`docs/alliance-duel.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Alliance Duel"
description: "How the client finds today's Alliance Duel (VS) entry, the activityid it must ask for, the live eventList fields, the score table behind each day's scoring list, the score push, and how goclient's duel-aware features read it."
---

The Alliance Duel ("VS") is a weekly alliance-versus-alliance event with one theme per server day. The client learns today's theme, scoring list, and chest thresholds from one detail read of activity `55000`. This page covers that read as the wire shows it, the tables that give the scoring list its meaning, and how `goclient`'s features use it. Facts confirmed against production on 2026-10-06 are marked **confirmed live**; everything else is static-analysis-only, from the 1.0.364 Lua and tables.

## Finding today's entry

### The init activity entry

The `init` push's `activity` map carries the duel as activity `55000` (type 14, `EnumActivity.AllianceCompete`). Confirmed live, the entry is:

```text
activity["55000"] = {
  id:           55000,           // the activity table row (type 14)
  activityid:   "70000",         // the heroactivity row: the id the detail read must send
  name:         "370026",        // locale key of today's theme name
  startTime, endTime:  <ms>,     // today's server-day window
  readyTime:    <ms>,
  matchGroupId: <int>,
  uuid:         <32 hex chars>   // equals today's eventList actId
}
```

It's the only entry in the live `activity` map, among the types `goclient` knows, that carries an `activityid` different from its `id` (confirmed live, 2026-10-06).

### The detail read must send `activityid`

`ActivityInfoData:ParseActivityData` sets `activityId` from the entry's `id`, then overrides it with `activityid` when one is present (`ActivityInfoData.lua:126-128, 160-161`). `AddOneActivity` sends that value for the duel, as a UtfString (`ActivityListDataManager.lua:158-163`):

```text
hero.event.info.get {activityId: "70000"}     // not "55000"
```

Confirmed live: asked for `"55000"`, the server answers with a bare `{success=true}` and no `eventList`, and no second message follows. The client would ignore that reply anyway: `ActivityEventInfoGetMessage` processes a reply only when it has no `success` key (`ActivityEventInfoGetMessage.lua:26`). Asked for `"70000"`, the reply carries the data directly.

### The reply

Top level, confirmed live: `activityId` (`"70000"`), `type` (`15`, the duel event type), `ranking`, `isFix`, and `eventList`. The client routes it by `type == 15` (`ActivityListDataManager.lua:1180-1186`).

Each `eventList` entry, field names as confirmed live:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `st`, `et` | The day window, unix ms. **The live entry has no `begintime`/`endtime`**, the pair `ActivityEventInfo:ParseData` reads first (`ActivityEventInfo.lua:69-74`); `st`/`et` are the fields `RefreshActivityTime` reads (`ActivityListDataManager.lua:1193-1198`). Read either pair, `begintime`/`endtime` first |
| `rt` | Ready time, ms |
| `t` | Event type, `15` |
| `eventId` | The theme: a `heroevent` row, `110000`-`110005` |
| `actId`, `actName`, `actDesc` | Today's event id (used by the chest claim) and locale keys |
| `score` | `\|`-joined `score` table ids: today's scoring list |
| `target` | `\|`-joined chest thresholds, ascending. Live: nine values, `40000\|150000\|540000\|660000\|1000000\|2300000\|2600000\|3600000\|7200000` |
| `value`, `reward`, `reward_science` | Per-chest valuation, per-chest reward lists, and the tech that unlocks each chest |
| `userScore` | `{score, rewardFlagList, newRewardFlagList, finishFlag, canRwdFlag, level, actId, hardMode, refreshTime, sendReward, uid}`: today's points and chest flags |
| `vsAllianceInfo[]` | One entry per side: `{allianceId, alName, abbr, icon, power, serverId, win, winScore, alScore, scoreHistory[{score, day}], mvpPlayer{uid, name, pic, picVer, monthCardEndTime}}` |
| `fightStartTime`, `fightEndTime`, `weekEndTime` | War-day and week boundaries, ms |
| `minDayScore`, `minWeekScore` | Victory-mail floors |
| `winReward`, `winWeekReward` | Daily and weekly win rewards |
| `isCrossFight`, `crossFight`, `canAttackCity` | War-day flags |
| `nextId`, `nextName` | Empty in the live reply |

Pick the entry with `t == 15` whose window contains now. Don't fall back to another entry: a stale entry's scoring list belongs to another day.

### The week

`TB:heroactivity#70000`, the type-15 row, maps the server weekday to a theme (static-analysis-only):

| Server weekday | `eventId` | Theme |
|---|---|---|
| Mon | 110000 | Radar Training |
| Tue | 110001 | Base Expansion |
| Wed | 110002 | Age of Science |
| Thu | 110003 | Train Heroes |
| Fri | 110004 | Total Mobilization |
| Sat | 110005 | Enemy Buster |
| Sun | none | Rest day: no entry, the detail read has no current entry |

The server day starts at 02:00 UTC, see [Identity, login & session](/auth#server-day-and-daily-reset). Confirmed live on Tuesday 2026-10-06: theme `110001`, with the window ending at 02:00 UTC.

## The scoring list

Each id in `score` is a row of the `score` table: `{id, type, value, points}`, where `type` is a `ScoreType`, `value` narrows it, and `points` is the base award per unit. The client gates its duel prompts by score type, not by theme (`AllianceCompeteDataManager.lua:631-654`). Its predicted award is `units × points × (1 + Σ effects)` (`GetAllyDuelScoreInfo.lua:39-43`).

Score types `goclient` uses (`ScoreType`, `EnumType.lua:15728-15744`, plus table types):

| Type | Meaning | `value` |
|---:|---|---|
| 4 | Train one unit | unit tier |
| 20 | Shop | |
| 23 | Building power up | |
| 42 | Recruit one hero | |
| 51 | One minute of speed-up | the queue sped up: `4` training, `6` research, `7` construction, `9` healing (`SpeedScoreValue`) |
| 82 | Complete one radar task | |
| 98 | Dispatch a UR trade truck | |
| 99 | Perform a UR secret task | |
| 119 | Use an item | `itemId\|count` |
| 120 | Recruit one survivor | |

Type 51 is keyed by the queue an item is used on, not by the item's own kind.

The 2026-10-06 (Base Expansion) entry listed eight ids, confirmed live:

| Id | Type / value | Base points |
|---|---|---:|
| 90201 | 51 / `7` (construction speed-up, per minute) | 50 |
| 90202 | 23 | 10 |
| 90203 | 98 / `5` | 100,000 |
| 90204 | 99 / `5` | 75,000 |
| 90000 | 20 | 30 |
| 100910 | 120 | 1,500 |
| 110301 | 119 / `801000\|1` | 1 |
| 110302 | 119 / `801001\|1` | 2,500 |

`goclient` embeds the whole table (1,475 rows, table version 39432) in `internal/game/duel_scores_gen.go`. The generator, `internal/game/genduelscores`, reads a decoded `score.json`, checks six known rows before writing, and refuses another table or shifted columns:

```bash
go generate ./internal/game    # with LASTWAR_TABLES and LASTWAR_TABLE_VERSION set
```

## The score push

`push.act.score.obtain` reports earned points for score events: Arms Race always, and the Alliance Duel when `type == 15` (`PushActScoreObtainMessage.lua:6-16`; static-analysis-only). The duel branch feeds `GetDuelScoreManager:PushScoreChangeByType`, which reads the added points and the alliance total. Nothing in the client waits for it.

`goclient` logs every one at Info as `activity score obtained`, with `afterCmd` set to the last request sent on the connection. A push that arrives after a run's last read isn't seen.

## Chest claims

A chest is claimed with the day's `actId` and the chest's threshold (static-analysis-only):

```text
accept.personal.reward {actId: UtfString, stage: Int (the target value), eventType: 15}
```

A chest is claimable when `userScore.score` has reached its target, its flag isn't in `newRewardFlagList`, and its index is within the number of chests the account's tech unlocks (3, 6, 9, or 12). Confirmed live: `newRewardFlagList` is a comma-joined list of claimed chest indexes, for example `1,2,3`.

## How goclient uses it

Every optional feature in `goclient` can declare the duel score types it earns (`Feature.Duel`, a list of `{Type, Value}`; an empty `Value` matches any). A feature with `Hold` set runs only on a day whose entry lists one of those types. With no current entry (Sunday, not in an alliance, the read failed) a held feature stays held. `-list-features` shows each feature's policy as `duel:hold`, `duel:always`, or `duel:-`.

- **`duelPolicy`** in the session config overrides a feature's default: `{"duelPolicy": {"radar-claims": "always"}}`. Valid values are `hold` and `always`.
- **`-run <feature>`** of a held feature is refused with the reason; **`-run-anyway`** runs it regardless. A spend feature still checks today's scoring list inside its run, so `-run-anyway` on a non-scoring day sends nothing.
- **Status line:** with any feature enabled, every run logs one `alliance duel` line: theme, score, next chest, and day end.

The duel-aware features are all off by default; see the README for the full list:

| Feature | Duel policy | What it sends |
|---|---|---|
| `radar-claims` | hold, type 82 | `receive.detect.event.reward` for finished radar tasks |
| `free-recruits` | always, types 42 / 120 | `useFree: 1` pulls only |
| `duel-speedups` | hold, type 51 / `4` `6` `7` `9` | owned speed-up items on running jobs, see [Speed-ups](#speed-ups) |
| `duel-recruit-tickets` | hold, types 42 / 120 | ticket pulls, only while a ticket is held |
| `duel-troop-training` | hold, types 4 / 51 `4` | `building.camp.training` on idle camps |
| `secret-tasks-start` | always, type 99 | `hero.dispatch.start` for UR tasks |
| `radar-execute` | always, type 82 | march-free radar task flows, see [Radar tasks](#radar-tasks) |

`duel-speedups-plan`, `secret-tasks-start-plan`, and `radar-inventory` are read-only previews.

### Speed-ups

The speed panel sends items in the items-only form (`UISpeedView.lua:1540-1586`):

```text
build.ccd.m.new     {bUUID: Long, isFixRuins: false, itemIDs: "tmpl;n|tmpl;n"}   // construction
queue.ccd.m.new     {qUUID: Long, itemIDs: "tmpl;n|..."}                          // research, hospital
building.camp.accel {uuid: Long, itemId: "tmpl;n|..."}                            // camp training
```

- **The diamond forms** are a `useGold` key (`BuildCcdMNewMessage.lua:12-16`, `QueueCcdMNewMessage.lua:10-12`, `BuildingCampAccelMessage.lua:9-11`) and, for `queue.ccd.m.new`, an empty `itemIDs`, which is the client's own instant finish (`ArmyManager.lua:199-203`). `golloesSpeedTime` spends a different free-time pool.
- **No `isGold` on the wire.** The UI passes `isGold` to `queue.ccd.m.new`, but the message class never puts it on the wire (`QueueCcdMNewMessage.lua:3-17`).
- **`goclient`'s guard.** `duel-speedups` refuses any key outside the three items-only sets above, an empty or malformed item string, and a count above the owned count from init `items`. It also stops for the rest of the process if a reply shows the diamond balance falling or lacks `itemCostArr` for the items sent.

Speed-up goods (`goods` table, static-analysis-only): `type2` is the menu, `para3` the seconds.

| Ids | `type2` | Seconds |
|---|---:|---|
| 200200-200207 | 1, universal | 60, 300, 900, 3,600, 10,800, 28,800, 86,400, 432,000 |
| 200210-200217 | 7, construction | same eight |
| 200220-200227 | 6, research | same eight |
| 200230-200235 | 3, training | first six |
| 200240-200245 | 4, healing | first six |

### Radar tasks

`radar-execute` runs the client's Quick Execute flows for the march-free task types `{6, 18, 26, 44}`, only while init `dataConfig` turns on `radar_quick_operation_switch` (`RadarFakeUIMarchManager.lua:105-111`):

```text
detect.event.batch.put.point.in.world {uuidList: "uuid|uuid"}       // state 3 → 0
start.pick.garbage {uuid} … ≥ 3 s … finish.sampling {uuid}          // types 6, 26; 44 adds finish.visitor
detect.event.help.start {uuid, eventType: 18} … detect.event.help.end {uuid, eventType: 18}
start.detect.event.talk {uuid} … end.detect.event.talk {uuid}       // type 14: finishes and claims at once
```

- **Never sent:** `reset.detect.event` (a diamond re-roll), any battle or march type, and any client-computed result.
- **Help stamina:** a Help Teammates task costs 10 stamina unless its `cost` is `1`.
- **Day gating:** the talk flow runs only on days whose entry lists type 82, because it claims as it finishes.

The client's bank model for reference: each refresh adds `N` tasks into free slots and then into stock, up to `detect_max_num`, so a refresh with a full bank loses `eventNum + N − max(show − slots, 0) − maxNum` tasks (`detect_level`; `UIDetectEventCtrl.lua:371-394`). `goclient` claims radar tasks only on days whose entry lists type 82 (`radar-claims`), and `radar-inventory` logs the bank figures.

## Open questions

- **When each duel action books its points.** Start, finish, or claim, per action type: radar tasks, UR secret tasks, power gains, and training. The client's own Claim All dialog points at the claim for radar tasks (en `detect_quick_reward_confirm_text`), and the `push.act.score.obtain` log is in place to settle each one live.
- **Are unclaimed chests mailed at the day's end?** A mail template exists; it isn't confirmed.
- **Does a finished radar task survive its `endTime`?** The live task list shows finished (state 1) tasks carrying an `endTime` like unstarted ones.
- **Is an empty or over-count `itemIDs` charged in diamonds?** `goclient` never sends either, so this stays a static reading.

See also [Live validation against production](/live-validation#alliance-duel-and-duel-spend-commands) for the reply shapes these features have round-tripped.

```

`docs/android-platform.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Android platform layer"
description: "Permissions, third-party SDK wiring, and the Java-native-C# bridge on Android, none of which gates the SFS2X/HTTP game protocol."
---

Everything outside the game protocol: permissions, third-party SDK wiring, and the Java↔native↔C# bridge. None of it duplicates or gates the SFS2X/HTTP game protocol; this layer is platform shell, cleanly separable from the client a Go reimplementation needs.

## Why the permissions you wouldn't expect

A war-strategy game asking for `CAMERA`/`RECORD_AUDIO`/calendar access looks suspicious until traced to real, named features:

| Permission | Actual use |
| --- | --- |
| `CAMERA` | Avatar/chat photo upload, plus Zendesk support-ticket attachments (when that support SDK is active) |
| `RECORD_AUDIO` | Tencent GME/TRTC voice chat rooms + short voice-message recording |
| `READ/WRITE_CALENDAR` | Genuine "remind me before this event" feature, writes to `CalendarContract` |

## Third-party SDK inventory

| Category | SDK |
| --- | --- |
| Analytics/attribution | AppsFlyer, Firebase (Analytics/Crashlytics/FCM), ThinkingData (China market) |
| Anti-fraud | ShuMei (数美), device fingerprint, heavily Obfuscator-LLVM hardened |
| Anti-cheat | Tencent ACE ("anogs"), root/inline-hook detection |
| Voice chat | Tencent GME/TRTC, own BoringSSL TLS stack, unrelated to game protocol |
| IAP | Google Play Billing **v8.3.0** (supports alt-billing programs) |
| Customer support | **Two full SDKs bundled**: Zendesk and AIHelp, switched server-side by a remote-config flag, not hardcoded |
| Ad mediation | **None found**: no AppLovin/ironSource/Unity Ads/AdMob anywhere. Monetization is IAP-only. |

<Warning>
**Cleartext HTTP is allowed, but the two cleartext endpoints are dead in 1.0.364.** `usesCleartextTraffic="true"` is set at the manifest level, and the network security config permits cleartext with system CAs only. The app still contains two FunPlus-owned plain-HTTP endpoints, but neither is called by this build (static-analysis-only):

- `analyse-aps.readygo.tech/{postback,clientevent}.php`, push-analytics beacons, lives in `RecordHttpUtil`, which has no callers, and the `PushRecordManager.RecordToHttp*` methods have empty bodies.
- `upload-img-aps.readygo.tech/get_apk_ver.php`, a side-loaded self-update check, runs only for the package `com.readygo.aps.gp`, not `com.fun.lastwar.gp`.

Neither gates gameplay; a Go client can ignore both. Earlier versions of this page said both were called.
</Warning>

## Remote kill switch

At startup, `libil2cpp.so` calls into the Java class `ConfigFetch`, which fetches a remote flag over a raw `SSLSocket` with a spoofed `okhttp/3.12.1` User-Agent (static-analysis-only; the call site is inferred from class, method, and base64 URL strings in the `.so`):

```text
GET https://storage.googleapis.com/remote-config-analytics/<base64(package name)>?t=<ms>
```

The integer body goes to the native `Java_com_common_ConfigFetch_setConfig`, which calls `exit(0)` when the value is `1` on a release build (`2` on a debug build), confirmed by arm64 disassembly. It's a vendor kill switch for the app process, not part of the game protocol, and a Go client never needs it. Whether the request even resolves is open: `Base64.DEFAULT` appends a newline to the encoded package name.

## The JNI split for anti-cheat is worth knowing

`libanogs.so` (Tencent ACE) has a full Java wrapper class (`com.gamesafe.ano.AnoSdk`) that turns out to be dead code. **C# calls into the native library directly via `[DllImport("anogs")]` P/Invoke**, bypassing Java entirely. Its detection/report data appears to travel over a local Unix pipe to Tencent's own backend, not the FunPlus game server's wire protocol.

```

`docs/auth.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Identity, login & session"
description: "How device identity, SFS2X zone login, the MD5 integrity fields, the access-token lifecycle, the post-login init sequence, and the separate chat channel authenticate a client against the game's servers."
---

The SFS2X username/password fields are vestigial; the password is always sent empty. Real authentication rides in ~50 fields on a custom SFSObject payload, most of them device fingerprints, three of them opaque MD5-based "integrity" tokens.

## Device ID

```text
deviceId = nativeCall("PM_getDeviceUDID")           // Android ID or GAID, or:
         ?? SystemInfo.deviceUniqueIdentifier + rand   // fallback, unstable across restarts
deviceId += CommonUtils.IsDebug() ? "_3d" : "_n3d"
airKey    = "lwDid_" + base64(utf8(deviceId))          // sent alongside deviceId everywhere
```

Persisted to `PlayerPrefs["DEVICE_ID"]`; on iOS additionally mirrored to the Keychain (survives uninstall). The `assets/deviceId.txt` file present in the install package contains a single byte, `"1"`; no code reads it anywhere; it does not appear to be the device id source. Unchanged in 1.0.364.

## SFS zone login

A stock SFS2X `LoginRequest` (`action=1`, system controller), but every call site passes an **empty password**. Real auth material is entirely inside the `parameters` SFSObject:

| Field | Value / derivation |
|---|---|
| `deviceId` / `airKey` | as above |
| `gameUid` | server-assigned account id (also used as the SFS username) |
| `serverId` | `zone` string minus its `"APS"` prefix |
| `at` | the HTTP-obtained access token, only if non-empty |
| `appVersion` / `versionCode` | the build identity. An access token is bound to the `packageName`/`platform`/`appVersion`/`versionCode` it was issued under (confirmed live). The 1.0.364 Android build is `1.0.364`/`1892`; the iOS app captured on 2026-10-04 still sent `1.0.344`/`786` |
| `SecurityCode` | `MD5(cmdBaseTime + "4d1c383ccbedf3d98320d6ea06d8dedc" + gameUid)`, hardcoded salt |
| `OneCode` | char-interleave of `MD5(rand32)` and `rand32` itself |
| `CoreV` | hash chain: `MD5(reverse(base64(rand32)))` then `MD5(that + rand32)`, interleaved |
| `packageSign` | despite the name, *not* a certificate check, just `SHA1(packageName)`, a constant public string, trivially reproducible without touching the APK's real signing certificate. The field that actually depends on the real signing cert is `psh`, below. |
| `psh` | `MD5(cmdBaseTime + hex(signing-cert DER bytes))`, the one field genuinely tied to the APK's real signing certificate; confirmed directly in the decompiled Android SDK source, `SdkManager.LW_PSH()`, which concatenates `cmdBaseTime` with each `PackageInfo.signatures[i].toCharsString()` and MD5s the result. Unchanged in 1.0.364, whose signing certificate is byte-identical to 1.0.351's. The iOS app's `psh` doesn't match this formula, see [Native binaries & security](/native-binaries) |
| `shumeiBoxId` | ShuMei anti-fraud device fingerprint — the ShuMei SDK's `smid`, assigned by the ShuMei backend in response to a `deviceprofile/v4` device-profile upload. **An empty string is a first-class, non-error client path**: the 1.0.364 C# sends `""` when the SDK isn't ready or `client_config` switch 25 is off. In the 2026-10-04 capture, a TLS call to a ShuMei endpoint preceded the game connection by 0.5 s, and the value had changed in both observed token rotations. The server doesn't require it: the same day, a captured iOS session reconnected into the established account with `shumeiBoxId` sent empty (confirmed live). The full flow is documented in [ShuMei device fingerprint](/shumei) |
| `dataConfigMd5` | not computed by the client: an echo of a server-issued value, omitted when the client has none, see [Live validation against production](/live-validation) |
| `resVersion` | built from check-version data, see [Startup, version-check & hot-update](/bootstrap#resversion) |
| `androidDid`, `IMEI`, `gaid`, `afuid`, `firebaseId`… | ~15 more device/ad identifiers, all static/spoofable strings |

All three integrity fields (`SecurityCode`/`OneCode`/`CoreV`) are ordinary client-side MD5 constructions with a hardcoded salt, fully reproducible in Go, no native dependency. [Native binaries & security](/native-binaries) found no evidence the server treats them as a hard gate versus a fingerprint for offline analysis, but a Go client should send them anyway (they cost nothing to compute). Checked against the 2026-10-04 capture, the `SecurityCode` and `OneCode`/`CoreV` formulas reproduce the real iOS app's values exactly.

## Token lifecycle

Everything in this section comes from the 1.0.364 C# (`AccountCredentialManager`, `AppStartupLoading`, `LoginState`, `LoginMessage`) and is static-analysis-only unless a line says otherwise. `goclient` implements little of it: it keeps no refresh token, so it can't refresh itself the way the real client does.

### Storage

| PlayerPrefs key | Holds | Written |
|---|---|---|
| `Login.access_token` / `Login.access_token_time` | `at` and the server-sent `at.time`: the moment of issue, in unix seconds (confirmed live) | after a successful GSL (Gate Server List) call, only when the new token is non-empty |
| `Login.refresh_token` / `Login.refresh_token_time` | `rt` and `rt.time`, also the moment of issue (confirmed live) | same as `at` |
| `Login.login_key` | one-shot account-resolution key | by Lua on account creation and role switch; cleared after every successful GSL call |
| `Setting.GAME_UID` | `gameUid`, also sent as the SFS2X `un` | overwritten from `init.user.uid` on every `init` |
| `SERVER_IP` / `SERVER_PORT` / `SERVER_ZONE` / `SERVER_CONNECTION_TYPE` | last game server | overwritten with the single winning gateway after each connect |

`at` and `rt` come only from `getserverlist.php` responses. No Lua code sets them.

### A GSL call on every cold start

`CheckResVersionState` clears the cached server IP, port, and connection type (keeping zone and `gameUid`), so `StartConnect` never finds a cached server and always runs `GetServerList`. The client then:

1. Picks the `serverList` entry matching the response's `lastLoggedServer`, falling back to `serverList[0]`. `goclient` first picks the entry carrying the session's `gameUid`, then falls back the same way.
2. Stores the new `at`/`rt` and clears `loginKey`.
3. Connects and logs in with the stored `at`.

### Choosing the GSL `opt`

```text
if loginKey != ""              -> opt=login   & loginKey=<loginKey>
else if gameuid == ""          -> opt=new
else:
    stale = attime > 0 && now_unix - attime >= 2592000     // 30 days
    if rt == ""                -> opt=fix
    else if at == "" || stale  -> opt=refresh & rt=<rt>
    else                       -> no opt field at all
```

So a returning client refreshes its token on its own once `at.time` is 30 days old, and right after an `E011` clears `at`. The form fields and their order are on [Gate-server RSA+AES handshake](/gate-server-crypto#request-fields). `goclient` sends `opt=login`, `opt=fix`, or `opt=new`, and sends `opt=refresh` only through the manual `-cs-rt` flag. Its game-server lookup sends no `opt` field (see [Looking up the game server](#looking-up-the-game-server)).

### GSL result codes

The client accepts a GSL response only when `code == 0` and `serverList` is non-empty.

| `code` | Client action |
|---|---|
| `0` | Success. An empty `serverList` still fails, as `E120` |
| `201` | Fails with `E116_201`, shows a "not available" dialog, then quits |
| `211` | Clears `at`, `rt`, and `loginKey`: the refresh token was rejected, so the account needs a full re-authentication |
| `212` | Clears the server info and `gameUid` as well: the account-to-device mapping is reset |
| `213` | Fails with `E213` (`ERROR_CHECK_SERVER_LIST_ENCRYPT`): an envelope or crypto error |
| any other non-zero | Fails with the generic `E116` |

`goclient` decodes `code` but doesn't branch on it.

### Login rejection codes

A rejected `Login` arrives as SFS2X `ec=28` with a reason string in `ep[0]` (see [Live validation against production](/live-validation)). `LoginState.OnLoginResponse` and the Lua `LoginErrorCode` table map them:

| `ep[0]` | Client's label | Client action |
|---|---|---|
| `E001`, `E002` | `ACCOUNT_NOT_EXIST` | Clears auth and server info, then reloads |
| `E005` | `ERROR_MAINTENANCE` | Maintenance dialog, no credential change. Live, the server also returned `E005` for a token presented under the wrong platform identity, and for an Android `Login` into an established account whose `ta` was `{}` (see [A device of its own](#a-device-of-its-own)) |
| `E010` | Account deletion pending | Dialog |
| `E011` | `ERROR_LOGIN_ACCESS_TOKEN` | Clears **only `at`** and keeps `rt`. Shows a dialog and reloads; the reload runs GSL `opt=refresh`, because `at` is now empty. Confirmed live as the whole failure signature of a rotated token |
| `E012` | Korean real-name authentication | Dialog |
| `E013`, `E015`, `E016` | Season register ban, season start, season stop or maintenance | `E013` clears all user data |
| `E014` | `ERROR_OLD_UID_USE_NEW_RT` | Clears `gameUid`, `at`, `rt`, and `loginKey`, then reloads |
| `4` (with `;` details) | Ban | UI only |
| `43`, `44` | IP blacklist, device blacklist | No C# case; falls through to the generic `E117` |
| `45`-`48` | Account deletion: applied, deleted, refused, confirmed | UI only |
| `49` (with `;` details) | `TRAFFIC_CONTROL_BANNED_USER` | UI only |
| `55`-`58` | Role deletion: applied, deleted, refused, confirmed. New in 1.0.364 | UI only |

None of the numeric codes is a credential problem, and none is worth retrying. The `E1xx` codes (`E101`-`E117`) are client-local loading and network codes; the server never sends them. `goclient` reports `E011` as `session.ErrTokenRejected` and every other rejection as `ErrAuthRejected`; both exit with code `2`.

The real client's recovery from `E011` needs the refresh token: clear `at`, run GSL `opt=refresh` with `rt`, store the new pair, and log in again. `goclient` doesn't persist `rt` from GSL responses, so its recovery is a fresh capture, see [Recovering from a rotated token](/capturing-and-decoding-traffic#recovering-from-a-rotated-token).

### Following a `serverInfo` redirect

When the `Login` response carries `serverInfo`, the real client saves the new ip, port, zone, and uid, clears its network config, runs the normal `Login`-response handler, and reconnects. The cached IP is now set, so the reconnect goes **straight to `ConnectGame`: no GSL call, and the same `at`**. `serverInfo.uid` replaces `gameUid`. `goclient` follows redirects too (confirmed live) and now does the same as the real client: it redials with the same `at` and adopts `serverInfo.zone` and `serverInfo.uid`. Earlier versions called GSL `opt=fix` before redialing. Under the iOS identity that call could only swap a working token for an Android-bound one, because that GSL request claimed `platform=Android`. The `-cs-rt` refresh and the guest login still send `platform=Android`; only the game-server lookup below sends `platform=iOS` for an iOS session.

### Looking up the game server

A session config's `ip` and `port` are optional. The game server's address comes from GSL `getserverlist.php`, as it does for the real client on every cold start, so you don't have to copy it from a capture. `goclient`'s session-config reconnect asks GSL in two cases:

- **No address given:** it looks the role's server up before dialing.
- **The given address doesn't answer:** every gateway refuses the connection, or the `Login` gets no reply. It looks the server up once and, if GSL names a different address, retries there. A rejected `Login`, such as `E011`, never triggers a lookup.

A working address costs no GSL call. Either way, `goclient` saves the address it connected to back into the session config.

The lookup sends no `opt` field, the request the real app makes on a cold start while it holds a fresh `at` and an `rt`. It sends the session's device, `zone` and `gameUid`, and `platform=iOS` for a session the iOS app issued. It takes only the address from the reply, picking the entry that carries the session's `gameUid` and refusing an entry that names another role. It keeps the session's `at` and logs whether the reply carried a different one.

Confirmed live on 2026-10-10 against a session captured from the iOS app, with the Android check-version reply's gate host and RSA key:

- **`opt=fix`**, which the table above gives a client with no `rt`, was rejected with code `212`. It returned no server list and no tokens, and the session's `at` kept working.
- **No `opt`** returned code `0` and one entry: `State#783`, zone `APS783`, port `10783`, the three `lastwar-game-tcp-*` gateway hostnames, and the session's `gameUid`. It returned no `at` or `rt`.
- **With no address in the session config**, `goclient` looked the server up, logged in, and saved the gateway list and port.
- **With the pre-August address** (the captured gateway IPs on port `17783`), the first gateway timed out and the second reset the connection. `goclient` looked the server up once, retried at the hostnames on `10783`, logged in, and saved the new address.

### A device of its own

A Go client that copies the real app's tokens shares them with the app, so either side's refresh may invalidate the other's. The real client's role-switch flow shows how a device gets a pair of its own: email verification, then `loginKey`, then GSL `opt=login`. `goclient` ran that flow on 2026-10-04 with a fresh, Go-generated device (confirmed live):

1. The existing `-email` and `-code-pipe` flow bound the new device to the real account. `push.account.login.new` returned the account's `gameUid` and a `loginKey`. The `LASTWAR_STATE_DIR` environment variable kept that device's state files apart from the existing ones.
2. The experimental `-own-device-session <path>` flag traded the `loginKey` for the device's own `at`/`rt` pair through GSL `opt=login`. The response named `lastLoggedServer` 783 and a one-entry `serverList` for `APS783`, whose `ip` held three gateway hostnames on port 10783 (see [SFS2X wire protocol](/wire-protocol#gateway-race-and-the-pre-login-probe)). `at.time` and `rt.time` both equaled the moment of issue. The flag writes these into a session config, including `refreshToken`, `accessTokenTime`, and `refreshTokenTime`, which later runs refresh with (see [Refreshing the access token](#refreshing-the-access-token)).
3. A base-zone `Login` with that token and `goclient`'s Android identity (1.0.364/1892, `un` = `gameUid`, `shumeiBoxId` empty) was rejected with `ec=28`, `ep=[E005]`.
4. On 2026-10-13 the same token, nine days old, logged in once the `Login` carried a filled Android `ta` analytics blob (confirmed live). The `init` push loaded 160 buildings. Minutes later the account's email got a "New Device Alert for Last War ID" naming an Android device in the United States, with a **Sign Out of This Device** button. So the account keeps a device list, and the server counts the Go client's device as one of them.

The gate was `ta`. `goclient` filled `ta` only for iOS and sent `{}` on Android. C485 found from real Android captures that an Android `Login` with `{}` gets `E005` and one with the platform markers filled in doesn't ([discussion #22](https://github.com/ljagiello/lastwar-client/discussions/22)). On 2026-10-13 one build sent the same token twice, changing only `ta`:

| Android `ta` | Result |
|---|---|
| `{}` | `ec=28`, `ep=[E005]` |
| `#os` = `Android`, `#bundle_id` = `com.fun.lastwar.gp`, `lw_platform` = `market_global`, the build in `#app_version`/`lw_version`/`lw_buildcode`, `lw_zone` = `APS783` | `Login` accepted, `init` arrived |

The `deviceId`, account, and server were the same in both runs, so the 2026-10-04 suspects don't block this `Login`: the Go-generated `deviceId`'s shape, the Android identity itself, and, nine days after binding, trust in the device. `ta`'s `lw_device_id`, `lw_shumei_id`, and `lw_airKey` stayed blank, as they are for iOS. A missing `shumeiBoxId` isn't the cause either, since the accepted `Login` sent none.

What the test settles and what it doesn't:

- **Established accounts only.** A guest `Login` was accepted with `{}` for months, and on 2026-10-13 a fresh guest was accepted with the filled blob too (confirmed live). The `-email` binding ran with it the same night (see [Setting up a device of its own in one run](#setting-up-a-device-of-its-own-in-one-run)); the `loginKey` fast path (`opt=login`, `un` empty) hasn't.
- **Which keys matter is open.** Both A/B tests, C485's and this one, compared `{}` with the whole blob. The platform markers (`#os`, `#bundle_id`, `lw_platform`) are the likely gate, but the build and zone keys changed with them.

### Setting up a device of its own in one run

`-email` together with `-own-device-session` binds a fresh device and writes its session config in one run:

```bash
mkfifo /tmp/lw_code_pipe
LASTWAR_STATE_DIR=~/.lastwar_own_device ./lastwar-client -email you@example.com \
  -code-pipe /tmp/lw_code_pipe -own-device-session ~/own_device_session.json &
echo 123456 > /tmp/lw_code_pipe   # the code from the email
LASTWAR_STATE_DIR=~/.lastwar_own_device ./lastwar-client -config ~/own_device_session.json -collect
```

The run logs in as a guest, verifies the email, and logs the account's roles: each role's server, zone, `gameUid`, level, and power. Then it trades the account's `loginKey` for the device's own `at`/`rt` through GSL `opt=login` and writes the session config. A device that already holds a `loginKey` skips the email and trades it.

`-server` picks the role to bind, by its server number (`783`) or zone (`APS783`), from the roles the run logs; a value that names no server number is refused before the code is requested. Without it, the role `push.account.login.new` names at its top level is bound. A server the account has no role on, or two roles on one server, fails after verification without saving the binding. By then the code is spent, so bind again from a fresh `LASTWAR_STATE_DIR` with a server from the logged list. If GSL's `opt=login` reply doesn't list the picked role, the trade fails rather than writing another role's server into the config.

Binding a role other than the top-level one is static analysis only: the real account has one role, so it was never tried live. The 1.0.364 role picker (`UIRoleLoginView.OnClickLogin`) takes the picked entry's `loginKey` and `gameUid`. The live entry carried no `loginKey`, so `goclient` uses an entry's own `loginKey` when it has one and the account's otherwise.

Confirmed live on 2026-10-13: one run bound a fresh device to the real account's role on 783 and wrote its config, and a `Login` with that config loaded 160 buildings. What the same night showed:

- **`accountArr` carries no `loginKey`.** The `loginKey` is the account's, at the push's top level. Each `accountArr` entry is a role: the server's `id`, `zone`, `name`, `ip`, and `port`, the role's `gameUid`, `gameUserName`, `gameUserLevel`, and `power`, and also the device `uuid` the role was created on and the server's internal database and cache hosts. `goclient` logs only the server and role fields.
- **A quick second code request sent no email.** A second `account.login.send.verify.code` about two minutes after the first was acknowledged, but no email came. Twelve minutes later one did. A code that already completed a binding was refused with `errorCode=208193`.
- **A failed bind leaves a guest behind.** After a bind that failed at the code, the same device's next guest `Login`, with the access token GSL `opt=new` returned for it, got `ec=28`, `ep=[E011]`. Bind again from a fresh `LASTWAR_STATE_DIR`; the run warns when the device already logged in as a guest.
- **Two own devices keep working tokens.** After a second device was bound and logged in, the first device's config still logged in. Each `Login` still takes the role's one live connection, so they don't play at the same time.

### Refreshing the access token

A session config with a `refreshToken`, such as one `-own-device-session` writes, renews its own access token the way the real client does (`csharp-native` §2.3):

- **Before the `Login`**, when the config has no `accessToken`, or its `accessTokenTime` is 30 days old (`gsl.ChooseOpt`), `goclient` sends GSL `opt=refresh` with the refresh token.
- **After an `E011`**, it refreshes once and logs in again. A token rejected again right after a refresh exits 2 with a message to bind the device again. A refresh that fails for another reason, such as the network or another GSL code, exits 1, and the next run tries again.
- **Every refresh is saved at once.** The new `at`, `rt`, and their times go into the session config before the `Login` uses them, so a rotated `rt` survives a `Login` that fails. A GSL code 211 or 212 means the device's credentials are gone and exits 2, except before the `Login` while an old access token is still on hand: then the run logs an error saying to bind the device again and carries on with the old token for as long as it works.

The refresh sends the session's device, `zone`, and `gameUid`, and `platform=iOS` under `iosMode`. A config captured from the real app has no refresh token, so its `E011` still needs a fresh capture (see [Recovering from a rotated token](/capturing-and-decoding-traffic#recovering-from-a-rotated-token)).

Confirmed live on 2026-10-13 with the own device's eight-day-old pair:

- **`E011`, then refresh:** a config whose `accessToken` the server never issued got `E011`. The refresh succeeded, and the second `Login` loaded 160 buildings.
- **Stale `at.time`:** with `accessTokenTime` set 31 days back, the refresh ran before the `Login`, which was accepted.
- **No access token:** a config holding only `refreshToken` refreshed and logged in.
- **What `opt=refresh` returned:** each time, the device's current `at` with its original `at.time`, and no `rt`. Eight days after issue, a refresh doesn't rotate either token.

### Open questions

These need live observation; [Findings & further work](/findings) tracks them.

- Does `opt=refresh` rotate `at` or `rt` once `at` is 30 days old? Eight days after issue it returned the current `at` and no `rt` (2026-10-13). The client stores whatever arrives non-empty.
- Does a device of its own leave the real app's tokens valid? Two own devices kept working tokens side by side (2026-10-13), but the real app's token wasn't checked against them.
- Does the server check `platform`, `uuid`, or `airKey` on `opt=refresh`? The client always sends the values the token was issued under.

## Post-login sequence

In the 2026-10-04 capture of the real iOS app, the server pushed one bare `init` (about 287 KB, 247 top-level keys) about 200 ms after `Login`. No `init.before`, `init.after`, or `push.init.build` arrived. A Go client doesn't send `init` itself; it just waits for it, see [Live validation against production](/live-validation#the-real-post-login-bootstrap-bare-init-not-push-init-build).

Around and after `init`, the real client sends, in order (observed in the capture, with the C# and Lua sources noted):

1. `change.user.parseid` and `check.device.change {_id}`, both from C#. The server answered `check.device.change` with `r:false`; the C# reads the result and ignores it.
2. About 45 requests from Lua's `RequestOtherLoginMsg`, nearly all reads: VIP, news, shop, alliance, world, and season info. The capture holds about 224 extension requests in the first 5 s.
3. `login.ext {info, add}`. `info` is a JSON device description: device name and model, OS version, network type, GPU, and CPU. When `init` carries `add {a, b, data, enc}`, the C# decrypts `data` with a hardcoded AES key, **executes it as Lua**, and returns the result as `add`: a server-pushed, executable integrity challenge. It's documented here as a protocol fact only; reproducing it is out of scope. In the capture, `init` carried `add` and the server answered `login.ext` with `{success:true}`.

4. Nine `mail.delete.batch {type: "auto", uids}` calls about 4.7 s in. The real client auto-deletes mail older than 30 days once a day, see [Alliance, chat & mail](/alliance-chat-mail).

The server also pushes `push.shumei.id {shumeiId}` about 0.5 s after `Login` (observed live). The client caches that value and reports it as `ta.lw_shumei_id` in its next `Login`.

`login.init` is an active pull that the real client never sent in the capture. The C# sends `dataConfigMd5` with it only when non-empty.

As far as the 1.0.364 Lua shows, none of these requests is a prerequisite for server-side state: production, idle rewards, visitors, and mail are all server-time-based, and daily VIP state arrives in `init` (static-analysis-only).

### `init` fields worth reading

| Field | Contents |
|---|---|
| `user` | 59 keys, including `uid`, `serverId`, and `deviceBindTimes`. `gold`, `gold1`, and `paidGold` are the total, free, and paid diamond balances (static-analysis-only). Also holds the account's **email address**: never log `user` unredacted |
| `building_new[]` | `uuid`, `bId`, `lv`, `pId`, and the production timers `prodST`, `prodT`, `prodET`, `pEndT`, `prodStatus`, see [City & building](/city-building#which-buildings-are-production-lines) |
| `visitor` | `{addNum, maxNum, list[]}`. Each entry is `{uid, eventId, startTime, visitorId, type, extendInfo, ...}`. Per the Lua, a visitor whose `startTime` (ms) is still in the future can't be greeted yet. `type` isn't the visitor's behaviour, see [Visitor type numbering](#visitor-type-numbering) |
| `vip.vipInfo` | `level`, `loginDays`, `score`, `loginScoreState`, `everyDayReward`, `endTime`, `privilegeReward` |
| `tomorrow` | Unix time of the next server-day boundary; every `*_times_expire` field uses the same instant. The `Login` response's `real_timezone_offset` (`-7200` on 2026-10-04) gives the server day's offset, see [Server day and daily reset](#server-day-and-daily-reset) |
| `mixedInfo` | `todayLoginTimes` (counts every login, including each `goclient` run), `scoreSwitch`, `materialBackup`, `popRate` |
| `freeRewardArr`, `todayFreeStamina`, `lastClaimFreeStaminaTime` | daily freebie and stamina state |
| `queue_new[]`, `collect_reward[]` | build and research queue timers; pending rewards with expiry. Field meanings are on [City & building](/city-building#building-and-queue-fields-in-init) |
| `allianceNewMail` | The number of unclaimed alliance gifts, which drives the client's gift red dot (static-analysis-only) |
| `dataConfig` | The live override of the `item` table's DataConfig defaults (`k1` to `k30`), replaced wholesale on every `init`, see [Game data tables](/data-tables) |
| `chatToken` | auth for the separate chat WebSocket, below |
| `add` | `{a, b, data, enc}`, the integrity-challenge input described above |

No gateway list, session hint, or token expiry appears anywhere in `init`.

### Server day and daily reset

The server day starts at 00:00 server time, which is UTC plus `real_timezone_offset`. With the live offset of `-7200` s, that's **02:00 UTC** every day, and `init.tomorrow` is 02:00 UTC of the next day (observed in the 2026-10-04 capture). The rest of this section is from the 1.0.364 Lua and C#, static-analysis-only:

- Day zero is `now - (now + real_timezone_offset * 1000) mod 86,400,000`, all in ms (`UITimeManager:GetTodayZero`). Weeks start on Monday at the same boundary: Monday 02:00 UTC, live.
- All server-day math uses UTC plus a fixed offset, so daylight saving time never moves the boundary.
- There's no "new day" push. The client fires `OnUnDelayPassDay` exactly at the boundary and `OnPassDay` 5 to 15 s later, with random jitter, when 61 DataCenter managers re-fetch their daily state. `OnPassWeek` fires 4 s after Monday's boundary.
- "Already claimed today" checks compare timestamps with `IsSameDayForServer`, not with 24-hour timers.
- The C# always sets its next reset from `init.tomorrow`, but applies `real_timezone_offset` only when `init` carries the key. The Lua falls back to `0` (UTC) when the key is absent, which would put its boundary at 00:00 UTC while `tomorrow` stays at 02:00 UTC. The 2026-10-04 capture shows the key in the `Login` response; whether `init` carries it too hasn't been checked. Anchoring on `tomorrow` (day zero = `tomorrow - 86400` s) works either way.

### Visitor type numbering

Two different numberings are both called "visitor type" (static-analysis-only):

| Field | Numbering |
|---|---|
| `init.visitor.list[].type` | The **queue type**, from `Scene/CityVisitor/Const.lua`: `0` GEN_BY_TIME, `1` CYCLE_REWARD, `2` STAGE, `4` WORKER_LOTTERY, `5` DOMINATOR, `6` AllianceCongratulation, `8` SystemGift, `11` ActivityVisitor, `12` AllianceInvite, `18` S0_ALLIANCE_BOSS, `19` SURVIVOR_PACK_GiFT, `20` ProtectCoverVisitor |
| `lw_base_visitor_event[eventId].type` | The **behaviour type**, the global `VisitorType` in `Global/EnumType.lua`: `1` MERCHANT, `2` GIFT, `3` RECRUITMENT, `4` BATTLE, `5` WORKER_LOTTERY, `6` NOTIFY, `7` OPEN_PANEL, `8` ALLIANCE_INVITE_MOVE_CITY, `9` DOMINATOR, `10` SeasonDayGift, `11` VisitorActivity, `12` ALLIANCE_INVITE, `13` DOMINATOR_COCKATRICE, `14` AllianceCongratulation, `15` AD_REMINDER, `16` SKY_BATTLE, `17` PLANE_FEATURE, `18`-`20` S0_ALLIANCE_BOSS, SURVIVOR_PACK_GiFT, ProtectCoverVisitor, `30` SystemGift |

What `visitor.operate {uid, operate}` does depends on the behaviour type, so look it up through the entry's `eventId`, not its `type`. For a MERCHANT (events 1001 and 1002), `operate: 1` **buys** the offered item with resources and `operate: 0` declines. A SystemGift visitor opens a gift-pack window first. Visitors with event ids 6001, 8001, 12001, and the S0-boss and ProtectCover visitors have client-made uids (`eventId + 100000000`) and never reach the server. Across 326 accepts on the real account over three months, every visitor's behaviour type was 2, 3, or 10 (confirmed live).

## Guest identity is sufficient

No OAuth is required to play: `account.login.new` with `type=1` and only `deviceId`/`airKey`/`pf` is the full "no external provider" path. Social binding (Google Sign-In `type=2`, Apple Game Center `type=4`, Play Games `type=5`) requires obtaining a provider token yourself, out of scope for a headless client, and optional. Per the 1.0.364 Lua, `account.login.new` sends `pf` as `"AppStore"` on iOS and `"market_global"` on Android; `goclient` always sends `market_global`.

### New-device account selection

With `client_config` switch 21 on and no stored `gameUid`, the 1.0.364 C# first connects to the `loginServer {ip, port, ws_ip, ws_port}` that the GSL response names, not to a game zone. The server's `login.push.shumei.exception.level` push then decides whether the account picker offers **New game** (static-analysis-only). That push is an anti-fraud surface, recorded here only as a protocol fact.

## A second, optional channel: chat

Real-time chat text runs over a **separate WebSocket** (JSON frames, not SFSObject), authenticated with the `chatToken` from the `init` push. Server discovery is its own HTTP bootstrap, signed with an MD5 formula keyed on a fixed app id `100017`: `/server/links` on the `lastwar-chat-*` hosts, or `chat_server_links.php` behind a DataConfig switch (see [Alliance, chat & mail](/alliance-chat-mail#chat-websocket-transport)). Every outbound message is signed: `MD5(uid + json(sortedParams) + sendTime + connectionSign)`. This channel is optional, skip it entirely if the Go client doesn't need real-time chat; "share to chat" and moderation commands still work over the plain SFS socket regardless (see [Alliance, chat & mail](/alliance-chat-mail)).

```

`docs/bootstrap.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Startup, version-check & hot-update"
description: "The 18-state cold-start machine and the three independently-versioned hot-update payloads it downloads and patches."
---

Cold start walks an 18-state machine from splash screen to a live game connection. Four independently-versioned payloads, asset bundles, the C# hot-update assemblies, the Lua bundle, and the data tables, are checked and patched separately, from a single version-check HTTP response.

## State machine (cold start, first launch)

| # | State | Does |
|---|-------|------|
| 1 | `Logo` | Splash screen |
| 2 | `Permission` | OS permission + jailbreak checks |
| 3 | `CheckResVersion` | **Version check**: races N hosts in parallel, first success wins |
| 4–5 | `DownloadManifest` / `DownloadUpdate` | Downloads/patches asset bundles, table data, and the Lua bundle |
| 6 | `LoadDataTable` | Loads config tables + localization into memory |
| 7 | `GetServerList` | **GSL request**: RSA+AES hybrid handshake ([Gate-server RSA+AES handshake](/gate-server-crypto)), on every cold start in 1.0.364 |
| 9 | `ConnectGame` | Races every gateway in the zone's list and keeps the first to answer (see [SFS2X wire protocol](/wire-protocol#gateway-race-and-the-pre-login-probe)) |
| 10 | `Login` | SFS2X `Login` request (see [Identity, login & session](/auth)) |
| 12 | `LoadScene` → `EnterGame` | Loads the actual game scene |

In 1.0.364, `CheckResVersion` clears the cached server IP, port, and connection type on every cold start, so `StartConnect` never finds a cached server and the GSL (Gate Server List) call always runs (static-analysis-only). The cached `ip/port/zone` short-cut from state 6 to state 9 still exists, but only a mid-session reconnect, such as following a `serverInfo` redirect, takes it. See [Identity, login & session](/auth#token-lifecycle) for what the GSL call does with the stored tokens.

## Check-version endpoint

```text
GET {host}/gameservice/getlsu3dversion.php
?packageName=com.fun.lastwar.gp&platform=...&appVersion=...
&gm=0&server=<cached zone>&uid=&deviceId=&table_env=table_online&buildId=<versionCode>
&returnJson=1&unityVersion=440
```

In 1.0.364, `table_env` is `table_online` and `server` carries the cached zone (static-analysis-only). `goclient` now sends the same: `table_env=table_online`, and the session zone in `server` on the cross-server path. Earlier versions sent both empty, and the server answered anyway (confirmed live). The empty `table_env` had one visible cost: the server returns `table_version` and `locale` only when the request carries `table_env=table_online`. Four anonymous check-version GETs on 2026-10-05, Android 1.0.364 and iOS 1.0.344 each with and without `table_online`, showed both fields (plus an empty `x_table_version`) only in the `table_online` variants, with every other field identical (confirmed live).

Host list (requests go out to every host in parallel and the first success wins; on total failure the client retries the same list once). About 5% of devices are A/B-bucketed to the `ea-` hosts by `GrayUtils.GetPercentageFromMd5`: `MD5(deviceId)` read as a little-endian uint64, `mod 100 + 1 <= 5`.

```text
https://lastwar-serverlist-cf.lastwarapp.net
https://lastwar-serverlist-us-aws-ali.lastwargame.com
https://lastwar-serverlist-us-gcp-ali.lastwargame.com

# ea- bucket
https://lastwar-serverlist-ea-us-aws.lastwargame.com
https://lastwar-serverlist-ea-us-gcp.lastwargame.com
```

`goclient` tries the three online hosts one after another, not in parallel.

Whichever host answers becomes the base URL for every subsequent call in this bootstrap (`getserverlist.php`, `getnotice.php`, `probe.php`); there is no separate "gate server" discovery step.

A response counts as valid when it has a non-empty `code` (which the client treats as an error), or when `updateType` is in `0`..`3` and `hotUpdateMsg` is non-empty. The 1.0.364 parser (`CheckResVersionState`) reads these fields:

| Response field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `code` | Error: the client throws and falls back to the versions packaged in the app |
| `resMsg` | Base64 DER RSA public key (no PEM armor), feeds the GSL crypto, see [Gate-server RSA+AES handshake](/gate-server-crypto). **Not hardcoded**, delivered fresh every check. |
| `updateType` | See the table below |
| `downloadurl` | Store link shown with a forced update |
| `hotUpdateMsg` | `;`-separated `name,version,size,crc32`, asset-bundle manifest versions (`GameRes`, `DataTable`, `Lua`, `Download`, `PackageRes`, `DllRes`). `size` and `crc32` describe the manifest file itself: the APK's `gameres.version` is `2342,18537644,856103597`, where 18,537,644 is the manifest's byte size, and the client writes the three fields verbatim into `<name>.version` (`CheckResVersionState.SaveManifestVersion`; static-analysis-only) |
| `lwfile2` | The Lua bundle: `version\|bzSize\|bzCrc[\|rawSize\|rawCrc];oldVer\|patchSize\|patchCrc;...`. A patch downloads only when the local version equals one of the `oldVer` entries |
| `table_version` | `version,size,md5[,crc][;patch chain]` for the game-data table archive. Returned only when the request carries `table_env=table_online` (confirmed live), see [Game data tables](/data-tables) |
| `locale` | `version,lang1,lang2,...`. Returned only with `table_env=table_online` (confirmed live) |
| `client_config` | Server-pushed feature flags: `\|`-separated `"0"`/`"1"` values indexed by switch id (`ClientSwitch.IsOn(N)` gates throughout the client). See [SFS2X wire protocol](/wire-protocol#server-controlled-transport-switches) for the ones that change the wire |
| `checkok` | Present only in review mode; the client then skips the table and locale updates |
| `warmup` | Opaque asset pre-download list; not protocol-relevant |
| `firstLaunchForceUpdateMsg` | Read only in a first-launch skip-update experiment; not protocol-relevant |

That's every field the parser handles. A live response carries fewer: the iOS check-version response for 1.0.344 (786), fetched on 2026-10-04, held only `client_config`, `downloadurl`, `firstLaunchForceUpdateMsg`, `hotUpdateMsg`, `lwfile2`, `resMsg`, `updateType`, and `warmup`. With `table_env=table_online`, the 2026-10-05 responses also carried `table_version`, `locale`, and an empty `x_table_version` (confirmed live).

`updateType` meanings (1.0.364 C#):

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | Proceed to download and hot-update |
| `1` | Optional store-update dialog: update or continue |
| `2` | Forced update, blocking. The server no longer accepts this build |
| `3` | Falls into the `default` branch, so it behaves exactly like `0`. The `Login` response handler also rewrites `3` to `0` |

The `Login` response can carry `updateType` too; with `2`, the client enters its app-update state instead of waiting for `init`. On 2026-10-04 the iOS 1.0.344 app got `updateType=3` from both check-version and `Login`, with the `Login` response naming `new_version` `1.0.350` (observed live). `goclient` now logs a warning when check-version returns `updateType=2`, since `Login`s claiming that build are likely to start failing too.

## resVersion

`Login`'s `resVersion` is `GetResVersion()` in the 1.0.364 C# (static-analysis-only):

```text
{GameRes}.{DllRes}_{lwfile2 version}F_{table_version}.{locale}
```

The `{GameRes}.{DllRes}_{lwfile2 version}F` prefix comes from the versions check-version installs: the `GameRes` and `DllRes` manifest versions from `hotUpdateMsg`, and the first `|` field of `lwfile2`. The real iOS app sent `2159.1505_821F_39516.23570` on 2026-10-04, and that day's check-version response returned `GameRes` 2159, `DllRes` 1505, and `lwfile2` version 821, matching the prefix.

The `{table}.{locale}` tail is **local state**, not a field copied from the response (static-analysis-only):

- `{table}` is `CURRENT_TABLE_VERSION`: the APK's built-in `table/version` until a newer table archive has been downloaded, then the highest downloaded version.
- `{locale}` is `LOCALE_VERSION`: the APK's built-in `locale/version` until a downloaded `locale/<ver>/` exists, then the highest such version.

After a successful update, those equal check-version's `table_version` and `locale`, which the server returns only for `table_env=table_online` (confirmed live). On 2026-10-05 a `table_online` request returned table version 39516 and locale 23570, exactly the iOS app's tail. Every part of the 1.0.364 APK's own baseline is in the APK: `2342.1501_825F_39432.23557` (`gameres.version`, `dllres.version`, `LWScripts.txt`, `table/version`, `locale/version`). `goclient` sends `"0"`, which the server has accepted for months.

## Hot-update transport & patch format

Four independently-versioned payloads, compared via the fields above and patched separately:

- **Asset bundles**: UnityFS bundles in the XAssetPro container, tracked by the `gameres` manifest (see [The XAssetPro asset container](#the-xassetpro-asset-container) below).
- **C# assemblies**: the APK ships 118 loose, XOR'd `.mdl` files in `assets/Assemblies/`, not bundles, plus `noUpdateAssemblies.json` = `[{"name":"SmartFox2X"}]`, which pins the SFS2X library to the APK copy. The `dllres` manifest (v1501 in the APK) lists 117 remote-only `<asm>.encrypt.bytes` bundles plus its own copy of that JSON; `mscorlib` has no entry, so it can't be hot-updated. Updated assemblies are written to `persistentDataPath/Assemblies/<asm>.mdl`, which FM_Mono searches before the APK (static-analysis-only).
- **Lua bundle**: one flat `LWLF` file, not wrapped in an AssetBundle at all.
- **Data tables**: the plain-ZIP `table_*.data` archive.

Downloaded patches/replacements may be wrapped in a lightweight on-disk XOR obfuscation (not real confidentiality, key material is hardcoded client-side) built on a **reduced-round ChaCha** stream cipher: 8 rounds (4 double-rounds) instead of standard ChaCha20, IETF layout, detected by a short (3–6 byte) magic-prefix swap:

| Plain magic | Wrapped magic | Content | Keystream starts at |
|---|---|---|---|
| `50 4B 03 04` (`PK··`) | `CHAC` | table `.data` ZIP | byte 4 |
| `42 5A 68` (`BZh`) | `PRB` | bzip2 (Lua bundle package) | byte 4 |
| `42 53 44 49 46 46` (`BSDIFF`) | `PURBDP` | bsdiff patch | byte 8, so bytes 6-7 stay plaintext |

The offsets come from the 1.0.364 `EncryptUtils` in `BaseUtils` (static-analysis-only).

Key/nonce are derived once from hardcoded dummy constants via two self-referential ChaCha8 passes (reproduced independently in Python and confirmed reproducible):

```text
_key   = 83aa6a90bdfb210e4742405500db2c0c80b30776f6441df7cd1504f830ad1f2b
_nonce = 2122232425262728292a2b2c
```

## The XAssetPro asset container

The `gameres` asset bundles aren't plain Unity AssetBundles on disk. XAssetPro (`VEngine`, API 6.1.5) packs them, and the APK's install-time asset pack holds one container. Except for the dated HEAD requests, everything in this section is static-analysis-only, checked against the shipped files:

- `assets/AssetBundles/BundleFragment0.bytes` (539 MB) is 8,059 UnityFS bundles laid end to end, with no gaps or padding. Their headers have the engine version stripped (`5.x.x` / `0.0.0`; the real engine is 2019.4.41f1), and their blocks are LZ4HC.
- `BundleOffsetTable.bytes` and `AliasOffsetTable.bytes` map a bundle's name, or its alias, to `(fragment index << 32) | offset`. Both hold the same 8,059 offsets. The client opens a bundle with `AssetBundle.LoadFromFile(fragment, 0, offset)`.
- Manifests are text, with `[Version]`, `[Directories]`, `[Paths]`, `[Bundles]`, and `[Groups]` sections. A bundle line is `id,name,crc32,size,pathIds,depIds,downloadModes,alias`. The alias is `sha256(name without extension)` plus the extension, and the 32-hex suffix of a bundle's name is the MD5 of its bytes. Each manifest has a `.version` stamp, `version,size,crc32`, which is where `hotUpdateMsg`'s fields land.
- The pack holds exactly the bundles whose `downloadModes` include `0` (`Base`): 8,059 of the 36,745 in the `gameres` manifest (v2342), 539 MB of 3.04 GB. Everything else downloads on demand, by download-mode group.
- Downloads use `<CDN>/hotupdate/com.fun.lastwar.gp/Android/<file>`. A manifest is fetched as the ZIP `<name>_small_v<version>` and CRC-checked against its `.version`. Bundles are fetched by **plain name**; the alias is only the on-device file name. On 2026-10-04, HEAD requests returned 200 for a manifest ZIP and for a bundle by name, and 404 for the same bundle by alias.

<Warning>
TLS certificate validation is disabled on the XAssetPro bundle download path, its `HttpWebRequest` downloader (static-analysis-only). Integrity there rests on the manifest's CRC-32 alone.
</Warning>

## CDN

```text
https://lastwar-cdn.akamaized.net/hotupdate/     (primary)
https://lastwar-cdn.lastwarapp.net/hotupdate/    (fallback)
https://cdn.lastwar.com/hotupdate/               (fallback)
```

The client rotates through the fallback bases on retry. The Lua bundle sits at a predictable path under each base (`NetworkURLConfig.GetDownloadURL`, `LWLuaFileUtil`):

```text
https://lastwar-cdn.akamaized.net/hotupdate/<app id>/<Android|iOS>/LWScripts_<version>_u440.bz2
https://lastwar-cdn.akamaized.net/hotupdate/<app id>/<Android|iOS>/LWScripts_<new>_<old>_u440.patch
```

`<app id>` is the bundle identifier: `com.fun.lastwar.gp` for Android, `com.lastwar.ios` for iOS. The `.bz2` is plain bzip2, not ChaCha-wrapped; if a download ever is wrapped (`PRB`), the client unwraps it first. On disk, the client re-encrypts the bundle as `LWLF` file version 2, which never affects the CDN payload. Old versions stay hosted: every version probed between 780 and 826 returned HTTP 200 on 2026-10-04.

Lua bundle versions seen on 2026-10-04:

| Bundle | `LWLF` version | Chunks |
|---|---|---|
| 1.0.351 APK baseline (recovered from the CDN) | 793 | 18,514 |
| 1.0.364 APK (tag `20260921_1892_App`) | 825 | 18,733 |
| Live Android (newest hosted; 827 and 830 returned 404) | 826 | 18,740 |
| Live iOS (matches the iOS app's `lwfile2`) | 821 | 18,740 |

At the command-catalog level, both live bundles match the 1.0.364 APK. Their differences are debug-only UI modules, a removed diagnostic, and a handful of changed chunks outside `Net/`. Every request schema `goclient` uses is identical across all four versions, see [Command reference](/command-reference).

```

`docs/capturing-and-decoding-traffic.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Capturing and decoding traffic"
description: "The exact, reproducible pipeline behind every live-confirmed finding in this dossier: capture real client traffic, find the right TCP stream, reassemble it, and decode it with the same codec the Go client runs on its own connection."
---

Every "confirmed live via a real packet capture" claim in [Live validation against production](/live-validation) and elsewhere in this dossier was produced by the same four-step pipeline. This page is that pipeline, written down once, so reproducing or extending any of those findings doesn't require re-deriving it from scratch.

It works at all because the SFS2X game socket is **plain TCP with no TLS**. Capturing it is exactly as simple as capturing any other unencrypted traffic, no certificate pinning to defeat, no interception proxy, no MITM setup. `tcpdump` against the real app while it plays through the same network interface as the analysis machine is sufficient.

## Step 1: capture

Run `tcpdump` with a filter that keeps every TCP flow except HTTPS and SSH, then launch and use the real app (`/Applications/Last War.app` on macOS, or the equivalent iOS/Android install) while it's running:

```bash
tcpdump -i en0 -w capture.pcap 'tcp and not port 443 and not port 22'
```

This filter catches every SFS2X gateway the client races, IPv6 ones included, without knowing their addresses or the zone's current port. Capture on the real network interface (`en0` above; `networksetup -listallhardwareports` lists yours). On macOS:

- You don't need `sudo` if Wireshark's ChmodBPF helper is installed, since it gives your user read access to the `/dev/bpf*` devices.
- `-i any` needs root on macOS, even with ChmodBPF.

Port 443 is excluded because everything on it is TLS, which this pipeline can't decode. That includes the GSL (Gate Server List) call, so a capture never contains the GSL response or the values that only arrive there (`at.time`, `rt`).

If you need a narrower capture, filter on the known hosts and ports instead:

```bash
tcpdump -i en0 -w capture.pcap \
  'host 104.17.133.15 or host 104.17.132.15 or host 172.65.210.24 or \
   host 3.33.246.23 or host 15.197.233.176 or host 34.145.128.94 or \
   host 136.107.113.253 or host 166.117.204.28 or \
   port 19292 or port 17783 or port 6088 or port 25092 or port 10783'
```

The host list is every IPv4 server address this project has seen the client actually talk to (GSL HTTP endpoints, CDN, and SFS2X gateways); the port list catches every SFS2X game port seen across captures so far. It misses IPv6 gateways, such as the Cloudflare one the client raced on 2026-10-04. Keep the filter broad; a capture with some irrelevant traffic in it costs nothing at the decode step, but a filter that's too narrow silently drops the packets you actually need.

<Info>
  **Why the host list has held up better than the port list.** An account can get moved to a different zone server-side, confirmed live via a real server merge that moved this project's account from zone `APS783` to `APS8092` with an entirely different port (`17783` → `25092`) mid-session (see [Live validation against production](/live-validation#a-real-server-merge-exposed-three-real-redirect-following-bugs) for the client-side fix this required). The *port* is zone-specific and will drift every time this happens, there's no way to keep it current in a static list. The *host* IPs above turned out to be shared CDN/infra-level addresses rather than zone-specific ones: the post-merge zone's actual game-server host (`lastwar-game-cf.lastwarapp.net`) resolved to `172.65.210.24`, already on this list. Since the filter is a flat OR, `host 172.65.210.24` alone captured the new zone's traffic on its new port without the port list needing to know about it. That's not guaranteed to hold forever, if you're capturing after your own account has moved zones and traffic isn't showing up, re-resolve the current game-server hostnames (they're in a login response's `serverInfo` field, or already-resolved in your session config after a redirect) and add any genuinely new IP to the host list.
</Info>

**Give it real time.** A rushed capture is the single most common failure mode: the real client's own SFS2X connection can churn through its login/bootstrap burst in under a second, so if you start `tcpdump`, immediately open the app, do one thing, and stop, you'll likely capture only the bootstrap burst and miss the actual action you were trying to observe. Let the app fully settle into its main screen (10–15 seconds after login) before doing anything you actually want captured, and let it sit a few seconds after before closing.

## Step 2: find the game socket

A single capture typically contains several TCP streams: the real game session, a few short-lived "losing" gateway connections, and unrelated TLS side-channels (chat, logging, CDN). The losing connections come from the gateway race: in the 2026-10-04 capture, the real client opened three gateways on the zone port at once (two IPv4, one Cloudflare IPv6), sent an `a=29` probe on each, logged in on the first to answer, and closed the other two about 30 ms later. Each losing stream holds one probe and one pong, see [SFS2X wire protocol](/wire-protocol#gateway-race-and-the-pre-login-probe). The `pcap` tool lists them, decodable **plain** streams first, then encrypted **tls** ones:

```bash
go build -o pcap ./cmd/pcap
./pcap -in capture.pcap -list
```

```text
idx  kind  endpoint A                     endpoint B                     bytes
0    plain 192.168.1.80:8883              192.168.1.182:49202               546032  (378 segments)
1    plain 136.107.113.253:10783          192.168.1.182:61637               308125  (620 segments)
2    plain [2001:4860:4860::8888]:443     [2600:1700:...:2920]:64063         66034  (329 segments)
```

The game socket is the **plain** stream to the game server's host and port, port `17783`, or whatever the current zone's port has drifted to (see the port note above). Note its index (`1` above). That's all you need: the tool auto-detects the client side (the connection initiator, or the private-address endpoint) and both directions, so there's no separate stream-index or client-IP lookup to do, and it reads both classic pcap and pcapng, with no `tshark` in the loop.

<Warning>
  If the game-socket stream has only a handful of segments and well under a second of activity, the capture likely caught only a "losing" race candidate or missed the real session, see Step 1's timing note. Re-capture with more time around the action.
</Warning>

## Step 3: reassemble and decode

One command reassembles the chosen stream **by TCP sequence number** (so out-of-order and retransmitted segments land correctly, rather than corrupting the stream the way arrival-order reassembly can) and decodes every SFS2X packet in both directions:

```bash
./pcap -in capture.pcap -stream 1 -decode
```

```text
[c2s] #233 @offset 25561: {c=1, a=13, p={c=al.science.donate, r=-1, p={scienceId=10011900, option=1, _id=229}}}
```

To keep the raw reassembled bytes (e.g. to re-run the client's own `-decode-stream`), use `-out` instead of `-decode`:

```bash
./pcap -in capture.pcap -stream 1 -out stream          # writes stream_c2s.bin / stream_s2c.bin
go build -o lastwar-client ./cmd/lastwar-client
./lastwar-client -decode-stream stream_c2s.bin -decode-label c2s
```

Pass `-client <ip>` to `pcap` to override the auto-detected client side if the heuristic ever picks wrong.

<Tip>
  **The whole pipeline is one Go module, so nothing can drift out of sync.** Both the reassembler (`internal/pcap`) and the decoder are pure Go with no external dependencies; `pcap -decode` and `-decode-stream` frame and decode using the exact same `ReadPacket` (`packet.go`) and `DecodeObject` (`sfsobject.go`) the client uses on its own live connection. Any fix or extension to the real codec is reflected the next time you decode a capture, with no manual sync step.
</Tip>

## Reading the output

Each decoded line is one SFS2X extension-call envelope: `c` is the SFSObject's top-level wrapper (`1` = extension call, `0` = system/heartbeat), `a` is the sub-action, and `p` holds the actual payload; for extension calls, `p.c` is the command name and `p.p` is its params object. Client→server calls almost always carry `_id`, an ever-incrementing per-connection request id; the matching server response echoes the same `_id`. See [Wire protocol](/wire-protocol) for the full packet-envelope and SFSObject binary format this output is decoded from, and [Command reference](/command-reference) for what a given `p.c` command name actually does.

## Recovering from a rotated token

When every run fails with `ec=28`, `ep=[E011]`, the server no longer accepts the session config's access token. A config with a `refreshToken`, such as an own-device one, recovers on its own (see [Refreshing the access token](/auth#refreshing-the-access-token)). For a captured config, the fix is a fresh capture of the real app logging in, and `pcap -session-out` turns that capture straight into a session config. Confirmed live on 2026-10-04: this procedure restored the scheduled runs after the 2026-10-02 rotation (see [Live validation against production](/live-validation)).

<Steps>
  <Step title="Start the capture">
    ```bash
    tcpdump -i en0 -w login.pcap 'tcp and not port 443 and not port 22'
    ```
  </Step>
  <Step title="Cold-start the real app">
    Quit the real app completely, launch it, and wait until its main screen loads, so the capture holds the whole connect-and-login sequence. Then quit the app and stop `tcpdump`.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Write the session config">
    ```bash
    go run ./cmd/pcap -in login.pcap -session-out ~/.lastwar_goclient_session.json
    ```
  </Step>
  <Step title="Verify">
    ```bash
    ./lastwar-client -collect
    ```
  </Step>
</Steps>

What `-session-out` does:

- It searches every plain (non-TLS) stream, or only the one you name with `-stream`.
- It picks the `Login` request (`c=0, a=1`) whose server reply carries no `ec`. It reports streams whose `Login` was rejected or never answered, and skips the `a=29` probe streams.
- It writes `ip`, `port`, `zone`, `gameUid`, `deviceId`, `shumeiBoxId`, `accessToken`, and `iosMode` (from `platform="0"`), plus the `appVersion` and `versionCode` the token was issued under. It overwrites the destination and sets mode `0600`, tightening an existing file's mode too.
- It appends every other gateway that answered a probe on the same port to `ip` as a `|`-delimited fallback list, after the gateway the accepted `Login` went through. `ip` and `port` are only a starting address: `goclient` looks the server up with GSL when they stop answering, see [Looking up the game server](/auth#looking-up-the-game-server).
- It prints `ip`, `port`, `zone`, `iosMode`, `appVersion`, and `versionCode`, but only the **lengths** of `gameUid`, `deviceId`, `shumeiBoxId`, and `accessToken`, so its output is safe to paste into an issue.
- It refuses when more than one stream holds an accepted `Login` (for example, the app relaunched mid-capture), because the conversations carry no timestamps to tell which is freshest. Pick one with `-stream`.
- It fails if the accepted `Login` is missing `zn`, `gameUid`, `deviceId`, or `at`. It copies `shumeiBoxId` when present but doesn't require it, since the server doesn't either: a captured session also reconnects with it empty (confirmed live, 2026-10-04).

Recording the build matters. An access token is bound to the identity it was issued under, build included (confirmed live, see [Live validation against production](/live-validation#solved-a-field-by-field-identity-mismatch-not-anti-fraud)). Once the real app updates, a fresh token only works if `goclient`'s `Login` claims that same `appVersion` and `versionCode`. Without the two fields, iOS mode falls back to the 1.0.344 (786) build of the original capture.

<Warning>
  The written file holds live credentials for a real account. Keep it outside the repository, as the default path in your home directory already is.
</Warning>

## Known limitation: some captures stop decoding partway through

Server→client decoding has, on several real captures to date, hit either a `DecodeObject error: expected top-level tag 18 (SFS_OBJECT), got ...` or a `zstd decode: ...` error, most often right around the same point in the bootstrap-burst response sequence, but not always at an identical byte offset. Client→server decoding has not shown this problem in any capture so far.

These two error kinds behave differently, and only one of them actually stops the decode. A `DecodeObject` error is non-fatal: `-decode-stream` logs it inline for that one packet and continues decoding every packet that follows in the stream (see `decode_test.go`'s "DecodeObject error on one packet continues to the next" regression test). A `zstd decode` error, by contrast, comes from a lower layer (packet framing/decompression, not the SFSObject decoder) and is fatal, it halts the rest of the stream, so only what was decoded before that point is usable.

The working theory was always that this is a reassembly edge case (a reordering/overlap pattern) rather than a decoder bug, since `-decode-stream` uses the identical codec the live Go client relies on and that connection has never shown equivalent corruption. Replacing the old `tshark`-fed Python reassembler with the pure-Go `internal/pcap` (Step 3 above) supports that theory: on a real August-2026 capture whose server→client stream the old path decoded only partway, the Go reassembler decoded the **entire** stream cleanly, every byte consumed as valid framed packets, ~35 more server→client packets than the old path recovered. The Go reassembler places each segment by its exact sequence offset (rather than relying on `tshark`'s own stream-reassembly opinion), which is what makes it more robust to the out-of-order/retransmit patterns that tripped the old pipeline. It's plausible this closes the limitation outright, but it hasn't been re-tested across enough captures to declare it gone. If a decode still stops partway: a `DecodeObject` error is isolated (that one packet is skipped, everything before and after is valid), enough to confirm a client→server request's exact shape even when its matching response is the corrupt one; confirming that one response instead means replaying the request live through the Go client (e.g. via `-interactive`) and reading its response directly. A `zstd decode` error is fatal to the rest of the stream, and the same live-replay approach then applies to everything after the cutoff.

```

`docs/city-building.mdx`:

title: "City & building"
description: "The base-building loop: two distinct queue systems, the building-id encoding scheme, core commands, and the two-part resource economy."

The base-building loop: two architecturally distinct "queue" systems that share a confusing name, a building-id encoding worth knowing, and a resource economy that's really two separate systems.

## Two "queues": don't conflate them

- **Build-queue slots** (`BuildQueueManager`): the small number of concurrent construction slots a player has. A building upgrade occupies one until it finishes.
- **Production queue** (`QueueDataManager`): a generic per-item timer reused by farming, pasture barns, troop training, hospital healing, and research alike. Same wire schema across all of them.

## Building ID encoding

Game-data rows are keyed `id = base_type_id + level`, where `base_type_id` is always a multiple of `BuildLevelCap = 1000`. So `bId=10100000, lv=5` → row id `10100005`.
