The original capture used `ta`'s real sub-fields; the shipped code replaced those with empty placeholders for security, and reconnect is now **re-confirmed working with the placeholders too**, an unattended cron running this client reconnected and collected real resources over multiple days (August 2026), re-verified after a live zone-server migration. On 2026-10-04 it also succeeded with `shumeiBoxId` sent empty. See the reconnect wall below and "What's still open" for the parts (minimal `ta` content, fully from-scratch login) that remain open |

## The reconnect wall

Picking a role from `accountArr` (after email verification) does a full reconnect, not a session continuation, decompiled precisely from `UI/UISetting/UIRoleLogin/View/UIRoleLoginView.lua:OnClickLogin`:

```lua
function UIRoleLoginView:OnClickLogin()
  CS.AccountCredentialManager.ClearAll()
  CS.AccountCredentialManager.SetServerNetInfo(self.param.ip, self.param.port, self.param.zone, 0)
  CS.AccountCredentialManager.SetLoginKey(self.param.loginKey)
  CS.AccountCredentialManager.SetUID(self.param.gameUid)
  CS.AccountCredentialManager.Save()
  EventManager:GetInstance():Broadcast(EventId.SwitchAccount, self.param.gameUid)
  SFSNetwork.SendMessage(MsgDefines.UserCleanPost)
end
```

This triggers the `CrossServerLogin` FSM state (`Assembly-CSharp.decompiled.cs:108752-108812`), which dials the role's own `ip:port` **directly, no second GSL HTTP call**, and sends the same base SFS `Login` request. This was reimplemented exactly and tested with every plausible field combination:

| # | `un` | `p.at` | `shumeiBoxId` | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `""` | GSL token (`opt=login`) | `""` | `ec=28, ep=[E011]` |
| 2 | composite gameUid | GSL token (`opt=login`) | `""` | `ec=28, ep=[E005]` |
| 3 | composite gameUid | *omitted* (matches decompiled `CrossServerLogin` exactly) | `""` | `ec=28, ep=[E011]` |
| 4 | composite gameUid | **real, GSL-validated token** (`opt=refresh` with a real device's refresh token) | **real ShuMei fingerprint**, extracted from a genuine prior login | `ec=28, ep=[E005]` |

Row 4 is the load-bearing result. `/Applications/Last War.app` (the iOS build, installed locally via Mac Catalyst) had previously logged into the exact same real account, its sandboxed PlayerPrefs equivalent (`~/Library/Containers/<uuid>/Data/Library/Preferences/com.lastwar.ios.plist`) contained a real device ID, a real refresh token, and a cached ShuMei device-fingerprint token. Feeding all three through the Go client, plus a fresh, GSL-validated access token obtained by actually exchanging that refresh token, still got rejected identically to a fully synthetic identity.

<Warning>
  **Reading the result.** The rejection doesn't depend on any field this client can construct or replay, not `un`, not `at`, not `shumeiBoxId`, not even a genuine previously-accepted device fingerprint's token value. It only fires for accounts with real history; the byte-identical guest path never triggers it. Most likely explanation: the real credentials were issued for the iOS bundle (`com.lastwar.ios`) while this client presents as the Android build (`com.fun.lastwar.gp`), and ShuMei fingerprints are very likely bound to the specific app/package that generated them, not something further trial-and-error on field values is likely to fix.
</Warning>

<Note>
  **Update, 2026-10-04: two live tests narrow this down further.**

  - **`shumeiBoxId` isn't required (confirmed live).** The captured iOS session, with the same `at` and the same identity, logged in fine with `shumeiBoxId` sent empty. The ShuMei explanation in the warning above doesn't hold for an established account.
  - **A device of its own gets tokens, but not a session (confirmed live).** `goclient`'s email-verification flow bound a fresh, Go-generated device to the real account, and GSL `opt=login` with the resulting `loginKey` issued that device its own `at`/`rt` pair. A base-zone `Login` with that token and `goclient`'s Android identity (1.0.364/1892, `un` = gameUid, `shumeiBoxId` empty) was then rejected with `ec=28`, `ep=[E005]`, reproducing row 2 above.

  **Update, 2026-10-13: the own-device `Login` works once Android `ta` is filled (confirmed live).** Every Android `Login` in the table above, and the 2026-10-04 own-device one, sent `ta` as `{}`; `goclient` filled it only for iOS. C485 found from real Android captures that an Android `Login` with `{}` gets `E005` and one with `#os`, `#bundle_id`, and `lw_platform` filled in doesn't ([discussion #22](https://github.com/ljagiello/lastwar-client/discussions/22)). One build sent the 2026-10-04 own-device token twice, changing only `ta`: `{}` got `ec=28`, `ep=[E005]`, and the filled blob logged in with 160 buildings in `init`. So rows 2 and 4 most likely failed on `ta` too. Row 4 also mixed an iOS-issued token with the Android identity, so it can't be separated after the fact. The gate applies to established accounts: guests were always accepted with `{}`, as the Warning above says. Which of the blob's keys the server reads isn't isolated, since both tests swapped the whole blob. See [Identity, login & session](/auth#a-device-of-its-own).
</Note>

## Solved: a field-by-field identity mismatch, not anti-fraud

**Confirmed.** The guess above was exactly right, and it's now proven rather than inferred. The proof came from a live packet capture, not more trial-and-error on field values: `tcpdump` against the locally installed `/Applications/Last War.app` (the real iOS / Mac Catalyst build), captured while manually logging into the exact same real account through the actual app UI. Because the SFS2X game socket is plain TCP with no TLS, this captured cleartext-after-XOR application data directly, no interception layer needed. The captured `Login` request was decoded field by field using the client's own codec and byte-diffed against what the Go client itself was encoding for the same fields, see [Capturing and decoding traffic](/capturing-and-decoding-traffic) for the exact, reproducible version of this pipeline.

First proof point, before touching the Go client's login path at all: replaying the captured `Login` packet **byte-for-byte, raw, over a fresh TCP connection** succeeded cleanly. That settles something earlier hypotheses left open, reconnecting was never blocked by session locking, token single-use, or anti-fraud in the way row 4 above seemed to suggest. The same access token, reused verbatim, worked fine when replayed on this second, fresh connection, ruling out session locking and token single-use as blockers in this test. Whether it remains valid across a third or further reconnects wasn't separately tested.

The field diff showed the actual gate: an access token is bound to the exact `packageName`/`platform`/`appVersion`/`versionCode` identity it was issued under, and the Go client had been hardcoding an Android identity unconditionally, even when replaying a token issued to a real iOS session. Fixing `identity.go`'s `BuildLoginParams` to match the token's real issuing identity got a live reconnect working **through the Go client's own from-scratch SFS2X implementation**, not the raw-replay hack. The fix: an `IOSMode` boolean that switches `packageName` to `com.lastwar.ios`, `packageSign` to `SHA1(packageName)` (confirmed this formula generalizes correctly to iOS too, it matches the captured value exactly), `platform` to `"0"`, `pf` to `AppStore`, `appVersion` to `1.0.344`, `versionCode` to `786`; adds the previously entirely-missing `dataConfigMd5` and the iOS-only `idfa`/`idfv`/`phone_native_screen` fields; drops the Android-only `AndroidID`/`IMEI`/`google_available` fields and makes `country`/`suggestCountry`/`timeoffset`/`gcmRegisterId`/`referrer` genuinely conditional on an empty `uid` instead of unconditional; and, critically, at the time, populated `ta` with the real captured analytics blob instead of an empty placeholder object. `crossserver.go` and `main.go` picked up `-cs-ios` and `-cs-at` flags to drive this path. Because the fix changed the platform fields and `ta` together, it didn't show which of them the server reads. The 2026-10-13 own-device test (see the update above) showed that, for an established account, a filled `ta` is required on its own.

<Warning>
  **`ta`'s real values were later replaced with placeholders; the reconnect result above no longer describes the shipped code exactly.** A subsequent security audit found that `ta`'s `lw_device_id`/`lw_shumei_id`/`lw_airKey` sub-fields, set from the same live `DeviceID`/`ShumeiBoxId`/`AirKey` values used elsewhere in the request, leaked those secrets in cleartext inside an opaque JSON string, outside the reach of `SFSObject.StringRedacted()`'s key-based masking. `identity.go`'s `BuildLoginParams` (`IOSMode` branch) now sends those three sub-fields as empty-string placeholders instead. The reconnect success documented above was first confirmed against the *pre-fix* code, which sent `ta`'s real captured content, but it has since been **re-confirmed against the shipped, placeholder code**: an unattended cron running this client reconnected and collected real resources over multiple days (August 2026), and it was re-verified manually after a live zone-server migration. So the placeholders are accepted; the server does not require `ta`'s real device sub-fields for reconnect. See "What's still open" below for what remains (the *minimal* required `ta` content, and a fully from-scratch login).
</Warning>

Live result: `Login` OK, followed immediately by a correctly Zstd-decoded `init` push containing the account's full real state, **162 real buildings** on this account.

## A real server merge exposed three real redirect-following bugs

<Warning>
  **Symptom, confirmed live:** a session config that had worked for weeks started logging in "successfully", `Login OK`, no `ec` error, while every single command after that timed out identically: `push.init.build` never arrived, and every hand-sent command got `i/o timeout`. Not one specific action failing; *everything* after login, uniformly.
</Warning>

Root cause: the account's zone had been migrated server-side (a routine live-game server merge, `APS783` → `APS8092`, entirely different host and port) mid-session. The old connection was still *accepted* at the login step, but the account genuinely no longer lived there, so nothing past that point could ever succeed. The server actually says this happens, directly in the `Login` response's `serverInfo` field, the client just wasn't reading it.

Three separate, real bugs, not one:

1. **`DoCrossServerLogin` had zero `serverInfo` handling at all.** The other login path (`Login`/`waitForInitPush`) had a redirect check; the session-config-driven cross-server path, the one actually used day to day, didn't check for it at all.
2. **The check that *did* exist was structurally unreachable.** It lived inside a `for attempt := 1; attempt <= maxLoginAttempts; attempt++` loop capped at 1 (deliberately, retrying on a *timeout* had been live-tested as actively harmful, see above). Go's `continue` in a C-style `for` loop still runs the post-statement before re-checking the condition, so hitting the redirect branch just silently exited the loop instead of retrying. It had never been exercised against a real redirect before this.
3. **Once both were fixed and actually reachable, the check itself was looking in the wrong place.** `serverInfo` isn't a top-level field of the `Login` response, it's nested one level down, under `p`: `{p: {eu_state, serverInfo: {ip, port, zone, ...}}, rs, zn, un, pi, rl, id}`. Confirmed by testing against the real redirect payload: reading `env.Content.Get("serverInfo")` directly, as both the original code and the decompiled `LoginMessage.CSHandleResponse` call site alone would suggest, found nothing.

A fourth thing surfaced immediately once the redirect actually started firing: `serverInfo.port` decodes as a **UTF string**, not a numeric SFS type, `GetInt("port")` silently returned `0`, resolving the redirect address to `host:0` and failing to connect. Every other numeric-looking field in the same object (`id`, for instance) is a real number; this one specifically isn't.

The fix: both login paths now follow the redirect (close the stale connection, redial the new address, resend `Login` with the new zone) up to a small bounded hop count; `findServerInfo` checks the nested location (falling back to top-level, in case a different response shape ever puts it there); `getIntFlexible` reads `port` as a number or falls back to parsing its string form. `crossserver.go`'s `DoCrossServerLogin` also now persists the resolved address back into the session config file after a redirect, so the *next* run connects directly instead of re-following the same redirect every single time.

Confirmed live, full loop: reconnecting with the stale `APS783` config correctly received and followed the redirect to `APS8092`'s real host and port, logged in cleanly, loaded all 163 buildings, and, on the very next run, connected straight to the new address with no redirect needed at all, because the config had been rewritten in place.

<Info>
  **This isn't a one-time fixed state; the account has genuinely moved zones more than once since.** A later capture showed the base `Login` targeting `APS783` again with no redirect needed, meaning the account either moved back or the merge target changed a second time. The fix here isn't "resolved to APS8092", it's "follows whatever `serverInfo` says, every time," which is the only version of this that stays correct across further merges without more manual intervention.
</Info>

## The 2026-10-02 token rotation (`E011`)

<Warning>
  **Symptom, confirmed live:** from 2026-10-02, starting somewhere between 12:00 and 15:00 PDT, every scheduled run failed at login with `ec=28`, `ep=[E011]`. The TCP connection and the `Login` request went through. The server rejected the access token, so nothing after login ran.
</Warning>

What's known from the failing runs and a fresh capture:

- **Nothing on the researcher's side triggered it.** Playing on a phone doesn't rotate the scheduled client's token, and the researcher didn't refresh it any other way. The invalidation happened server-side, around the 1.0.364 rollout window (the Android build was posted 2026-09-23). Nothing ties the two together beyond timing.
- **Both credentials had changed.** A fresh capture of the real Mac Catalyst app showed a new `at` **and** a new `shumeiBoxId`, with the same `deviceId`. That app's binary was still 1.0.344 (build 786), hot-updated to `resVersion` `2159.1505_821F_39516.23570`.
- **Recapturing fixed it.** Writing the new values into the session config with `pcap -session-out` (see [Recovering from a rotated token](/capturing-and-decoding-traffic#recovering-from-a-rotated-token)) restored the scheduled runs, and a full `-collect` run then succeeded.
- **It has happened before.** The first rotation, on 2026-08-16, failed identically for 16 consecutive runs over about 42 hours, and `shumeiBoxId` had changed then too.

`goclient` now reports an `E011` rejection as `session.ErrTokenRejected`, which wraps `ErrAuthRejected`, so the exit code stays `2`. The log line names the recapture procedure.

What static analysis of 1.0.364 adds (static-analysis-only, see [Identity, login & session](/auth#token-lifecycle)):

- The client labels `E011` `ERROR_LOGIN_ACCESS_TOKEN`. It clears only the access token, keeps the refresh token, reloads, and runs a GSL (Gate Server List) `opt=refresh` call that issues a new `at`. `goclient` keeps no refresh token, so its only recovery is a fresh capture.
- Two mechanisms fit the observation, and static analysis can't tell them apart: (a) the real app's own 30-day proactive refresh superseding a copied token, or (b) server-side expiry or invalidation. The researcher didn't run anything that would refresh the token this time, which fits (b) better, but this stays open.

`at.time` is an issue time, not an expiry (confirmed live). A GSL `opt=login` response on 2026-10-04 carried `at.time` and `rt.time` equal to the moment of issue, in unix seconds. So the client's 30-day rule counts from issue. That still doesn't show whether the server expires tokens on its own, so which mechanism caused the 2026-10-02 rotation stays open. The capture itself couldn't show `at.time`, because the GSL call runs over HTTPS on port 443, which the capture filter excluded.

## The complete `Login` params field list ([Identity, login & session](/auth) was a partial reconstruction)

`LoginMessage.CSSetData` (`Assembly-CSharp.decompiled.cs:122440-122598`), read in full, in call order:

```text
_id, netType, ta, distinct_id, phone_screen, configVersion
  -- only if uid (args[0]) is empty (brand-new device):
  country, suggestCountry, timeoffset, gcmRegisterId, referrer
AndroidID, IMEI, psh, mt, deviceId, airKey, cmdBaseTime,
SecurityCode = MD5(cmdBaseTime + "4d1c383ccbedf3d98320d6ea06d8dedc" + uid),
OneCode, CoreV, googlePlay, androidDid, googleName, deeplinkParams, pfId,
dataConfigMd5 (only if non-empty), google_available, fromCountry, packageName,
packageSign, platform="1" (hardcoded in this decompiled Android assembly -- not confirmed to hold "both platforms": the live iOS capture used for the reconnect fix above required platform="0", so this literal is almost certainly baked in per-platform build rather than shared), lat (hardcoded 0 in the 1.0.364 Android assembly; the iOS captures send 1), device_string, pf,
firebaseId, afuid, phone_model, configNumber=0, gaid, osVersion, parseRegisterId,
gameUid = uid (SAME string object as `un`, not independently derived), appVersion,
resVersion (1.0.364: GetResVersion(), built from check-version data; goclient sends "0"), versionCode, lang, serverId = zone.Substring(3), gmLogin=0,
KCPMode="0", forbidden_froce_merge=1, shumeiBoxId, simOp, simOpName,
delete_account_status, isUseLz4 (only if NetPacketConst.useNewPacket && useZStd)
at (only if AccountCredentialManager.AuthTokens.at is non-empty)
```

`un` and `p["gameUid"]` are proven the literal same string object in every call site, no divergence possible. `rt`/`loginKey`/`attime`/`rttime` are read **only** at the GSL HTTP layer to pick `opt=`; none are ever placed in the SFS `Login` request. `pw` is always `""` at this layer regardless of new/returning.

**1.0.364 re-read (static-analysis-only).** `LoginMessage.CSSetData` in 1.0.364 sends the same fields in the same order. Every derivation (`cmdBaseTime`, `SecurityCode`, `OneCode`/`CoreV`, `psh`, `packageSign`, `airKey`) is unchanged, and the APK signing certificate is byte-identical to 1.0.351's. Two values are worth knowing:

- `dataConfigMd5` isn't computed by the client. The C# reads it from a cache of a value the server sent in an earlier `init`, and omits the key when the cache is empty. In the 2026-10-04 capture, the Login's `dataConfigMd5` equaled `init.add.a` from the same session. Whether the server expects it to persist across sessions is open.
- `resVersion` is built from check-version data, see [Startup, version-check & hot-update](/bootstrap#resversion).

## The 2026-10-04 capture: real client versus `goclient`

A cold-start capture of the real iOS / Mac Catalyst app (1.0.344, hot-updated) was decoded and diffed against what `goclient` sends. The real `Login` and `goclient`'s `BuildLoginParams` in iOS mode carry the **identical 51-key set with identical SFS2X types**; only key order and values differ. SFSObject is a map, so key order is harmless. Everything in the left column was observed in the capture of the real client; "tolerated live" means `goclient` logs in and works with its own behavior.

| Real client (observed in the capture) | `goclient` | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Opens every gateway in the zone's list in parallel, sends an `a=29` probe on each, and sends `Login` about 45 ms after the first pong | Dials the list in order, sends no probe, sends `Login` straight after connecting | Tolerated live, see [SFS2X wire protocol](/wire-protocol#gateway-race-and-the-pre-login-probe) |
| Sets header bit `0x04` plus a 2-byte id (`0x030F`, the zone's server id 783 in this one sample) on every client-to-server frame | Never sets it | Tolerated live |
| Heartbeat payload nested one level deeper: `p={p={clientTime}}` | Flat: `p={clientTime}` | Tolerated live |
| A monotonic `_id` on every extension request | `_id` only on `Login` (`1`) and `login.init` (`2`) | Tolerated live |
| No SFS2X `Handshake` (`a=0`) | None by default (`-handshake` is an experiment) | Match |
| `netType=1` on Wi-Fi (`1` = Wi-Fi, `2` = mobile, inferred) | `netType=2`, while its own `ta` says `WIFI` | Tolerated live |
| `resVersion` = `2159.1505_821F_39516.23570` | `"0"` | Tolerated live for months |
| `dataConfigMd5` = a server-issued value | `""` | Tolerated live |
| After `init`: `change.user.parseid`, `check.device.change` (answered `r:false`), about 220 mostly read-only requests in 5 s, and `login.ext {info, add}` | None of these | Tolerated live |
| Never sends `login.init` | Sends `login.init` as a fallback if `init` is slow | n/a |
| Sends `mail.delete.batch {type:"auto", uids}` nine times on login: the real client auto-deletes mail | Never deletes mail | n/a |
| iOS `psh` | The Android-derived `psh`, which doesn't match the iOS value | Tolerated live for weeks; see [Native binaries & security](/native-binaries) |

Other facts from the same capture, all observed live:

- The server sent only a bare `init`, about 287 KB with 247 top-level keys. No `init.before`, `init.after`, or `push.init.build` arrived.
- `push.shumei.id {shumeiId}` arrives about 0.5 s after `Login`. The real client reports that value as `ta.lw_shumei_id` in its next `Login`; it isn't the `shumeiBoxId` sent in the same request.
- `init.user` carries the account's email address. `goclient` now masks `email` and `shumeiId` in every redacted dump, alongside `mail` and `shumeiBoxId`.
- `init.mixedInfo.todayLoginTimes` counts logins per server day, including every `goclient` run.
- Over 328 s, the server answered all 83 heartbeats. There was no kick, no redirect, and no token-expiry hint anywhere in `init`.

`psh`, `dataConfigMd5`, `init.add`, `login.ext`, and the probe template are app-integrity and anti-fraud surfaces. They're recorded here as protocol facts only; reproducing them is out of scope for this project. `shumeiBoxId` is in scope: `goclient` reproduces the ShuMei device-profile registration that mints it, see [ShuMei device fingerprint](/shumei).

## `ec`/`ep` vs `errorMessage`: two distinct error channels

`ec`/`ep` are SFS2X's own built-in protocol error fields, not app-level ones; the game's `BaseUtils` transport reads them and formats them through the stock SFS2X error table (`BaseUtils.decompiled.cs:31893-31958`). `ec=28` is SFS2X's generic custom-error passthrough (`SFSErrorCodes.errorsByCode[28] = "{0}"`), it fires when the server's Zone Login Event Handler throws a rejection carrying an arbitrary string, which shows up as `ep[0]`. Observed live: `"E002"`, `"E005"`, `"E011"`. `E011` maps client-side to `ClearAccessToken()` (despite firing even when `p.at` is omitted entirely, so the name isn't a literal description of the server check). The 1.0.364 C# names it `ERROR_LOGIN_ACCESS_TOKEN` (static-analysis-only).

`E005` was previously read as a generic, uncategorized bucket. The 1.0.364 C# maps it to its own `ERROR_MAINTENANCE` code and shows a maintenance dialog (static-analysis-only). Live, though, the server returned `E005` for a token presented under the wrong platform identity (rows 2 and 4 of the reconnect-wall table above), not during maintenance. Read "maintenance" as the client's UI bucket for the code, not as the server's reason. See [Identity, login & session](/auth#login-rejection-codes) for the full code table.

## The real post-login bootstrap: bare `init`, not `push.init.build`

`push.init.build` exists and is wired but never fired once across roughly a dozen live sessions. The actual all-in-one bootstrap is the bare `init` push (`InitMessage.HandleMessage`), which fans one payload out to essentially every data manager in one shot:

```lua
local HandleMessage = function(self, t)
  print("[PushInit] lua PushInit")
  ...
  DataCenter.BuildManager:InitData(t)          -- buildings come from HERE: t.building_new
  DataCenter.ProductLineManager:HandleInit(t)
  DataCenter.AccountManager:InitData(t)
  ...
```

<Check>
  **Resolved: a silent Zstd decompression bug, not rate-limiting.** The `init` push was never actually missing, it was arriving and being silently discarded. `packet.go`'s `ReadPacket` already correctly *detected* the server's Zstandard-compressed frames (header bits `0x20` compressed + `0x10`, the `useLZ4` flag repurposed as "useZstd"), but simply returned an error instead of decompressing, decompression was never implemented. Every read loop waiting on the post-login `init` push treated that error exactly like a closed connection: no crash, nothing that read as a decode error, just silence indistinguishable from "the push never came." That's the entire mystery this investigation originally chased, the `Handshake` experiments, the active-pull `login.init` attempt, the longer timeouts, the 3-attempt reconnect loop, none of it could have worked, because none of it touched the real bug. Confirmed via live capture: the server's init bootstrap push is roughly 313KB of Zstd-compressed data on the wire. The fix was a real decoder (`github.com/klauspost/compress/zstd`, a shared lazily-initialized `zstd.Decoder`, `DecodeAll`) dropped into the compressed branch of `ReadPacket`. Getting that 313KB payload to then parse correctly surfaced two further bugs in `sfsobject.go`'s array-tag decoding, see the root-cause section below. Once both were fixed, `init` arrived cleanly on the very first login in every post-fix login tested; neither the reconnect loop nor the active-pull fallback ever actually had to fire. Of the two mechanisms built to chase this symptom, only the three-attempt reconnect-on-timeout loop has since been removed (`maxLoginAttempts` reduced back to 1, live testing showed any reconnect attempt reliably breaks a working session with `ec=28`/`E011` or `E005`, it doesn't recover a missing `init`; see `login.go`'s comment above `maxLoginAttempts` for the full history). The halfway active-pull `login.init` send inside `waitForInitPush` is a separate mechanism and was *not* reverted, it remains live, unconditional code: partway through the `init`-wait window, if the push hasn't arrived yet, it still sends `login.init` as a real, currently-registered active-pull command, kept in place as a genuine fallback for a server that stays silent for a reason other than this bug.
</Check>

**Correction from earlier static analysis:** Training Base was previously placed on `building.camp.collect`, reasoned as troop training rather than a `ProductLineManager` type. Live testing disproves this directly, `building.camp.collect` against a real Training Base `uuid` returns `errorCode=E000001`, `"Building type error"`. Reading the actual handler, `2944_Net_Msgs_BuildingCampCollectMessage.lua`, shows `building.camp.collect` only covers three building types: Military Camp (`LW_BUILD_MILITARY_CAMP`, 10103000), Smith Shop (`LW_BUILD_SMITH_SHOP`, 10101000), and Tactical Chip Factory (`LW_BUILDING_TACTICAL_CHIP_FACTORY`, 10232000), not Training Base. Training Base belongs with the other production-line buildings after all, the table above is corrected accordingly.

**"Spore Factory" was also previously documented as non-permanent, uncollectible seasonal content, also corrected.** The four Season 6 tiers (`LW_BUILD_SEASON6_QUARTZ_FACTORY1`-`4`, internal codenames left over from an earlier season's reskinned content) are real, currently-active, collectible buildings on a real account, confirmed live via `building.production.collect` against each of their four real `uuid`s.

**Four more building types beyond the original six were confirmed live in a follow-up pass:** Oil Well, Drone Parts Workshop, Tactical Center, and Armament Institute. All four accept `building.production.collect` (in the one wrong-type case actually tested, Training Base sent to `building.camp.collect`, see above, the server returned `errorCode=E000001`, not `602026`; that single precedent is what's relied on below to read a `602026` response from Tactical Center or Armament Institute as confirming the pairing is correct even though their timers hadn't completed, a wrong-type request was never directly tried against `building.production.collect` itself). At the time, the requested names "Tactical Institute" and "Component Factory" had no exact 1:1 locale match found by static analysis, so `Armament Institute` and `Drone Parts Workshop` were used as closest-guess stand-ins. **That guess was wrong, see the correction below.** Both Tactical Center and Armament Institute responded live with `errorCode=602026` ("in production, please be patient") rather than completing a collection, which was read at the time as confirming the command pairing. That reading turned out to be wrong; see the resolution below.

**A further four Truck Station tiers were added in a later pass, on the same "command pairing looks real" basis as Tactical Center/Armament Institute, also still unconfirmed.** These were found while chasing "Armed Truck" specifically: `SHAKE_COLLECT_TRUCK_RES` (a setting key dedicated to trucks, parallel to the general `SHAKE_COLLECT_RES`) and `BuildBubbleType.TruckReady`/`TruckReward`/`TruckTravelling` (modeling a dispatch-travel-collect lifecycle) both looked like promising matches for "Armed Truck." All four `LW_BUILD_TRUCK_STATION_1`-`4` exist on the real account and accept `building.production.collect` without an `E000001` type-mismatch, but, like Tactical Center and Armament Institute, every attempt across multiple full `-collect` runs got `602026`, never a real collection. This lead turned out to be a dead end for "Armed Truck" specifically (see below). The buildings stayed wired in only because the command pairing looked valid, until the resolution below.

<Check>
  **The "Tactical Institute"/"Component Factory" naming guess above was wrong, corrected via a live packet capture of the real game client tapping both buildings directly.** The uuids the real client sent to `building.production.collect` resolved to `bId=10214000` (`LW_BUILD_SQUAD_EQUIP_FACTORY`) and `bId=10235000` (`LW_BUILD_DOMINATOR_TRAIN`), neither matches Drone Parts Workshop or Armament Institute. Both are locale-confirmed: `10214000`'s `building.lua` row names it via loc-key `2000574` = "Component Factory"; `10235000`'s name loc-key resolves directly to "Tactical Institute" (its description: "Produces items for Overlord training levels", the same "Overlord" idle-reward track from `lw.pve.idle.reward`). Finding the second one took extra digging: a naive lookup of the key `building_name_10235000` in the flat length-prefixed locale key/value store initially returned nothing at all. The key and its value were actually still there, just merged into an adjacent malformed entry by a parser desync a few bytes earlier in the stream (a length byte that happened to also be valid ASCII, throwing off alignment until the parser resynced), re-scanning for the substring rather than an exact key match recovered it.

  **Component Factory (10214000) is now genuinely confirmed**, a real `status=1` collection (item `630011`) on first live test. **Tactical Institute (10235000)** got `errorCode=602026` on its first test, but unlike Tactical Center/Armament Institute/Truck Station, its raw `building_new` data carries real `prodST`/`prodStatus=1`/`prodET` timestamps, a genuinely active production cycle, not a dormant one. It has since collected successfully 321 times. Drone Parts Workshop stays in the client as a confirmed production line; Armament Institute turned out not to be one at all.
</Check>

<Check>
  **Resolved (2026-10-04): the six "pairing looks real" buildings are not production lines.** Live evidence and the 1.0.364 Lua agree:

  - **Confirmed live:** across 342 consecutive scheduled runs, Tactical Center, Armament Institute, and Truck Station I-IV returned `errorCode=602026` on every attempt and never `status=1`. Over the same runs, Tactical Institute collected successfully 321 times.
  - **Static-analysis-only:** the real client sends `building.production.collect` only for buildings in `Global/EnumType.lua`'s `ProductLineBuilds`, plus the current season week card's farm building. None of the six is in either set. The real client also skips any building without `prodST` (`ProductLineManager:GetNextCollectTime` returns `-1`) and shows tip 602026 locally instead of sending anything.

  So a 602026 response doesn't confirm a command pairing: the server returns it for buildings the real client never collects. `goclient` no longer sends a collect for these six, and it now skips any building without `prodST`. See [City & building](/city-building#which-buildings-are-production-lines) for the full set.
</Check>

Confirmed live, end to end: two separate full `-collect` runs against the real account (before the Truck Station tiers existed in the client) produced 38 and 39 successful collections (out of 41 attempts each) across what were then the **12 confirmed building types**, the original six, Oil Well, Drone Parts Workshop, and the four Spore Factory tiers all completed real collections with resource deltas visible in the live `push.resource.info` / `push.resource.item.update` server pushes (food, iron, gold, refined metal, refined material, training points, petroleum, Drone Parts, and obsidian all observed increasing). The remaining attempts in both runs got `errorCode=602026`, `"In production please be patient"`: for buildings whose production timer hadn't finished yet, and for every attempt on Tactical Center and Armament Institute, which turned out not to be production lines at all (see above). Component Factory's later confirmation brought the total to 13, and Tactical Institute's later collections bring it to **14 confirmed building types**.

## Armed Truck: an account-level idle reward, not a building

<Check>
  **Resolved.** "Armed Truck" is not a building at all. It's also not `LW_BUILD_TRUCK_STATION` above, despite that being a real, suggestively-named lead. `Scene/LWHummerScene` turned out to be the same feature, not a separate minigame: it's the "Jeep Adventure" 3D scene behind this reward panel. It reads `stage_idle_reward` and `lastIdleRewardTimeStamp`, fills the truck's cargo bed as the pool accrues, and its **reward** button sends `lw.pve.idle.reward {action: 0}` to open the claim popup. Nothing played in the scene changes the reward (1.0.364 Lua, static-analysis-only). An earlier version of this page called it an unrelated driving/combat minigame with no network commands; that was wrong. Confirmed via a live packet capture of the actual game client: "Armed Truck" is one of two independent tracks (the other is "Overlord") in a dedicated **"Truck Rewards" idle/AFK reward panel**, collected through a single account-level command with no building `uuid` involved at all: `lw.pve.idle.reward`, with an `action` field, `0` peeks at the accumulated pool without claiming it, `1` claims it.
</Check>

The real client's own captured traffic called `action=0`, then `action=1`, then `action=0` again, peek, claim, refresh. Replaying the same three-call sequence through this Go client got the identical shape of result:

```
lw.pve.idle.reward {action: 0}  ->  reward=[{type=1, value=18636}, {type=20, value=18636}, {type=31, value=11849}, {type=27, value={num=176628, id=8001}}], dominatorReward=[]
lw.pve.idle.reward {action: 1}  ->  reward=[{total=1824399742, type=1, ...}, {total=1342422740, type=20, ...}, {total=818689169, type=31, ...}, {type=27, value={addNum=176628, itemId=8001, number=672979884, ...}}]
lw.pve.idle.reward {action: 0}  ->  reward=[]
```

The `action=1` response is the load-bearing evidence, not just an echo of the peek: it includes real post-collection account `total` values for each resource, and the immediate follow-up `action=0` peek showed the pool reset to genuinely empty, proving the claim actually drained a real accumulated reward, not that the command merely succeeded superficially. `dominatorReward` (the "Overlord" track) was empty in this particular capture, so its claim payload shape wasn't directly observed, but the same `action=1` call is expected to cover both tracks together since they share one panel and one command.

Wired into the Go client as `CollectIdleReward` (`buildings.go`), called automatically at the start of every `-collect` run, independent of the building-uuid loop since this command needs no `uuid` at all.

## Visitors: delivered free in `init`, greeted with `visitor.operate`

<Check>
  **Confirmed live.** City visitors, the `?`-bubble NPCs that occasionally appear near the base, need no separate discovery request at all. They're delivered as a sibling field of `building_new` in the same bare `init` bootstrap push (see [The real post-login bootstrap](#the-real-post-login-bootstrap-bare-init-not-push-init-build) above): `visitor={addNum, maxNum, list=[{uid, eventId, startTime, type, extendInfo, visitorId}, ...]}`. `maxNum` was observed live as `5`. Greeting one is `visitor.operate {uid, operate: 1}`, confirmed via a live packet capture of the real game client tapping two visitors in its city, one `visitor.operate` call per tap.
</Check>

Replaying the same request shape through this Go client, against the one visitor the real client's own session had left ungreeted, got a real, well-formed business-logic response rather than a protocol error or an "unknown command":

```
visitor.operate {uid: 1389862050553073568, operate: 1}  ->  errorCode=visitor_err_coming, errorMsg="visitor not started"
```

That single response is more informative than it looks. Cross-referencing the three visitors present in that capture's `init` payload, this was the most-recently-arrived of the three (`eventId=2005`, the newest `startTime`), the real client had greeted the other two (`eventId=2002` and `eventId=2001`, both older) and left this one alone. Read together: visitors apparently go through an arrival delay/animation window after showing up before they're actually greetable, and `visitor_err_coming` is the server's real, typed way of saying "not yet." This confirms the full path end to end, parsing visitors out of `init`, building the request, round-tripping it, decoding a real typed response. The real client's own capture *did* successfully greet those other two visitors (`visitor.operate {uid, operate: 1}`, one call per tap), but the response to those two specific calls fell outside the successfully-decoded portion of that capture (a stream-reassembly artifact past a certain point, the same class of issue seen with the Truck Rewards capture above), not because no visitor was greetable. So a **successful** greet's reward payload has still not been directly observed, but the gap is a capture-decoding artifact, not a missing greetable visitor.

Wired into the Go client as `GreetVisitors` (`visitors.go`), called automatically on every `-collect` run alongside `CollectIdleReward`, for the same reason: no building `uuid` involved.

## Alliance automation: help-all and gift claiming, both true bulk commands

<Check>
  **Confirmed live**, both via real packet captures of the actual game client. Unlike mail (below), neither of these needs per-item uids at all, both are genuine "do everything of this kind" bulk commands, closer in shape to the Armed Truck idle reward than to mail claiming.
</Check>

**Helping alliance members** (`al.help.all`) bulk-completes every pending alliance-member help request (construction/research speedups other members asked for) in one call. Reading the request-construction Lua directly (`extracted/lua_decompiled/4368_Net_Msgs_Alliance_AlHelpAllMessage.lua`) shows the wire request carries exactly one field, `cmdBaseTime`, everything else the UI passes in (`helpBtnPos`, `toPos`, `isOnlyDisperse`, `isOnlyShowDiff`) is purely local animation state, never sent. The real client sent an absolute Unix-epoch-milliseconds value; replaying the same shape through this Go client with a live `time.Now().UnixMilli()` got a real response echoing the account's own `allianceId` back with no error. The Lua handler shows this call is unconditional and safe even with nothing pending, it's a no-op success, not an error, in that case.

**Claiming alliance gifts** (`alliance.reward.allreceive`) is the "Claim All" button on the Alliance Gifts panel, and needs only a `type` field. The panel has two independently-claimed tabs; reading the handler's own tip-string branch (`extracted/lua_decompiled/4428_Net_Msgs_Alliance_AllianceReceiveAllGiftMessage.lua`) pins the mapping exactly: `type == 1` shows locale key `alliance_system025` ("Premium Alliance Gifts"), everything else shows `alliance_system024` ("Regular Alliance Gifts"), so `type=1` is Premium, `type=2` is Regular. Only Regular was actually packet-captured live (the tips banner afterward read "2 Regular Alliance Gifts were claimed," confirming `type=2`); `type=1` for Premium is included on the strength of that same code branch, not independently packet-captured. Replaying both through this Go client got real, well-formed responses for each: `{type=1, receiveResult=0}` and `{type=2, receiveResult=0}`, `receiveResult=0` means nothing was pending at test time (the account had just been cleared manually moments before), not an error.

Wired into the Go client as `HelpAllianceMembers` and `ClaimAllianceGifts` (`alliance.go`), both called automatically on every `-collect` run.

## Alliance tech donation: bulk tree discovery, then one targeted donate

<Check>
  **Confirmed live**, end to end, through this Go client. Unlike help-all and gift claiming above, this isn't a single blanket "do everything" call, donating requires first discovering which one tech (out of dozens) is currently marked "Recommended" by the alliance, then targeting that specific `scienceId`. Both steps are confirmed with real evidence, not just static analysis.
</Check>

**Discovery** uses `science.data.refresh`, no parameters at all, which returns the account's *entire* alliance tech tree in one response: every `scienceId` with its `currentPro`/`needPro` donation progress and a `state` field. A live call returned ~45 entries; exactly one had `state=1`, every other had `state=0`. That one entry's progress, `currentPro=4951850`/`needPro=8000000`, matched the "4.9M/8.0M" bar shown under the thumbs-up-badged "Senior Scientist" tech in the real game UI at essentially the same moment, confirming `state=1` is the recommended-tech flag. (`al.science.recommend {scienceId, state}` is the real client's own way of *setting* this, an alliance-officer action, matching the "Cancel Recommend" button seen in the UI, but nothing here ever calls it; this only reads the current value.)

**Donation** is `al.science.donate {scienceId, option: 1}`, confirmed via a real packet capture of the actual game client tapping the free (coin-cost) donate button. `option`'s exact range of valid values wasn't determined (only `1` was ever observed, for a successful donation), so `1` is reused as-is rather than guessed at.

**"Holding the donate button longer adds a multiplier in the UI"** turned out to be pure client-side behavior, not a server feature. Reading both donate messages' request-construction Lua directly (`extracted/lua_decompiled/4380_Net_Msgs_Alliance_AlScienceDonateMessage.lua` and `..._AlScienceGoldDonateMessage.lua`), neither has a count/times/multiplier field on the wire. Holding the button just fires the same single-donation request repeatedly while held; the "multiplier" is a running visual counter on the client, not a batched call. That distinction matters because the free donate path is real-rate-limited server-side: `al.science.refreshNum` (also confirmed live) returned `maxNum=30` (donations per day), the size of a pool of donation charges: `useNum` is the number left, and one charge refills every `refreshTimeBlock` (`1200000` ms, 20 minutes). A real `errorCode=120471` response was first read as a per-donation cooldown, but the 1.0.364 Lua shows it means the charges are used up (see the note below), which also explains why two live `-collect` runs roughly 3 minutes apart both donated successfully. The gem-cost "Unlimited Attempts" path (`al.science.donate.gold {scienceId}`, no `option` field) has no such cooldown, `useGoldNum`/`maxGoldNum` both came back as `999999999`, but spends real premium currency per use, so it's deliberately not wired into automatic collection.

Live-tested through this Go client end to end: `science.data.refresh` correctly found `scienceId=10011900` as the recommended tech, and `al.science.donate` against it returned a real, well-formed response, `errorCode=120471, "Donate science CD time is not finish"`, the expected cooldown error, since the real account had just donated minutes earlier in the same capture. That confirms the full discovery-then-donate path end to end, even though this particular attempt was correctly blocked by a real, working rate limit rather than a client bug.

<Info>
  **1.0.364 Lua: `120471` is a donation-charge limit, not a per-donation cooldown (static-analysis-only).** The locale text for `120471` is "Donation Count has reached its limit, please wait." The free donate path holds regenerating charges: `useNum` of `maxNum`, refilled every `refreshTimeBlock` ms, with the next refill at `timePoint`. The real client reads `useNum` from `al.science.refreshNum {scienceId}`, sent right after `science.data.refresh` with the first `scienceId`, or from the `al.science.donate` response. It shows `120471` itself when `useNum <= 0`, without sending a donation. That fits the two runs 3 minutes apart that both donated: each spent a charge. The live `errorMsg` string ("Donate science CD time is not finish") differs from the locale text; both are facts about the same code.
</Info>

Wired into the Go client as `DonateRecommendedAllianceTech` (`alliance.go`), called automatically on every `-collect` run, one free donation attempt toward whatever the alliance currently has recommended, treating `120471` as a benign "no charge left" answer.

## Mail: claimable, but scoped per category with string-GUID uids

<Check>
  **Confirmed live**, via a real packet capture of the actual game client tapping "Claim All" across several mailbox category tabs (Alliance, Event, Season). Two things this contradicted from a naive read of the command catalog: mail uids are **string GUIDs** (e.g. `1f9f236259ff4ae285bf5b20bdac2586`), unlike every other uuid this project deals with (buildings, visitors, all int64s); and claiming is scoped **per category** (`type`), not global, the real client sent one `mail.reward.batch` call per tab, each with only that tab's mail uids and that tab's `type` (observed live: `3`, `4`, and `9` for three different tabs; the 1.0.364 Lua later identified these as mail group ids, see the note below).
</Check>

Discovery uses `chat.get.system.mails`, paginated via the response's `more`/`lastUid`/`lastMailTime` fields, following the real client's own request shape (`extracted/lua_decompiled/5018_Net_Msgs_Mail_MailGetMutiMessage.lua`: `clientseq`, `time`, `count`, `firstCmd`, `isAll`). One real gap: the captured request already had a non-empty `clientseq`/`time` matching a specific already-known mail uid, because the real client was mid-session with a warm local mail cache built from a long history of `push.mail` notifications, the true cold-start values were never directly observed. This Go client sends `time: 0`, `clientseq: ""` on its first call (still with `firstCmd: "YES"`, exactly as captured), on the theory that's the correct "give me everything" cold-start shape. That theory held up well in testing: a fresh call returned **326 real mailbox entries** across multiple paginated pages, not just a handful, but whether that's genuinely the account's full history or just a large recent window hasn't been independently verified against the real client.

Each mail object reports `uid`, `type`, and `rewardStatus`; `rewardStatus == 0` is read as "has an unclaimed reward," matched by direct observation (the one fresh mail seen in a `push.chat.get.system.mails` push had `rewardStatus=0` and real embedded reward data, and had not yet been claimed by the user's actions in that capture).

<Warning>
  **Bug, found and fixed: marking mail as read and claiming its reward are two genuinely independent actions, not one paired step.** An earlier version of `ClaimAllMail` only sent `mail.read.status.betch` for mail that *also* had an unclaimed reward, silently never touching notification-only mail (alliance markers, battle reports, and similar) that never carries a reward at all. In practice this meant those mail categories' unread badges never cleared, no matter how many times `-collect` ran, since the function never sent a read-status call for them.

  A follow-up live capture caught the real client doing exactly the opposite: tapping "Claim All" on a Regular-category tab (all battle reports, no gift icons visible in the UI) sent `mail.read.status.betch` for all 21 visible mail uids, but **no** matching `mail.reward.batch` call at all. Reading `Net.Msgs.Mail.MailReadStatusBatchMessage`'s own request-construction Lua confirms why this split is safe: the wire request needs only `uids`, no `type` at all, unlike the reward claim below, marking mail as read isn't scoped by category, so every discovered mail can be marked read in one pass regardless of type. `ClaimAllMail` now does exactly that: marks every mail returned by `ListMail` as read (batched, 100 uids per call), independent of reward status, then separately groups only the reward-bearing mail by `type` and claims it the same way as before.
</Warning>

Claiming a reward sends `mail.reward.batch {uids, type}` per category, grouped by whatever `type` each reward-bearing mail object reports.

<Info>
  **The 1.0.364 Lua sends a different `type` than `goclient` does, and the server accepts `goclient`'s shape.** Static-analysis-only: the real client's `MailRewardBatchMessage` sends `type` as a **UtfString** holding an internal mail *group* id, not the mail's own raw `type`: `2` report, `3` alliance, `4` activity, `5` system, `6` daily, `7` charge, `8` favor (also any mail with `saveFlag==1`), `9` season. Mail whose raw type has no group id never gets claimed in bulk. The `3`, `4`, and `9` in the original capture are exactly the alliance, activity, and season group ids. `goclient` sends `type` as an **Int** holding the raw mail type. Confirmed live: with that shape, `mail.reward.batch` returns `{success=true}` and each unclaimed mail disappears from the inbox after one run. Which of the two values the server actually reads is unknown.
</Info>

Wired into the Go client as `ClaimAllMail` (`mail.go`), called automatically on every `-collect` run. Live-tested end to end after the fix: a full mailbox of 350 real entries, correctly paginated across 4 pages, all successfully marked read in one run. The reward claim has since run against real unclaimed rewards too: `mail.reward.batch` returns `{success=true}`, and each unclaimed mail is gone after one run.

## Alliance Duel and duel spend commands

<Check>
  **Confirmed live on 2026-10-06** (a Tuesday, Base Expansion), through `goclient`'s `-run` path against the real account. Field names and shapes only; values that identify the account are left out. The protocol background is on [Alliance Duel](/alliance-duel).
</Check>

### Duel detection: `activityid`, not `id`

The first live run of the duel scheduler reported "no duel day running" on a duel day. Two things were wrong, and both were only visible live:

- **The detail read asked for the wrong id.** The duel's `init` entry is `{id: 55000, activityid: "70000", name, startTime, endTime, readyTime, matchGroupId, uuid}`. The client sends `activityid` when an entry has one (`ActivityInfoData.lua:126-128, 160-161`). `hero.event.info.get {activityId: "55000"}` got a bare `{success=true}` and nothing else, even with the session held open for another 10 seconds. `{activityId: "70000"}` got the full reply: `{activityId, type: 15, ranking, isFix, eventList}`.
- **The day window is `st`/`et`.** The live `eventList` entry has no `begintime`/`endtime`, the fields the client's `ActivityEventInfo:ParseData` reads first.

After both fixes, the status line read the right theme (`110001`), the eight scoring ids, all nine chest thresholds, and a day end of 02:00 UTC. `-run radar-claims` was then refused with "today's duel theme (Base Expansion) doesn't score it". The arms-race duel-chest claim had used the same read, so it had never seen duel data either.

### `build.ccd.m.new`, items only

```text
request: build.ccd.m.new {bUUID: Long, isFixRuins: false, itemIDs: "200211;25"}
reply:   {remainGold, finished: false, isFixRuins: false,
          itemCostArr: [{itemId: 200211, costNum: 25, count: 0}],
          buildInfo: {uuid, bId, lv, state, sT, uT, qS, pEndT, hp, pId, help, gValT, lCT, lStaT, AssignedHero[]}}
```

- **Diamonds:** `remainGold` equaled the balance from `init` `user.gold`.
- **Items:** `itemCostArr` lists each item spent: `costNum` is how many were used, `count` how many remain.
- **Timer:** `buildInfo.uT` came back earlier by the item time.
- **Duel score:** read again on a fresh login, it rose by 150 per item-minute. That's the score row's 50 multiplied by the account's duel effects, matching the client's `units × points × (1 + Σ effects)`.

`queue.ccd.m.new` and `building.camp.accel` are static-analysis-only so far.

### Radar: Help Teammates, executed and left unclaimed

```text
get.detect.info {openWnd: false}
  → {worldMainPoint, detectInfo: {level, eventNum, nextRefreshTime, specialOpsNum, recoverTime, type2Data, …},
     events: [{uuid, eventId, type, state, cost, num, pointId, startTime, endTime, reward, helpInfo, …}]}
detect.event.help.start {uuid, eventType: 18}   → {uuid}
detect.event.help.end   {uuid, eventType: 18}   → {success=true}
```

- Each event's `type` matched the `detect_event` table's type for its `eventId`, for every listed task.
- After `help.end`, three Help Teammates tasks were listed in state `1` (finished), each with `cost` now `1`.
- Stamina fell by 10 per task, read from `init` `playerInfo.stamina` on the next login.
- No `receive.detect.event.reward` was sent.
- `detectInfo.eventNum` is the stock and `nextRefreshTime` the next refresh, in ms. The next refresh time moved by about 50 minutes between two reads 8 minutes apart, with the help tasks run in between, so it isn't a fixed wall-clock schedule.

### Other reply shapes seen

- **`lottery.hero.card`** with `useFree: 1` replied `{id, isTen, totalLottery, lotteryHero: [{id, num, type}], dailyFree, dailyFreeLimit, dailyFreeNextFreshTime, pityType, pityCurProtectNum, pityProProtectNum, pityMaxProtectNum, pityProType, pityProNum, wishPityCurNum, …}` and no itemised `reward`.
- **`worker.lottery.info {officerId}`** returns `nextFreeTime` in ms.
- **`al.science.donate`** replies `{scienceId, useNum, maxNum, refreshTimeBlock, donateAvailable, dp, point, para1, para2, gold, allianceId, maxdonate: {count}, options: {…}}`. It carries the diamond balance as `gold`.
- **`al.science.refreshNum`** replies `{scienceId, useNum, maxNum, useGoldNum, maxGoldNum, goldNum, timePoint, refreshTimeBlock}`.
- **`hero.dispatch.list`** replies `{todayAssistNum, todayStealNum, ls: [{uuid, heroList, completionTime, actEndTime, ownerId, allianceId, conditionIndex, followCount, stealInfoList, …}]}`, with **no** `gold` field. A diamond check after a dispatch can't read the balance from it.

Static-analysis-only, from the `goods` table and DataConfig:

## Firework chests and world tiles over SFS2X

Firework chests normally reach the client as alliance-chat posts 693 and 695 on the separate chat WebSocket. On 2026-10-06 the real account confirmed a game-socket path that needs no chat:

- `get.fireworks.info.list` with no params replies `errorCode=firework_tips_1013` ("Target player is in a different Warzone"). It looks up one player's firework shows; it isn't a chest list.
- `al.rank {allianceId: Utf}` lists the alliance's members. Each `list[]` entry carries `uid`, `pointId`, `serverId`, `curServerId`, `online`, `offLineTime`, `mainCityLv` and `rank`, among others.
- `get.al.points {serverId}` replied normally when `serverId` was sent as an SFS2X Long, although the client declares it Int. The server coerced the type here; don't assume it does everywhere.
- `world.get.block` is sent with the client's typing (`WorldGetBlockMessage`): Int scalars `bigMap`, `x`, `y`, `serverId`, `worldId`, `type`, `viewLvl`, `timeStamp`, `blockSize`, `leftBottom`, `rightTop`; an IntArray `index` of block ids, `(y/10)*100 + x/10` on the 1000×1000 map; and `clearUuidSet` on the first request only. One request covered every member HQ (70 points). Each point's protobuf `WorldPointInfo` decoded, with the HQ's `BuildInfo` carrying the owner uid. **The server answers tile reads from a session that never entered the world scene.**
- Confirmed live: none yet. The chest list itself is `BuildInfo` field 54 (`fireWorksGiftList {uuid, configId, sendTime, num, max, index}`, tag bytes `B2 03`). No chest was live during the test, so field 54 is static-analysis-only so far.
- Static-analysis-only: the claim is `get.fireworks.gift {uuid: Long, ownerUid: Utf, type: Int}`, where `type` is 1 for firework configs 671001-671005 and 0 otherwise. The error codes are `firework_tips_1009` (daily cap), `1014` (expired), `1015` (full), `1016` (already claimed) and `1017` (too fast).

### Allies' dug radar treasures

The alliance channel's "{owner}'s treasure at (x, y) has been dug up!" (post 600) also reaches the client only over the chat WebSocket, but the treasure itself is an ordinary world point. Everything here is static-analysis-only:

- The point is a `WorldPointInfo` of `pointType` 21 carrying `TreasurePointInfo` (field 11): `uuid`, `ownerUid`, `eventId` (a string), `completionTime`, `allianceId`, `rewardUserList` (the claimers), `complete`, `expireTime`, `type` (1 radar, 3 activity radar, 11 off-season) and `multiple`.
- The server places a radar task near its owner's HQ, at a distance nothing in the client states. `alliance-treasures-plan` reads every block within 3 blocks of each member HQ's block (at least 30 tiles each way) and logs each treasure's distance from its owner's HQ.
- The claim is `detect.event.claim.treasure {uuid: Long, targetServer: Int}`, the point's own uuid and serverId. It is free and needs no march. A treasure takes `detect_event.para2`'s cap × `multiple` claimers: 20 for radar treasures 25001-25198, 10 for 1025001-1025168.
- `801348` ("Already taken. One reward per player.") and `activity_wajueji_27000_tips13` (expired) are taken as benign. The daily cap's code is unknown, so any other error stops the run.

## Dig mini-games: what the live account showed

All of these are confirmed live, read-only, on 2026-10-06:

- `get.detect.info` and init carry no radar-ruin or city-ruin dig board when none is active.
- `hero.dispatch.treasure.v2.get.info {}` replies `rewardList[{isReward, rewardInfo[], target, quality}]` and a score.
- `alliance.boss.act.info {serverId}` replies `digGameInfo {uid, mapConfigId, rewardState, endTime, uuid}` alongside the drill data. `rewardState=2` means that vault is finished.

Static-analysis-only: the free hammer for a radar-ruin or city-ruin board (`detect.event.dig.game.receive.hammer {eventUuid}`, `building.dig.game.receive.hammer {buildingUuid}`) is offered while the board's `rewardState` is 4 (NotBegin). The dispatch dig's `isHammerGetMax` is the daily cap on hammers received from allies, not this gate (`DigTreasureManager.lua:244-249`).

## Root cause: packet-decode bugs, not protocol or anti-fraud gates

Both of the "blocked" results elsewhere in this section trace back to the same live packet capture, even though they turned out to be mechanically distinct bugs. The capture: `tcpdump` against the locally installed `/Applications/Last War.app` (the real iOS / Mac Catalyst build) while manually logging into the same real account through the actual app UI. Since the SFS2X game socket is plain TCP with no TLS, this recorded cleartext-after-XOR application data directly, no TLS interception needed. The same `packet.go`/`sfsobject.go` the Go client already used decoded the capture directly, see [Capturing and decoding traffic](/capturing-and-decoding-traffic) for the full reproducible pipeline.

Decoding that one real session did two things at once: it surfaced the real `Login` request's exact field values, byte-diffed against the Go client's own encoding (which is what led directly to the identity-mismatch fixes above), and it handed the decoder a real ~313KB Zstd-compressed `init` payload to chew on, which is what exposed both the missing Zstd path in `packet.go` and two SFSObject array-decode bugs in `sfsobject.go`. None of the small packets decoded earlier in this research happened to exercise those code paths, so both bugs sat latent until something this size and this well-populated came through.

`packet.go`'s `ReadPacket` had always correctly detected the compressed frames (header bits `0x20` + `0x10`, the `useLZ4` flag repurposed as "useZstd") but simply errored instead of decompressing, never implemented. Every read loop waiting on `init` silently treated that error as connection-closed. The fix: a real Zstd decoder (`github.com/klauspost/compress/zstd`, a shared lazily-initialized `zstd.Decoder`, `DecodeAll`).

Getting that decompressed payload to parse correctly then surfaced two bugs in `sfsobject.go`'s array-tag decode switch. **(a)** `LONG_ARRAY` (tag 13), `FLOAT_ARRAY` (tag 14), `DOUBLE_ARRAY` (tag 15), `BOOL_ARRAY` (tag 9), and `SHORT_ARRAY` (tag 11) weren't implemented at all, only `BYTE_ARRAY`/`INT_ARRAY`/`UTF_STRING_ARRAY` existed, because those were the only array types any previously-decoded (small) packet ever happened to contain. Fixed by implementing all five against the decompiled Unity SDK's `BinDecode_BOOL_ARRAY`/`SHORT_ARRAY`/`LONG_ARRAY`/`FLOAT_ARRAY`/`DOUBLE_ARRAY` functions, each a 2-byte (`i16`) count plus N big-endian elements, via a shared `GetTypedArraySize` helper. **(b)** `BYTE_ARRAY` (tag 10) specifically had a real length-prefix bug: it read the same 2-byte count as every other array type, but the real Unity SDK's `BinDecode_BYTE_ARRAY` doesn't go through `GetTypedArraySize` at all, it calls a bare 4-byte (`i32`) `ReadInt` instead. That's a genuine SFS2X wire-format asymmetry, not an implementation guess, confirmed by reading the decompiled function directly. It silently corrupted decoding partway through any packet containing a real byte-array value, which, like the missing array types, never happened to matter until this payload.

<Check>
  **Net effect.** Once both fixes landed, `init` arrived cleanly on the *first* login attempt in every post-fix login tested, no reconnect loop, no extended timeout, and no active-pull fallback ever needed to actually fire. Of the two mechanisms built earlier in this investigation to chase the missing-`init` symptom, only the three-attempt reconnect-on-timeout loop was solving the wrong problem, and only that loop has been removed (max login attempts reduced back to 1), especially since repeated reconnect attempts against a stale or identity-mismatched token were themselves tripping `E005`/`E011`, meaning even "reconnect gets blocked after one attempt" was downstream of the same identity-mismatch root cause above, not a separate rate-limit or session-lock mechanism. The halfway active-pull `login.init` send inside `waitForInitPush` is a separate, still-live mechanism, a real, currently-registered active-pull command sent partway through the wait window as a fallback in case the push itself never arrives (report 15's `init_push_missing_after_login` finding #2), and was deliberately kept in place, unconditionally, not reverted: it's still the correct behavior for a genuinely silent server, even though this particular investigation's root cause turned out to be the Zstd bug above rather than a missing push. No rate-limiting, no session-lock, no already-connected gate was ever found to exist anywhere in this path.
</Check>

**What's still open (narrowed, the big one is now closed):** the placeholder-`ta` question is no longer open. Reconnect is **confirmed working against the shipped code**: an unattended cron running this from-scratch Go client reconnected into the established account and collected real resources over multiple days (August 2026), re-verified after a live zone-server migration, all with `identity.go`'s `BuildLoginParams` (`IOSMode` branch) sending `ta`'s `LwDeviceID`/`LwShumeiID`/`LwAirKey` sub-fields as the empty placeholders a security audit put in (they had leaked the same live `DeviceID`/`ShumeiBoxId`/`AirKey` secrets in cleartext inside an opaque JSON string that `StringRedacted()`'s key-based masking couldn't see into). So the server does **not** require `ta`'s real device sub-fields for reconnect. What genuinely remains: **(1)** the `ta` blob's exact *minimal* required content still isn't isolated, the client sends a `ta` object with those three sub-fields blank but others populated, and which of the rest actually matter (a zone/`deviceId` echo, a game-session id, ...) vs. which are ignored was never pinned down; a fresh capture still needs its own fresh `ta` regardless, since it carries session-specific fields. **(2)** This was first proven via the captured-access-token path. A fully from-scratch login using iOS identity mode from the very first GSL call (no captured token) hasn't been tried. The *Android*-issued-token mirror case has: on 2026-10-04 a Go-generated device bound by email verification got its own token pair from GSL, and on 2026-10-13 that pair logged in once Android `ta` was filled (see the updates under the reconnect wall above). **(3)** The captured game-server address drifts on every zone/server migration (the port moved `17783` → `10783` in August 2026, silently breaking the cron with a login that connects but never gets a response, until the address was recaptured). The session config's `ip` now holds the zone's whole `|`-delimited gateway list, which `-session-out` fills from every gateway that answered the real client's probe, so one dead gateway no longer breaks a run. `ip` and `port` are now optional: when they are missing, or when every gateway refuses the connection or the `Login` goes unanswered, `goclient` looks the role's server up with GSL `getserverlist` (no `opt` field, `platform=iOS` for an iOS session), retries there, and saves the new address. Confirmed live on 2026-10-10: the lookup returned the role's server with no tokens, and both a config with no address and one with the pre-August port `17783` logged in through it. GSL rejected `opt=fix` for the same session with code `212`. See [Looking up the game server](/auth#looking-up-the-game-server). **(4)** The access token itself can be invalidated server-side, as on 2026-08-16 and 2026-10-02. `goclient` keeps no refresh token, so each time the fix is a fresh capture; see "The 2026-10-02 token rotation" above.
