`docs/lua-architecture.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Lua scripting architecture"
description: "How the C# hot-update tier hands off to xLua, the module tree, boot sequence, require() resolution, and the BaseClass OOP convention used across the codebase."
---

Once the C# tier finishes booting, it spins up xLua and mostly gets out of the way, keeping only the transport, the login plumbing, and the world-map viewport protocol. Nearly everything a player experiences, city, army, hero, world map, chat, and all 3,115 commands in the Lua catalog, is Lua. The exceptions are the 54 commands only C# handles, see [Dispatch order](#dispatch-order).

## Module tree

Counts are from a walk of the 1.0.364 `LWLF` bundle (version 825, 18,733 modules); the rest sit in `Common/`, `Global/`, `Util/`, `RedPoint/`, and a few smaller trees.

| Directory | Files | Purpose |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `UI/` | 11,709 | Per-screen UI logic, the largest tree by far |
| `Net/` | 3,117 | Networking: dispatch core + 3,104 command (`Message`) classes |
| `DataCenter/` | 2,483 | Client-side state managers, the "model" layer, 833 lazy-singleton manager names in the registry |
| `Scene/` | 951 | In-world/3D scene & rendering glue |
| `Chat/` | 172 | The dedicated chat subsystem (see [Alliance, chat & mail](/alliance-chat-mail)) |
| `Framework/` | 113 | The actual engine: base classes, event system, logger, loaded first |

An earlier version of this table, built from the 1.0.351 manifest, undercounted `UI/`, `Net/`, and `DataCenter/` because of a path-truncation artifact.

## Boot sequence

```text
XLuaManager.Initialize()
  → new LuaEnv(); AddLoader(CustomLoader)     // the one game-specific require() hook
  → require("Common.Main")                     // table/string/bit/Unity-math utils
  → require("Framework.FrameworkMain")          // BaseClass OOP, DataCenter service locator, event system
GameEntry.Lua.StartGame()
  → require("GameMain"); GameMain.Start()
      LuaEntry:init()                           // player/session state root
      PBController.InitPBConfig()               // no-op in this build (misleadingly named, real proto loading is PBController.InitBytes/LoadBytes)
      ~90 × DataCenter.<Manager>:Startup()      // one per gameplay system
```

## `require()` resolution: how a module path finds its bytes

A single custom loader, layered under stock xLua's searcher chain, resolves `"DataCenter.Global.LuaEntry"` in order: a dev-only local override → a table-config ZIP lookup (if the path contains `LuaDatatable`) → raw disk read in the Unity Editor → **the `LWLF` bundle** (production path, confirms and refines [Extraction methodology](/methodology)'s reverse-engineered format exactly) → a TextAsset fallback.

## The `BaseClass(...)` OOP pattern

Every Lua file in the codebase uses one convention: prototype-chain classes over plain tables, via `OptClass.Declare` (a from-scratch, self-optimizing class system, not stock Lua OOP). Constructors chain automatically root-to-leaf; a computed-property ("getter") mechanism only attaches its extra metatable indirection to classes that actually define getters.

```lua
local MailGetMessage = BaseClass("MailGetMessage", SFSBaseMessage)
local base = SFSBaseMessage
local OnCreate = function(self, mailId, mailType, senderUid)
  base.OnCreate(self)                              -- explicit super-call convention
  self.sfsObj:PutUtfString("uid", mailId)
  ...
end
MailGetMessage.OnCreate = OnCreate
return MailGetMessage
```

## Relationship to the C# hot-update layer

Four independently-versioned payloads, confirmed by reading the version-check parser directly: asset bundles, the C# `.mdl` assemblies (through the `dllres` manifest), the Lua bundle, and the data tables each carry their own version field and can update independently (see [Startup, version-check & hot-update](/bootstrap)). They are *not* fully independent, though; the Lua bootstrap itself (`XLuaManager`, the custom loader) lives inside the hot-update C# tier, so a broken C# release could in principle break the Lua loader before any Lua code runs.

## Dispatch order

Every incoming extension response goes to C# first (1.0.364 C# `MessageFactory.DispatchResponse`; static-analysis-only):

- C# `MessageFactory` handles 71 wire names itself. Everything else becomes a Lua table and goes through `GameMain.Protocal`, then `SFSNetwork.HandleMessage`, then the handler that `MsgMap[wire]` names. A reply with no `MsgMap` handler falls through to the chat manager.
- 18 of the 71 are also in the Lua catalog, and for those **C# wins**: the Lua `HandleMessage` never runs. Lua still builds some of the requests, among them `world.march.formation.new`, `world.march.change`, `world.march.speed.up`, `train.send`, and `train.batch.send`.
- 54 commands exist only in C# (53 of the 71, plus `world.get.cross`) and are missing from any Lua-derived catalog. They include `login.ext`, `check.device.change`, `change.user.parseid`, `init.error`, the world-map viewport pulls (`world.get.block`, `world.get.new`, `world.get.cross`), `push.world.march.new` / `.del`, and `push.user.off`.
- Lua-originated and C#-native requests share one `_id` counter, which resets on reconnect.
- There's no protocol-level request timeout or retry: `FutureManager.update()` is a no-op. Each feature handles a missing reply on its own.
- Duplicate wire names resolve to one class for both directions: `SFSNetwork.GetMsgType` uses `MsgMap[wire]` for sending and receiving.

## At-rest Lua obfuscation ("SuperEncrypt")

Besides the non-standard header that [Extraction methodology](/methodology) describes, `BaseUtils`' `EncryptUtils` has an at-rest obfuscation for individual Lua chunks (static-analysis-only):

- An encrypted chunk starts with `0B 45 4E 43`, and the rest of the 32-byte Lua 5.3 header is replaced by `S` bytes.
- The source-name string is XORed with a 32-byte key derived through ChaCha.
- The body is XORed with a ChaCha8 keystream, and the `_ENV` tail is masked.

The keys come from the same dummy-constant derivation as the file wrappers on [Startup, version-check & hot-update](/bootstrap).

## Hot-patching C# from Lua

Lua can rewrite the C# layer, not only itself (static-analysis-only):

- `CommonUtils.Lua_File_Write` gives Lua arbitrary file IO inside the app sandbox, including `persistentDataPath/Assemblies/*.mdl`, which FM_Mono loads on the next start. A Lua hot update could therefore ship a replacement C# assembly. No use of this path was found in 1.0.364.
- xLua's `[Hotfix]` IL injection isn't active in 1.0.364. The attribute appears on some C# message classes, but `HotfixDelegateBridge` is never called, so those classes can't be patched that way.
- `DevPatchRuntime` is unused developer tooling.

```

`docs/methodology.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Extraction methodology"
description: "How three custom, undocumented file formats were reverse-engineered from first principles to recover readable Lua and C# source from the APK."
---

Three custom, undocumented formats stood between "an `.xapk` file" and readable source. All three were cracked from first principles, without any prior tooling built for this game.

### 1: Hot-update assembly de-obfuscation

The hot-update C# assemblies ship as `assets/Assemblies/*.mdl`, renamed, single-byte-XOR-obfuscated `.dll` files. At runtime they're loaded by FunPlus's FM_Mono bridge (upstream Mono 6.13.0 behind the il2cpp ABI in `libil2cpp.so`), not by HybridCLR as earlier versions of these docs said; no `hybridclr` or `huatuo` symbol or string exists in any shipped native library (static-analysis-only, see [Native binaries & security](/native-binaries)). The header is deliberately corrupted just enough to defeat naive static scanners:

```python
key = raw_bytes[3]          # the XOR key is stored in the file itself
n   = key                    # and doubles as the run length
for i in range(n):
    raw_bytes[i] ^= key       # XOR only the first `key` bytes, the rest is untouched
```

In the 1.0.351 pass, all 117 files decoded cleanly to valid PE/.NET assemblies on the first try; 9 of the most relevant (`Assembly-CSharp.dll`, `SmartFox2X.dll`, `BestHttp.dll`, and friends) were decompiled to C# with [ILSpy](https://github.com/icsharpcode/ILSpy).

### 2: The `LWLF` Lua bundle container

The 105 MB `assets/lwScripts/LWScripts.data` is a custom archive bundling every compiled Lua module (18,514 in 1.0.351, 18,733 in 1.0.364). Format, reverse-engineered by scanning for Lua's bytecode signature and reading backward:

```text
LWLF magic (4B) | fileVersion (u32) | version (u32) | entry_count (u32)
per entry:
  name       .NET BinaryReader 7-bit-length-prefixed string
  byte_len   u32
  data       byte_len raw bytes (Lua 5.3 bytecode, itself self-delimiting)
```

(Later corroborated exactly against the C# reader, `LWLuaFile._Load`, see [Lua architecture](/lua-architecture).)

### 3: A deliberately non-standard Lua 5.3 bytecode header

Every compiled chunk sets the Lua chunk header's `format` byte to `1` instead of the standard `0`, and, the actual obfuscation, **omits the 1-byte "instruction size" field** that stock Lua 5.3 headers always include. Every other header field (int/size_t/integer/float sizes, the `LUAC_INT`/`LUAC_NUM` sanity values) is stock. This is enough to make every off-the-shelf Lua decompiler reject the file outright.

<Info>
  **Fix**: A two-line patch to [unluac](https://github.com/HansWessels/unluac)'s `LHeaderType.java`, accept `format == 1`, and skip the instruction-size read when it's set, was enough to decompile all 18,514 chunks of the 1.0.351 bundle with a stock unluac release otherwise unmodified. Instruction encoding itself is completely standard Lua 5.1+, so nothing past the header needed touching.
</Info>

Once patched, this recovered readable Lua source for all 2,855 `Net/`+`Common/` modules of 1.0.351 (all 2,777 network command classes, the dispatch core, and the protobuf schemas) and all 1,279 of its game-data tables, the entire raw material for everything documented below.

### 4: Game data tables

`assets/table/table_*.data` is, despite the odd filename, a plain ZIP archive (magic `PK\x03\x04`): 1,279 entries in 1.0.351 and 1,291 in 1.0.364, each itself Lua 5.3 bytecode encoding a data-only module (building costs, hero stats, activity config, etc). No new format needed; unluac with the same header patch handled these too.

The sizes and counts below are from the 1.0.351 pass; the next section has the 1.0.364 numbers.

| Artifact | Raw size | Decoded to |
|---|---|---|
| `assets/Assemblies/*.mdl` ×117 | ~42.7 MB | Valid .NET assemblies, 9 decompiled to C# |
| `assets/lwScripts/LWScripts.data` | 105 MB | 18,514 raw `.luac` chunks; 2,855 decompiled (Net/Common) |
| `assets/table/table_*.data` | 18.6 MB | 1,279 decompiled Lua data tables |
| base APK Java/Kotlin (dex) | ~42.3 MB | 16,867 files via jadx |
| native libs, `lib/arm64-v8a/` | 7 relevant of 23 | Symbol/string survey only, no disassembly |

### Re-running the pipeline on 1.0.364

The same three techniques worked unchanged on 1.0.364 (versionCode 1892, posted 2026-09-23). All 118 `.mdl` files decoded with the same single-byte XOR scheme, and the patched unluac decompiled every one of the 18,733 chunks in the `LWLF` bundle (version 825, tag `20260921_1892_App`) and all 1,291 data tables with zero failures. Of the 118 assemblies, the `dllres` hot-update manifest lists remote replacements for 117 (`mscorlib` has no entry), and `noUpdateAssemblies.json` (`[{"name":"SmartFox2X"}]`) pins SmartFox2X to the APK copy. The 1.0.364 pass also decompiled all 118 assemblies with ILSpy, not just 9, see [Findings & further work](/findings) for the full coverage method. The signing certificate is byte-identical to 1.0.351's. Older Lua bundles stay hosted on the CDN, which is how the 1.0.351 baseline (`LWLF` 793, 18,514 chunks) was recovered for an exact diff, see [Startup, version-check & hot-update](/bootstrap).

```

`docs/military-battle.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Military, hero & battle"
description: "Combat resolution is server-authoritative for marches, arena, and world combat, while about 20 PVE and mini-game commands self-report their outcome; recovered BattleReport/LwBattleReport proto schemas and the core army/hero/formation commands."
---

Combat resolution is server-authoritative for marches, the arena, and world combat: the client sends only identity references (hero uuids, formation ids), never stats or an outcome, and the server ships back a full protobuf-encoded action-by-action combat log. The exceptions are the PVE stages and mini-game modes, where about 20 commands report a client-computed result.

## Server authority: proven

```lua
-- StartArenaBattleMessage.OnCreate, the entire request:
self.sfsObj:PutUtfString("target", target)
self.sfsObj:PutInt("type", type)
self.sfsObj:PutLong("power", power)        -- client's own number, display only
self.sfsObj:PutSFSArray("heroes", heroesArray)  -- {index, uuid}, IDENTITY ONLY, no stats
```

The client cannot send hero level, rank, skill, or equipment, only uuids the server already has authoritative records for. The response contains a full protobuf combat log; the server decides win/loss, damage, and rewards.

<Warning>
**About 20 exceptions, not one**: The scripted "story stage" PVE minigame (`Net.Msgs.Battle.*`) renders a real-time 3D scene locally and then **self-reports the outcome**: `lw.save.pve.record` sends `isWin` directly, `user.finish.pve.level` sends `isSuccess` directly, and no server-computed combat log accompanies either. The 1.0.364 Lua has about 20 commands of this kind across the PVE and mini-game modes (static-analysis-only), among them `lw.save.sky.battle.stage`, `lw.save.plane.stage`, `lw.save.pve.feature`, `lw.save.towerup.record`, `lw.save.count.record`, `lw.save.monopoly.record`, `end.detect.event.pve`, `parkour.fight.end`, `ghost.parkour.fight.end`, `user.finish.pve.trigger`, and `sync.pve.resource`. Surfing and Ghost Parkour also upload frame logs over HTTPS, outside the game socket, and several of these modes have server-side run validation. This is an inventory of the surface only: forging results is cheating and out of scope for this project. If building a server (not just a client), these are the subsystems needing their own out-of-band validation.
</Warning>

## Combat report delivery: two channels

- **Inline** (arena, PVE monster fights): a base64 `battleContent` field on the SFS response itself, chunked into `battleContentArr` if oversized. Decode: base64 → raw protobuf bytes → `protobuf.BattleReport`.
- **Out-of-band** (world combat, city sieges): the response carries only a `uuid`. Fetch separately:

  ```text
  GET https://lastwar-fight-report.akamaized.net/report/{uuid}.bin
  ```

  Check `Content-Encoding: zstd`, BestHTTP doesn't auto-decompress it, the client does it manually. Decode as `protobuf.LwBattleReport` (the richer, per-action-log schema, inferred by naming/structural convention; the exact CDN→proto-type pairing wasn't directly confirmed against a call site).

## `BattleReport.proto`: recovered in full

```proto
message ArmyUnitInfo { repeated SoldierProto soldiers=1; repeated HeroInfoProto heroes=2; string name=3; ... }
message FightReport {
  int64 uuid=1; ReportPlayerInfo selfInfo=2; ReportPlayerInfo otherInfo=3;
  ArmyResult selfArmyResult=4; ArmyResult otherArmyResult=5; ReportReward reward=6;
  int32 fightResult=7; repeated BattleEffectGroup otherBattleEffectGroups=8;
}
message BattleReport {
  int32 battleResult=1; int64 startTime=2; int32 startRound=3;
  BattlePointInfo battlePointInfo=4; repeated FightReport fightReports=5;
  FightLost fightLost=6; repeated BattleEffectGroup selfBattleEffectGroups=7;
}
```

The newer `LwBattleReport.proto` goes further, a genuine per-skill-cast, per-target action log (`FightAction`/`TargetHit`, with hit/miss/crit/damage/shield deltas), strong independent confirmation the server runs a full deterministic battle simulation (RNG included) purely for client-side replay:

```proto
message TargetHit { int32 index=1; int32 miss=2; int32 crit=3; int32 damage=4; ... }
message FightAction {
  int32 id=1; int32 order=2; int32 time=3; int32 casterIndex=4; int32 phase=5;
  int32 skillId=6; repeated TargetHit targets=7; int32 skillLevel=9; ...
}
message LwBattleReport {
  int64 uuid=1; int32 type=2; int64 battleTime=3; int32 fightResult=5;
  repeated LwBattlePlayerStat player=6; Reward reward=10; LwBattleDetail detail=12; ...
}
```

## Core commands

| cmd | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `army.add` | Add trained soldiers to garrison |
| `save.normal.formation.info` | Save which heroes occupy which squad slot |
| `world.march.formation.new` | Dispatch an army on a march to a target tile |
| `world.march.change` | Redirect an in-flight march |
| `find.resource` | Server-side "find nearest" search, no coordinates sent |
| `find.monster` | Same "find nearest" search, but (unusually for this family) also sends a `pointId` alongside the search criteria |
| `user.arena.fight` / `arena.battle` | Initiate arena combat |
| `hero.exp` / `hero.star.up` / `upgrade.hero.rank` | Hero leveling, star-up, rank-up |

<Note>
**Duplicate-cmd gotcha**: `MsgDefines.HeroRankUpgrade` and `MsgDefines.UpgradeHeroRank` both resolve to the wire string `"upgrade.hero.rank"`, `MsgMap` is a plain table literal, so the **later** assignment in file order silently wins at runtime. `command_catalog.json` preserves both entries since it's a mechanical dump, not a resolved map; when duplicates collide, trust whichever handler class appears last in `MsgMap.lua`. `SFSNetwork.GetMsgType` uses that one class for both sending and receiving, so in 1.0.364 `upgrade.hero.rank` always goes out as `{uuid: Long, exchange: Int}` (static-analysis-only).
</Note>

`docs/native-binaries.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Native binaries & security posture"
description: "Symbol/string survey of the game's native libraries and an assessment of whether anything below the protocol layer blocks a clean-room Go client."
---

Best-effort symbol/string survey of the native libraries. The first pass surveyed the 7 most relevant libraries, plus one targeted ARM64 disassembly of `libxlua.so`'s `CalcChatSign` helper (see the feasibility table below and [Findings & further work](/findings)). The 1.0.364 coverage pass surveyed all 39 libraries across both ABIs by symbols, strings, and P/Invoke maps, with two more targeted arm64 disassemblies. `libsmsdk.so` (ShuMei) is the one library that has since been fully decompiled — its Obfuscator-LLVM string encryption was reversed by emulating the `.datadiv_decode*` init functions, and the resulting device-profile/`deviceprofile` protocol is documented in [ShuMei device fingerprint](/shumei). The question that matters: does anything below the protocol layer block a clean-room Go client? For the one existing account tested against production, the answer is no, see the Warning below for the full scope.

## `libil2cpp.so` is a Mono bridge, not an IL2CPP build

Only 1.8 MB, small for a Unity IL2CPP binary, and for good reason: it contains **zero** strings for `AESHelper`, `NetworkManager`, `SendLuaMessage`, or even generic Unity type names. Assembly-CSharp is never AOT-compiled here at all; everything gameplay-relevant lives in the hot-update `.mdl` tier.

What runs that tier is FunPlus's **FM_Mono** bridge, not HybridCLR as earlier versions of these docs said (static-analysis-only):

- In both ABIs, `libil2cpp.so` exports the `il2cpp_*` ABI plus `FM_Mono::*`, `LoadAssemblyByName`, `AddAssemblySearchPath(…, NativePersistType)`, `SetAssemblyOnlyReadFromPackage`, `LoadAssemblyWithImageBinary`, and `visitNoUpdateAssemblies`.
- It implements them on upstream **Mono 6.13.0** (`libmonoboehm-2.0`, the same build in both ABIs). There's no `hybridclr` or `huatuo` symbol or string in any of the 39 libraries.
- The Java launcher `com.rivergame.fm_mono.FMMonoBaseActivity` loads it, and the managed side is `FM_MonoLib.dll`.
- It adds `persistentDataPath/Assemblies/` as a search path for hot-updated `.mdl` files and skips the persistent copy for any name in `noUpdateAssemblies.json`, which lists only `SmartFox2X`.

The `.mdl` XOR scheme itself is unchanged, see [Extraction methodology](/methodology).

## Feasibility table

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th>Mechanism</th>
      <th>Where it enters the wire protocol</th>
      <th>Blocking risk</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>ShuMei device fingerprint (<code>boxId</code>)</td>
      <td><code>login</code> field <code>shumeiBoxId</code></td>
      <td>
        <strong>None identified</strong>, <strong>live-tested (see [Live validation against production](/live-validation)):</strong>
        empty/synthetic values are accepted without issue for a brand-new guest account; reconnecting into an
        <em> established</em> account initially looked ShuMei-gated but turned out to be an unrelated
        <code>packageName</code>/<code>platform</code>/<code>appVersion</code> identity mismatch against the access
        token. Once that was fixed, reconnect worked, and it still works against the shipped code after a later
        security fix replaced part of the request with placeholders. On 2026-10-04 a captured iOS session also
        reconnected with <code>shumeiBoxId</code> sent empty, see [Live validation against production](/live-validation).
        No ShuMei-specific block was ever found. Fully decompiled (Obfuscator-LLVM strings reversed); the device-profile protocol is documented in [ShuMei device fingerprint](/shumei)
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Tencent ACE anti-cheat report</td>
      <td>Not found on the game-server protocol at all, local IPC to Tencent's own backend</td>
      <td><strong>None identified</strong></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><code>SecurityCode</code>/<code>OneCode</code>/<code>CoreV</code></td>
      <td><code>login</code> request, ~3 fields</td>
      <td><strong>None</strong>: plain MD5 with a hardcoded salt, fully reproducible</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><code>packageSign</code> (despite the name, <em>not</em> a cert hash, see [Findings & further work](/findings))</td>
      <td><code>login</code> request</td>
      <td>
        <strong>None</strong>: actually <code>SHA1(packageName)</code>, a constant public string; trivially
        reproducible without touching the APK's real signature. The field that genuinely depends on the signing
        cert is <code>psh</code> (see [Identity, login & session](/auth)), and the Go client reproduces it correctly
        for the Android identity; 1.0.364 is signed with the same certificate, so the value is unchanged. Under iOS
        mode it still sends the Android-derived value. The 2026-10-04 capture of the real iOS app shows its
        <code>psh</code> doesn't match that formula, yet the server accepted the Android-derived value from the
        iOS-mode client for weeks. <code>psh</code> is an app-integrity signature, so the iOS routine is left
        unexamined; reproducing it is out of scope for this project.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><code>libxlua.so</code> <code>CalcChatSign</code>/AES/MD5 helpers</td>
      <td>None in 1.0.364: the native chat branch in <code>ChatNetManager:InitWebSocketInst</code> is unreachable, so chat always uses the C# <code>ChatService</code></td>
      <td>
        <strong>None</strong>, resolved via direct ARM64 disassembly (see [Findings & further work](/findings)):
        plain unkeyed <code>MD5(MD5(appId+uid)+timestamp)</code>, byte-identical to the known C# formula, no custom
        key material. Only the armeabi-v7a <code>libxlua</code> registers <code>rg_websocket</code>; arm64's
        <code>luaopen_native</code> registers only <code>rg_sqlite</code>, <code>rg_async</code>, <code>cutils</code>,
        <code>md5</code>, <code>base64</code>, and <code>crypt</code>, and <code>LuaEntry:__InitCModule()</code>, the
        only code that would expose the native socket, is never called (static-analysis-only)
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>TLS / certificate validation</td>
      <td>All HTTPS traffic</td>
      <td><strong>None</strong>: no pinning evidence found anywhere. Standard chain validation everywhere except the XAssetPro bundle downloader, which disables certificate validation (see [Startup, version-check & hot-update](/bootstrap))</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Google Play Integrity / SafetyNet</td>
      <td>, </td>
      <td><strong>Not used at all</strong> in this build</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<Warning>
**Bottom line, updated after live testing, see [Live validation against production](/live-validation).** Static analysis alone said nothing here blocks impersonation, and live testing against production confirms it fully for guest accounts: nothing blocks a pure Go client from **creating and driving new guest accounts** or from **completing the email-verification bind** of a guest session to a real account, both work end-to-end, repeatedly, against the real account used for testing. **Reconnecting into an already-established account's live game state** also worked end-to-end at the time it was tested, but that test used the `ta` analytics blob's real captured device/anti-fraud sub-fields; a later security fix (see [Live validation against production](/live-validation)) replaced those sub-fields with placeholders, and reconnect is now **re-confirmed still working with those placeholders**, an unattended cron reconnected and collected real resources over multiple days (August 2026), so the server does not require `ta`'s real device sub-fields. The reconnect step initially looked like a genuine protocol-level session gate (reproducibly rejected, even replaying that account's own genuine device credentials from a real prior login), but turned out to be a `packageName`/`platform`/`appVersion`/`versionCode` identity mismatch against the access token, not a security check, see [Live validation against production](/live-validation) for the full methodology, test matrix, and the current state of the reconnect open question.
</Warning>

## ABI parity

The two Android ABIs don't ship the same native code (1.0.364; static-analysis-only):

- arm64-v8a ships 21 libraries and armeabi-v7a ships 18. Tencent GME voice (`libgmesdk`, `libtxffmpeg`, `libtxsoundtouch`) is arm64-only, and the C# has no ABI guard around it.
- `libxlua` is built from different source trees per ABI: the WebSocket code exists only in v7a, and the marshalling, ZLib, and async exports exist only in arm64.
- `libsqlite3` is 3.28.0 on arm64 and 3.19.3 on v7a, and `libxlua` embeds its own SQLite 3.38.0.
- The engine is Unity **2019.4.41f1** (from `libunity.so`), while a Java crash string says 2019.4.40f1 and the C# hard-codes `unityVersion=440` in check-version requests. `goclient` sends the same `440`; keep it rather than "fixing" it to 441.

```

`docs/shop-iap.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Shop, trading & real-money IAP"
description: "The full purchase flow, Google Play to server credit, traced end to end, including how the client smuggles its own order-correlation id through Google's generic obfuscated account id field."
---

The full purchase flow, Google Play to server credit, traced end to end, including the exact trick the client uses to smuggle its own order-correlation id through Google's generic "obfuscated account id" field.

## Purchase flow (Google Play, Android)

1. Lua UI sends `pay.action` (analytics), then `pay.before.check` with the internal product id + detected currency.
2. Server returns a fresh `selfOrderId`, a server-issued correlation token, plus a confirmed `productId`.
3. Client calls into native code with `{skuId, itemId: selfOrderId, uid}`. Billing Library's `launchBillingFlow` is built with:

   ```text
   setObfuscatedAccountId(itemId)                       // = selfOrderId
   setObfuscatedProfileId(currencyCode + "_" + priceMicros)
   ```

 , the game smuggles its own order id and the exact price/currency through Google's two generic "obfuscated id" fields, since Play Billing doesn't support custom purchase metadata otherwise.
4. Google Play handles the actual purchase UI entirely outside game code. On success, the client reads its smuggled values back out of the completed `Purchase` object.
5. Client sends the SFS command `pay`: `{orderId, productId, purchaseTime, signData (raw receipt JSON), signature, itemId: selfOrderId, pay_closingCurrency, pay_PriceOfClosingCurrency}`, this is the actual receipt-verification call. The server independently validates `signData`/`signature` against Google's purchase-verification API server-side; **the client-submitted receipt is untrusted input from the server's perspective and not forgeable without a genuine Google Play receipt.**
6. Only after server confirmation does the client call `ConsumeProduct` on Google Play, making a consumable product re-purchasable.

## Full command family

| cmd | Platform / purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `pay.before.check` | Pre-flight, always first, all platforms |
| `pay` | Google Play receipt submission |
| `pay.ios` | App Store (StoreKit) receipt submission |
| `pay.amazon` / `pay.tstore` | Amazon Appstore / Korean OneStore |
| `pay.gold.brick.new` | First-party web-payment rail (external checkout, US/JP alt-billing) |
| `pay.refund.request` / `.list` | Player-initiated refund flow |
| `get.week.card.info` / `receive.week.card.reward` | Subscription ("week card") claims |

## Non-IAP economy: no cryptography involved

Trading Center (`get.r.exchange.info`, `money.buy.resource`, `resource.sell.money`), the item shop (`item.buy`, `user.shop.buy.new`), and the player-to-player Storage Shop marketplace are plain request/response RPCs gated only by server-side currency balances, no receipts, no signing, directly drivable once authenticated.

<Note>
**Naming trap.** `purchase.order.refresh`/`.finish`/`.delete` is **not** IAP despite the name; it's an unrelated production-queue feature (grocery store / resident orders). Only the `pay*`/`Pay.*`-namespaced commands above are real-money purchases.
</Note>

```

`docs/shumei.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "ShuMei device fingerprint (shumeiBoxId)"
description: "How the ShuMei (数美) anti-fraud SDK produces the shumeiBoxId device fingerprint, and how a clean-room Go client can generate one without the native library."
---

`shumeiBoxId` is the value the SFS2X `Login` request sends as its ShuMei anti-fraud device fingerprint. It is **not** a locally-invented token: it is the `smid` (ShuMei Machine ID) that the ShuMei backend assigns in response to uploading a device profile to `/deviceprofile/v4`. This page documents that flow, recovered from the Obfuscator-LLVM-hardened `libsmsdk.so` and the `com.ishumei.smantifraud` Java classes, so a from-scratch Go client can register a device and mint its own `shumeiBoxId`.

## Three names, three different things

The protocol uses three ShuMei-related identifiers that are easy to conflate:

| Name | Where | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `smid` | `deviceprofile/v4` response, `detail.deviceId` | The ShuMei Machine ID that the server assigns (88 characters). |
| `shumeiBoxId` | `Login` request field | What the SDK's `getDeviceId()` returns: `"B"` + `smid` (89 characters) once the server has assigned one. Before that, it returns a `"D"`-prefixed local value instead. Empty is a first-class, non-error client path. |
| `shumeiId` | server push `push.shumei.id`, ~0.5 s after `Login` | A separate server-issued value; the client caches it and reports it as `ta.lw_shumei_id` in its *next* `Login`. It is **not** the `shumeiBoxId` sent in the current request. |

## The flow

```
SmSdkManager.callCreate()
  └─ SmOption:
       organization = "9dNCYkjHeFMYZMOjxgX8"        (app-specific, from the game)
       appId        = "default"
       publicKey    = X.509 cert (CN=e.ishumei.com, OU=SM, C=CN)
       area         = AREA_FJNY
       url          = https://shumei-api.lastwargame.com:19091/deviceprofile/v4
       confUrl      = https://shumei-api.lastwargame.com:19091/v3/cloudconf
       usingHttps   = true
  └─ SDK collects device data (SubCollector / AbsDetector)
     └─ native `w1` returns two JSON objects; the first one is the request body:
        POST <url>            Content-Type: application/octet-stream
        body = w1's first JSON object, unchanged (Java adds nothing)
        -> {"code":1100,"detail":{"deviceId":"<smid>","oldDeviceId","sid","c","t"},"requestId"}
        "B" + detail.deviceId  <-- this is the boxId the Login sends
```

Only the background resend (`l11l11l1l1Il`) adds `"retry":1`. The error
handler starts it for codes other than `1902`, so the first request never
carries `retry`.

```
getDeviceId()
  ├─ a server smid is cached        -> "B" + smid
  ├─ a smid is stored on disk       -> "B" + smid
  └─ no smid yet                    -> "D" + a locally built fallback value
```

## Configuration values (byte-exact)

All recovered from `com.sdkmanager.SmSdkManager` and `com.ishumei.smantifraud`:

| Constant | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `organization` | `9dNCYkjHeFMYZMOjxgX8` | `SmSdkManager.setOrganization` |
| `appId` | `default` | `SmSdkManager.setAppId` |
| `publicKey` | 2048-bit RSA cert, `CN=e.ishumei.com, OU=SM, C=CN` | `SmSdkManager.setPublicKey` |
| `os` | `android` | `l11l11lI1lll.l111l1111l1Il` |
| `sdkver` | `3.14.3` | `l11l11lI1lll.l111l11111I1l` (a cloudconf field, not a top-level deviceprofile one; deviceprofile carries it only as `a7` inside the protected `data`. `getSDKVersion()`'s `3.14.3_build1` is a separate public API) |
| `area` | `fjny` → numeric `011` | `SmAntiFraud.AREA_FJNY`, `l11l11lI1lll` region map |
| device-profile path | `/deviceprofile/v4` | `l11l11lI1lll.l11l1111I1ll` |
| cloud-config path | `/v3/cloudconf` | `l11l11lI1lll.l11l1111Il` |

The SDK's own built-in datasites are region-pinned on `fengkongcloud.com`
(`fp-it` / `fp-sa-it` / `fp-na-it-acc`, each with an `api-fp-retry-*`
companion). Last War bypasses them entirely with the
`shumei-api.lastwargame.com:19091` proxy above, so the region mapping matters
only as documentation.

## Cryptography

The SDK's protection is **hybrid RSA-OAEP + AES-256-CBC**, decompiled from
`l11l11l1lIl.java` and `l11l111l1lll.java`:

```java
// l11l11l1lIl: generate a per-request AES-256 key
KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES").init(256).generateKey();

// l11l11l1lIl: RSA-OAEP encrypt a value with the embedded cert
Cipher.getInstance("RSA/ECB/OAEPWITHSHA-256ANDMGF1PADDING")
      .init(ENCRYPT_MODE, CertificateFactory.getInstance("X.509")
          .generateCertificate(der).getPublicKey(),
        new OAEPParameterSpec("SHA-256","MGF1",MGF1ParameterSpec.SHA256,
                              PSource.PSpecified.DEFAULT));

// l11l11l1lIl: AES-256-CBC-PKCS5, IV "0102030405060708" (16 ASCII bytes)
Cipher.getInstance("AES/CBC/PKCS5Padding").init(mode, aesKey,
        new IvParameterSpec("0102030405060708".getBytes()));
```

The `data` sub-object wires it together: `pri` carries the RSA-OAEP-encrypted
AES key (`rsaOaep(cert, aesKey)`), so the server can encrypt its reply with
that same key and the client decrypts it AES-CBC. This shape belongs to the
**cloudconf** request (`/v3/cloudconf`), not the deviceprofile request.
Its `data` sub-object looks like this (from `l11l111l1lll`'s request builder):

```json
{ "os":"android", "sdkver":"3.14.3", "md5":"<config>", "enc":1,
  "bb":"<value>", "sid":"<value>", "pri":"<rsaOaep(aesKey)>" }
```

That is RSA-OAEP with SHA-256 as both the message digest and the MGF1 hash,
and an **empty** OAEP label (`PSpecified.DEFAULT`). In Go,
`rsa.EncryptOAEP(sha256.New(), rand.Reader, pub, msg, nil)`.

### The deviceprofile protection (native `w1`)

The **deviceprofile** request (`/deviceprofile/v4`) uses a different, simpler
hybrid than the cloudconf request above. It is built by the native `w1`, and
it is the scheme the Go client reproduces. In the decompiled `libsmsdk.so`,
the `w1` JNI stub at `0xa07c` calls `FUN_0010f8d0`, which calls
`FUN_0010c160`:

```
r    = 16 random alphanumeric chars
key  = MD5(r) as lowercase hex ASCII (32 bytes, the AES-256 key)
data = Base64( AES-256-CBC( rawDeflate(aNN-json), key, IV "0102030405060708" ) )
ep   = Base64( RSA-OAEP-SHA256(cert, r) )   // wraps only r, not the payload
tn   = Base64( RSA-OAEP-SHA256(cert, "0") ) // ignored by the server
```

`rawDeflate` is raw DEFLATE (RFC 1951, no zlib header) — Go's
`compress/flate`, not `compress/zlib`. The server decrypts `ep` to recover `r`,
derives the AES key from `MD5(r)`, decrypts `data`, and inflates the result to
recover the `aNN` device-data JSON. A body whose `data`/`tn`/`ep` it cannot
decrypt gets `1902`.

## Profile fields (byte-exact names)

The device-profile body is built by the native `w1`, which writes exactly these
top-level fields:

```
organization, os, appId, encode (2), compress (3), data, tn, ep
```

The `a1 … a174` device-data slots live *inside* the protected `data` payload
(the `aNN` fingerprint), not at the top level. The other names in the SDK's
name table (`l111l1111lI1l.java`) belong to other requests: `sdkver`/`md5`/
`pri`/`bb` to **cloudconf** (`l11l111l1lll.java`), and `smid`/`appname`/
`sessionId`/`wevent` to the **v3** event flow (`l1l1l111Il.java`). No
decompiled Java builder references `enc` or `sid`.

## Response codes

| `code` | Meaning | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `1100` | success, device assigned | `l1l11I1l.l111l1111l1Il` |
| `1902` | generic "can't use this" reply; live-tested 2026-10-10, any body the server can't decode gets it | `l1l11I1l.l111l1111llIl` |
| `1903` | hard error | `l1l11I1l.l111l1111lI1l` |

The `detail` object (`l1l11I1l.l11l1111I11l`) carries `deviceId` (the smid),
`oldDeviceId`, `sid`, `c`, `t` (`l11l111llI1l.java`).

## iOS

The iOS app (1.0.344, build 786) links the ShuMei SDK statically into
`Frameworks/UnityFramework.framework/UnityFramework`. Its `SmSdkManager`
configures the same organization and the same `deviceprofile/v4` and
`v3/cloudconf` URLs, but a different public key: a 1024-bit RSA
SubjectPublicKeyInfo, stored as base64 at file offset `0x863ffdf`, right after
the organization string:

```
MIGfMA0GCSqGSIb3DQEBAQUAA4GNADCBiQKBgQDXoi5fkXgG1nCQZdII4lLQT2VzbygcRlwve53AypO1AHW+3G6nqMUTu3SrLH6jdAHHi7y8FIGnx3q52is6LBqW1EpkWQCqjGGfcHl7wjk9IG7seV6E5mWiGz0k4gfR//GXRDUcVhjr5Uo6Hd4o8GyPFkbIi/k5T3Ggp6OfTZ8cYQIDAQAB
```

On 2026-10-12, each of these requests sent the Android `aNN` template,
protected with the `w1` scheme above (confirmed live):

| Key | `os` | RSA padding | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| iOS 1024-bit | `ios`, `iOS`, `iphone`, `iPhone` | OAEP-SHA256 | `1902` |
| iOS 1024-bit | `android` | OAEP-SHA256 | `1902` |
| iOS 1024-bit | `ios` | OAEP-SHA1 | `1902` |
| iOS 1024-bit | `ios` | PKCS#1 v1.5 | `1902` |
| Android 2048-bit | `ios` | OAEP-SHA256 | `1100`, 88-char `smid` |
| Android 2048-bit | `android` | OAEP-SHA256 | `1100`, 88-char `smid` |

The server can't use the iOS key with the `w1` scheme under any of those
paddings, so the iOS SDK protects its profile some other way. That scheme, and
the iOS SDK's device-data fields, haven't been reversed.

The server does accept `os: "ios"` with the Android key and fingerprint, but
`goclient` doesn't use that. Only the outer `os` field would change: the
protected fingerprint would still describe an Android phone (`a6: "android"`,
the `com.fun.lastwar.gp` package and paths, a Samsung model), which is the
pairing the iOS-mode skip below avoids. A real iOS `shumeiBoxId` needs the iOS
protection scheme and an iOS fingerprint template.

## Go implementation

`internal/shumei` reimplements this. `BoxID(client, deviceID, device)` builds
the `aNN` device-data fingerprint, protects it with the hybrid scheme above,
POSTs it, and returns `"B"` + `detail.deviceId` (the full `shumeiBoxId`). `main.go`'s
`-cs-shumei-gen` flag calls it before building `Login` params when no
`shumeiBoxId` was supplied; a failure only logs a warning and falls back to
the empty value the server already accepts. In iOS mode (`-cs-ios` or a
session config's `iosMode`) the flag is ignored, because the fingerprint is an
Android device profile, which an iOS `Login` never carries.

**Status (live-tested 2026-10-11):** the full fingerprint, protected with the
hybrid scheme, returns `code:1100` and a real `smid`, so `BoxID` now mints a
real `shumeiBoxId` (`"B"` + 88-char `deviceId`). The server validates the
protection: an empty or minimal `data`/`tn`/`ep` returns `1902`, and an empty
body returns `9101 "invalid organization"`. The `aNN` fingerprint is a spoofed
Android device profile (a Samsung SM-G988N on Android 12), because this client
runs on a desktop and has no real device telemetry — so the `smid` it mints is
for a device that does not exist. The game server does not require a real
`shumeiBoxId` (an empty one is accepted), so this is an optional best-effort
path, not a hard gate.

**What is byte-exact vs. reconstructed:** the configuration values, field
names, endpoint, response shape, and crypto primitives (RSA-OAEP spec, AES-256
CBC IV, the MD5-derived key) are byte-exact from decompilation and confirmed
live. The `aNN` device-data values themselves are a spoofed profile, not
collected from a real device. The clock fields below come from the host, and
the per-install values below are generated in the formats a real phone uses.

**Credit:** the `aNN` template started as C485's C# `ShumeiInnerTemplate`, and
the `FUN_0010c160` address comes from their `GetShumeiBoxId`. Both were shared
in [discussion #21](https://github.com/ljagiello/lastwar-client/discussions/21).

### Fields that change between collections

The SDK samples some fields fresh on every collection. `BoxID` fills them the
same way, from the host by default:

| Field | SDK source | `goclient` |
|---|---|---|
| `a9` | `System.currentTimeMillis()` | the current time |
| `a171` | `SystemClock.elapsedRealtime()` | the host's uptime: `/proc/uptime` on Linux, time since `kern.boottime` on macOS |
| `a170` | `SystemClock.uptimeMillis()`, which leaves out deep sleep | the same as `a171`: `goclient` doesn't measure the host's sleep time |
| `a40` | median of 11 `currentTimeMillis() - elapsedRealtime()` samples, the boot time | `a9 - a171` |
| `a80` | SDK session ID: `<millis at SmAntiFraud.create()>-<5 digits>`, the digits from `java.util.Random` seeded with those millis (`l11l11Il11l`) | the same, one second before `a9`, with a Go port of `java.util.Random` |

`-cs-shumei-boot` (RFC 3339) replaces the host's boot time.

**Wi-Fi details (`a19`, `a30`, `a31`) are absent by default, as on a real
device.** The SDK reads the BSSID, SSID and Wi-Fi IP only when the app holds
both `ACCESS_WIFI_STATE` and `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION` (`l1l11l1Illl`). Last War
1.0.364's manifest doesn't declare `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION`, so all three come
back empty. The SDK's reflection serializer (`l1l1l11Ill`) then skips them,
along with every other null, empty-string, empty-list and empty-map field.
`BoxID` serializes the same way: compact JSON, with empty top-level entries
dropped. Its keys come out in alphabetical order, while the SDK's follow
Java's field order. The server accepted the alphabetical order live. `-cs-shumei-ssid` and `-cs-shumei-bssid` add Wi-Fi details for a
device that holds the location permission. The SSID gets the quotes
`WifiInfo.getSSID()` adds, and `a31` becomes the host's LAN IPv4. Both
shapes returned `1100` and an 88-char `smid` on 2026-10-12 (confirmed live).

`a133` changes too: it's how long the collection took, in milliseconds
(`l111l1111llIl`). `BoxID` picks a random 150 to 600 ms on each call.

### Values one install keeps

Some fields stay the same for the life of an app install. `goclient` keeps them
per session, in the session config's `shumeiInstall` object. The first
`-cs-shumei-gen` run for a session generates whatever the object leaves out and
writes it back, so every later registration reports the same phone. A value
already in the object stays, such as a real phone's Android ID.

One install belongs to one Login `deviceId`, so the object records the one it
was made for, in its own `deviceId` key. A run under a different `deviceId`
registers a fresh install instead. That includes a run where `-cs-deviceid`
overrides the config's. The registration doesn't save the fresh install over the
config's when the config belongs to the other `deviceId`. The owner is the
config's top-level `deviceId`, or, if there's none, the `deviceId` of the
install already saved.

There's one exception. If that same run also follows a server redirect,
refreshes its token, or looks its server up after a failed connect, it saves
the whole config back under the `deviceId` it used, together with that run's
install. That is how the config has always treated `deviceId`. A run that
never had an install (no `-cs-shumei-gen`, or iOS) writes none.

Without a session config (`-no-config`, or bare `-cs-*` flags and no file),
there's nowhere to keep the values, so every run reports a new phone.
`goclient` logs a warning saying so. Without `-cs-deviceid`, all those phones
share the one persisted `deviceId`.

`goclient` checks the object only on runs that register: `-cs-shumei-gen`, no
`shumeiBoxId`, and not iOS. It exits on a value a real install couldn't hold.

| Field | SDK source | `shumeiInstall` key | Fresh value |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a24` | `Settings.Secure.ANDROID_ID` (`l1l11I111ll`), unhashed because Last War doesn't set `needUsingMD5` | `androidId` | 16 random lowercase hex digits |
| `a84` | the base64 `deviceUniqueId` of the Widevine, ClearKey (W3C and DASH-IF UUIDs) and PlayReady `MediaDrm` schemes, in that order, joined with `_` (`l1111l111111Il`), cached in the `auc` prefs | `mediaDrmId` | 32 random bytes for Widevine, then `___`. Android's ClearKey plugin keeps its test ID under `deviceId`, not `deviceUniqueId`, and the Samsung has no PlayReady |
| `a163` | `UUID.randomUUID()` without dashes, cached as `puuid` in the `seq` prefs (`l1l11I11l`) | `puuid` | a random version 4 UUID |
| `a125` | `{fit, lut}`: `PackageInfo.firstInstallTime` and `lastUpdateTime` | `firstInstallTime`, `lastUpdateTime` | installed 30 to 400 days ago, updated in the last 20 days |
| `a126` | `getDeviceId()` unless it's a `D` fallback: the `"B"` + `smid` cached from the last registration | `boxId` | absent until the first registration |
| `a167`, `a168` | the smid cache file's timestamp (`SMSDK.u2`), and the copy the SDK records as `bfic` right after writing that file | `boxIdSavedAt` | 0 until the first registration |

The three times are RFC 3339 strings, such as `2026-03-04T10:22:31.123Z`. The
wire and `dumpsys package` show them as milliseconds or in other formats. A
number there fails to parse, and every run then exits while loading the config.

The template used to send fixed values for all of these, including an `a84` in
the wrong format and `a167`/`a168` timestamps next to an empty `a126`, a pairing
a real install doesn't produce.

After a registration succeeds, `goclient` stores the box ID in `boxId` and the
time in `boxIdSavedAt`. The next run sends them back as `a126`, `a167` and
`a168`, as the SDK does on every launch. Android rewrites a prefs file only when
a value changes, so getting the same `smid` again keeps the earlier time. In
practice that doesn't happen: on 2026-10-12, three registrations with one
throwaway install all returned `1100`, each with a different 88-char `smid`. The
first was a fresh install, the second sent the first `smid` back as `a126`, and
the third was the same install with no `a126` (confirmed live). The `smid` looks
like an opaque token re-issued on every reply, so `boxIdSavedAt` moves on every
run. A failed registration still saves the generated values. The minted box ID stays
out of the config's top-level `shumeiBoxId`: that field means "send this one
and don't register", so storing a minted ID there would stop later runs from
registering.

Three assumptions remain. `SMSDK.u2` is native and hasn't been traced, so "0
for a missing file" comes from its Java wrapper, which returns 0 when the call
fails. The Widevine ID length (32 bytes) is the common one, not one read from an
SM-G988N. And the `a133` range of 150 to 600 ms is a guess: the real collection
waits up to 3 s on one of its threads (`thread.join(3000L)`), and no real
timing has been measured.
```

`docs/wire-protocol.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "SFS2X wire protocol"
description: "How the game's hand-rolled SmartFoxServer 2X packet envelope, header flags, XOR obfuscation, gateway race, heartbeat, and binary SFSObject codec work on the wire, validated against the official SmartFoxServer JS SDK."
---

The client bundles the real SmartFoxServer 2X SDK but never actually uses its socket layer. Every byte on the wire is written by a hand-rolled reimplementation that only reuses SFS2X's data model, and the "encryption" bit is a length-derived XOR, not a cipher.

## Transport

Plain TCP socket, **no TLS**. Host/port/zone/connection-type arrive dynamically from the GSL response. Two connection types exist:

- `connectionType 0`: raw TCP, straight into the packet framing below.
- `connectionType 1`: a one-shot literal HTTP/1.1 `Upgrade: websocket` preamble is sent first, purely to satisfy load balancers that require a valid HTTP handshake, then the exact same raw SFS2X binary framing runs on the same socket. **This is not a real WebSocket**: there's no RFC 6455 frame masking anywhere in the read/write path. A Go client can dial TCP directly, or replay the literal handshake bytes if a load balancer demands them.

The 1.0.364 preamble is fixed (`NetHandShakeInterceptor` in `BaseUtils`; static-analysis-only):

- `Sec-WebSocket-Key: cmFuZG9t`, which is base64 for `random`, on every connection.
- `User-Agent: LastWarWebSocket`, plus fixed `Cache-Control`, `Pragma`, `Accept-Encoding`, `TE`, and `Content-Length` headers.
- The request path comes from the `ws://host/path` line URL and defaults to `/`.
- The client accepts the response on status 101, any 2xx, or 304. It never checks `Sec-WebSocket-Accept`.
- On these lines the first ping is a plain ping, not the `a=29` probe described below.

In 1.0.364, `client_config` switch 26 selects connection type 1 to the `ws_ip` host on port 80, and switch 44 makes every second connect retry use it (see [Server-controlled transport switches](#server-controlled-transport-switches)). `KCPMode` is always `"0"`, and the game socket never uses UDP; only the real-time PvP mini-games do, over a separate transport (see [Mini-game PvP transport](#mini-game-pvp-transport)). Sockets set `NoDelay`, a 2 MiB receive buffer, a 64 KiB send buffer, and 30 s send and receive timeouts (static-analysis-only).

## Gateway race and the pre-login probe

The GSL `serverList[].ip` field is a `|`-delimited list of gateway hosts for one zone, all on the same port. Two live GSL responses on 2026-10-04 listed the same three hostnames, with only the port differing by zone: `10783` for `APS783` and `10072` for a guest account on `APS72` (confirmed live):

```text
lastwar-game-tcp-aws-1.lastwargame.com|lastwar-game-tcp-gcp-1.lastwargame.com|lastwar-game-tcp-cf-1.lastwarapp.net
```

The Lua also carries two fallback "proxy lines", `ProxyList` in `Global/EnumType.lua`, named `aws` and `cf` by `ProxyName`. They use the zone's current `GameServerPort`, the C# reads them through `CSharpCallLuaInterface.GetAllProxy()`, and the in-game ping screen lists them. When C# switches to them wasn't traced (static-analysis-only):

```text
lastwar-game-us-aws-ali.lastwargame.com
lastwar-game-us-cf-ali.lastwarapp.com
```

A related helper, `CommonUtil.GetPortId(zoneId)`, returns `17000 + zoneId`.

A packet capture only shows the addresses these resolve to, so a session config written by `pcap -session-out` holds IP addresses; the hostnames work in its `ip` field too. The shipped client connects to all the gateways at once and keeps whichever answers first. This comes from the 1.0.364 C# (`ChooseLine`, `NetRawProxy`) and matches the 2026-10-04 capture of the real iOS app:

1. Open a TCP connection to every gateway in parallel.
2. On each, immediately send a `CustomPingPong` request (`c=0`, `a=29`).
3. The first gateway to answer with a pong wins. Close the others and save the winner as `SERVER_IP`.
4. Only then send `Login`.

The capture showed the race across three gateways, two IPv4 and one Cloudflare IPv6:

| | Winner (IPv4) | Cloudflare (IPv6) | IPv4 (the address an older session config pinned) |
|---|---|---|---|
| SYN-ACK | 19 ms | 14.5 ms | 77 ms |
| Probe sent | 25 ms | 26 ms | 88 ms |
| Pong | **154 ms** (first) | 162.5 ms | 162.5 ms |
| Afterwards | `Login` at 200 ms, 45 ms after the pong | FIN at 187 ms | FIN at 188 ms |

The three pongs carried `serverTime` values within 11 ms of each other, so all three front-ends reach one backend. The winner varies from run to run; an earlier capture had the pinned address winning.

The probe's `p` object is fixed: a masked, Android-login-shaped template with literal placeholder values, into which the client splices only the device's real `deviceId`, plus a `clientTime`. It's byte-identical across all three sockets apart from `clientTime`. Its purpose is unknown, and it may be an anti-fraud surface, so it's documented here as a protocol fact only. The reply is a plain pong, `{p:{serverTime, clientTime}}` with `serverTime` in ms. After the probe, every keepalive is a plain ping.

Per the C#, a gateway that times out at `Login` (7 s) is blacklisted and the connect is retried. A separate `NetLineSpeedTester` re-probes every gateway the same way for analytics, at most once per 25 s, and never switches lines (static-analysis-only).

`goclient` doesn't race. `DoCrossServerLogin` dials the `|` list in order, 10 s per host and IPv6-safe, sends no probe, and sends `Login` straight after connecting. The server accepts that order (confirmed live). The fallback is confirmed live too: with an unreachable TEST-NET address first in the list, the dial timed out after 10 s and the login went through on the next gateway. When `goclient` writes a changed address or token back to the session config, it keeps the list as long as the gateway it reached is on it.

## Packet envelope: three nested layers

```text
[1-byte header][2/4-byte length][ optional zlib compress → XOR "encrypt" ]
  body = SFSObject {
    "c": BYTE    controller id   (0 = System, 1 = Extension)
    "a": SHORT   action id       (1 = Login, 13 = CallExtension, 29 = PingPong)
    "p": SFS_OBJECT  content
  }
```

For every gameplay `cmd`, the `"p"` content is itself another SFSObject:

```text
SFSObject {
  "c": UTF_STRING   cmd        e.g. "mail.read"
  "r": INT          roomId     always -1 (SFS "Rooms" are unused entirely)
  "p": SFS_OBJECT   params     the command's own fields, plus an injected "_id" int
}
```

So a full `mail.read` request is schematically `{c:1, a:13, p:{c:"mail.read", r:-1, p:{uid:..., type:..., toUser:..., _id:42}}}`.

The real client puts `_id` on every extension request: `Login` carries `1`, and requests count up from `2`. The server echoes `_id` and adds `_time` (observed in the 2026-10-04 capture). `goclient` sets `_id` only on `Login` and `login.init`, and the server accepts that (confirmed live).

## Packet header bits

| Bit | Flag | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `0x80` | binary | always set |
| `0x40` | encrypted | always set on what the client sends, see XOR "encryption" below. Server-to-client frames in the 2026-10-04 capture (`0x80`, `0xB0`, `0xB8`) didn't set it and weren't XORed; `goclient`'s reader XORs only when the bit is set |
| `0x20` | compressed | set iff the uncompressed serialized payload > 1024 bytes (zlib deflate, level 9) |
| `0x10` | useLZ4 (repurposed) | never set on send; on receive the "LZ4" bit actually triggers **Zstandard** decompression, not LZ4, leftover naming from a migration. With `0x20` and `0x10` both set, a 4-byte big-endian uncompressed length follows the length field. **Implemented**: `ReadPacket` (`packet.go`) previously detected this branch correctly but just returned an error instead of decompressing, which read as connection-closed; now decodes via `github.com/klauspost/compress/zstd`, confirmed live against the server's ~313KB Zstd-compressed init bootstrap push |
| `0x08` | bigSized | set iff payload > 65535 bytes → 4-byte length instead of 2. The game's own sender is `NetPacket` in `BaseUtils` (`BaseUtils.decompiled.cs:33284-33324`); the embedded SmartFox2X 1.7.8 SDK's `SFSIOHandler` uses the same threshold (`SmartFox2X.decompiled.cs:31762-31783`). See [Which SDK is the reference](#which-sdk-is-the-reference). The 1.0.364 sender tests the uncompressed length; `goclient` tests the compressed length, which is harmless because it never sends packets that large |
| `0x04` | forward | a 2-byte big-endian server id follows the header byte, before the length. The 1.0.364 client sets it on **every** send when `client_config` switch 29 and the Lua switch `EnableServerRangeRouting` are both on. The id is the zone number: `BaseUtils`' `ParseSid("APS783")` returns 783 (static-analysis-only). The 2026-10-04 capture agrees: it shows the bit on every client-to-server frame (headers `0xE4` and `0xC4`), including the probe, with id `0x030F` = 783 for zone `APS783`. Likely gateway routing. `goclient` never sets it, and the server accepts that (confirmed live) |

### Send and receive framing differ

The 1.0.364 client writes and reads packets with two different classes (static-analysis-only):

- **Send** always uses the legacy `NetPacket`: header `0x80 | 0x40`, plus `0x20` with zlib when the uncompressed body is over 1024 bytes, plus `0x08` when it's over 65535, plus `0x04` and the server id when forwarding. The body is XORed against the little-endian bytes of its final length. The maximum is 1,000,000 bytes.
- **Receive** uses `NetPacketNew`: when `0x20` and `0x10` are both set, the 4-byte uncompressed length follows, and the body is Zstd-decompressed. When only `0x20` is set, it's zlib.

`goclient`'s `packet.go` already matches both sides.

<Warning>
**The "encryption" is not encryption**

```go
func Encrypt(data []byte) []byte {
    key := uint32LE(len(data))          // the on-wire length field, sent in cleartext
    for i := range data {
        data[i] ^= byte(key >> (8 * (i % 4)))
    }
    return data
}
```

The XOR keystream is derived entirely from the packet's own (cleartext) length field. No secret material, no negotiation, no per-session state. This is obfuscation, not confidentiality, and needs zero cryptographic material to implement in Go, just XOR the body against the little-endian length, computed after compression.
</Warning>

## `SFSObject` binary format

Big-endian throughout. A standalone serialized object is self-describing, it starts with its own tag byte and count.

| Tag | Type | Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `NULL` | - |
| 1 | `BOOL` | 1 byte |
| 2 | `BYTE` | 1 byte |
| 3 | `SHORT` | 2 bytes, signed |
| 4 | `INT` | 4 bytes, signed |
| 5 | `LONG` | 8 bytes, signed |
| 6 | `FLOAT` | 4 bytes, IEEE-754 |
| 7 | `DOUBLE` | 8 bytes, IEEE-754 |
| 8 | `UTF_STRING` | u16 byte-length + UTF-8. The u16 allows 65535 B, but the client's encoder refuses strings over 32,767 B (SmartFox2X `ByteArray`), so a compatible sender should cap there too |
| 10 | `BYTE_ARRAY` | i32 count + N × element, the one array type that skips the shared size helper; the decompiled Unity SDK's `BinDecode_BYTE_ARRAY` calls a bare 4-byte `ReadInt` instead of `GetTypedArraySize`. A genuine SFS2X wire-format asymmetry, confirmed decoding the live 313KB init payload. |
| 9, 11–16 | `*_ARRAY` | i16 count + N × element (`GetTypedArraySize`) |
| 17 | `SFS_ARRAY` | i16 count, then N × (tag + payload), recursive |
| 18 | `SFS_OBJECT` | i16 key count, then N × (UTF_STRING key + tag + payload), recursive |
| 19 | `CLASS` | *not implemented*, never emitted |
| 20 | `TEXT` | i32 byte-length + UTF-8 (uncapped) |

*`BIG_NUM`, present in some SFS2X SDK builds, doesn't exist in this game's enum at all, no gap in the numbering. Not needed.*

## Which SDK is the reference

The APK carries two SFS2X C# libraries, and only one of them is live in 1.0.364 (static-analysis-only):

- **SmartFox2X** is the official SFS2X C# API 1.7.8. The game uses its data model, binary codec, and request envelopes (`ExtensionRequest`, `LoginRequest`, `LogoutRequest`), but never constructs its socket stack.
- **BaseUtils** holds the game's own socket layer and framing (`NetConnection`, `NetPacket` for sending, `NetPacketNew` for receiving), which replaces SFS2X's BitSwarm. There's no `BitSwarmManager` anywhere on the shipping path.
- **Smartfox2xLw** is a 2024 in-house fork of SmartFox2X stripped down to a codec. It's dead code: the only reference to it is a placeholder field that's never assigned, and its system controller has an empty handler table, so it can't even process `Login`. Earlier versions of this page cited it; the citations now point at SmartFox2X and BaseUtils.

`noUpdateAssemblies.json` pins SmartFox2X to the APK copy, so the codec changes only with an app release, unless a hot update replaces that pin list. BaseUtils, which writes the actual frames, can still be replaced through a hot update.

## Validated against the official client: `sfs2x-api` (npm)

SmartFoxServer publishes its own JS client SDK (`npm install sfs2x-api`, the official reference implementation, not a third-party reimplementation). Pulling it and diffing its packet/codec internals against everything above turned into a genuinely useful correctness check:

<table>
<thead><tr><th>Checked against the official SDK</th><th>Result</th></tr></thead>

The JS client's <code>65335</code> is an idiosyncratic quirk of that specific (different) implementation, not a shared protocol constant. Reverted after a later audit pass caught the discrepancy; a good reminder that "official" only means authoritative for the exact client it ships with.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Encryption flag (<code>0x40</code>) / XOR obfuscation</td><td><strong>Refined</strong>, the bit itself is real vanilla SFS2X: the C# SDK sets it exactly when a <code>CryptoKey</code> (a real AES-CBC key+IV pair) is present (<code>SmartFox2X.decompiled.cs:31766</code>). In stock SFS2X that key comes from an HTTPS call to <code>/BlueBox/CryptoManager</code> (<code>SmartFox2X.decompiled.cs:20760-20836</code>), not from the <code>Handshake</code>. This game never fetches a <code>CryptoKey</code> at all, yet the client always sets <code>0x40</code> anyway and the server expects the length-derived XOR instead of real AES, a deliberate override of the vanilla semantics, not evidence the bit is undocumented. The server's own frames don't set it (2026-10-04 capture). The JS SDK's read/write path (which never sets or checks this bit) simply never implements the CryptoKey path at all, consistent with this reading.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>0x10</code> LZ4-repurposed-as-Zstandard flag</td><td><strong>Game-specific meaning, stock bit</strong>: in the C# SDK, header bit <code>0x10</code> is <code>BlueBoxed</code> (HTTP tunnelling; <code>SmartFox2X.decompiled.cs:31328-31331</code>), and the game's own old header class still calls it that (<code>BaseUtils.decompiled.cs:33142-33175</code>). The game repurposes it on receive to mean Zstandard, under the name <code>useLZ4</code>. The JS SDK doesn't use it</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>

The official SDK's connection sequence also revealed a real gap: it sends a `Handshake` request (action `0`, fields `api`/`cl`, a step this dossier previously called out below as unused) *before* every Login, receiving back a session token / max-message-size / compression-threshold. Sending it against this game's real server got a clean, correctly-shaped response, `{ct=3072, ms=1000000, tk=<32-hex>}`, so the server-side handshake handler is real and working, even though the shipped client never uses it (see below). Practically, though, adding it to the Go client changed nothing: at the time this was tested, the init-push and reconnect-block problems were still unresolved, and this `Handshake` step made no difference to either, guest login and email-bind behaved identically with or without it. Both problems have since been resolved by unrelated fixes (a Zstd decompression bug and a token-identity mismatch, respectively, see [Live validation against production](/live-validation)), confirming the `Handshake` step was never the missing piece.

## Heartbeat & reconnect

A `PingPongRequest` (system controller, action 29) fires every **4000 ms**. On the wire, the real client nests its `clientTime` one level deeper than the action's own `p`: `{c:0, a:29, p:{p:{clientTime}}}` (observed in the 2026-10-04 capture). `goclient` sends it flat, `p:{clientTime}`, and the server answers that too (confirmed live). The pong carries `serverTime` in ms and echoes `clientTime`; the client uses the pair for server-time sync. In the capture, the server answered all 83 heartbeats over 320 s.

Client-perceived timeout is **12s** since the last pong or response, at which point the client disconnects and re-runs the entire connect→login sequence; there is no lightweight session-resume. No exponential backoff was found; retry cadence is a fixed timer.

The 1.0.364 timers (static-analysis-only):

| Timer | Value |
|---|---|
| Keepalive | 4000 ms; the first ping (the probe) goes out immediately on connect |
| Ping-pong timeout | 12 s since the last pong or response, then reconnect |
| `ConnectGame` | 6 s, 3 tries |
| `Login` response | 7 s, up to 3 tries |
| `init` push | 13 s, then reconnect and re-send `Login` with the same `at`, up to 3 times |
| GSL HTTP | 5 s, 4 tries, alternating UnityWebRequest and BestHTTP |

`goclient` sends its first heartbeat 4 s after connecting rather than immediately, waits up to 45 s for `init`, and makes a single attempt. That's more conservative than the real client, and the server accepts it.

## Error conventions

Errors on extension responses are per handler; the 1.0.364 Lua has no generic error layer (static-analysis-only):

- A failed request carries `errorCode`, a UtfString holding either an error code or a locale key.
- An optional `errorPara2` (UtfStringArray) carries tip parameters. The client shows `Localization:GetString(errorCode, table.unpack(errorPara2))`.
- `E000000` is the generic "unknown error" (`SeverErrorCode` in `ConstDefine.lua`). A few handlers treat it as a soft "no data" result, for example a rank preview with nothing to rank.
- `Login` rejections don't use `errorCode`. They arrive as SFS2X's own `ec` (a short) and `ep` (a UTF string array), formatted through the stock SFS2X error table. Code `28` is that table's `"{0}"` passthrough, which carries the game's `E0xx` strings in `ep[0]`, see [Identity, login & session](/auth#login-rejection-codes).
- Fatal conditions come only from the C#: a `Login` rejection, `push.user.off` (kicked: the client quits and doesn't reconnect), `push.server.stop` / `push.server.tostop`, and connection loss.

## Server-controlled transport switches

The check-version response's `client_config` field is a `|`-separated list of `"0"`/`"1"` flags, indexed by switch id (`ClientSwitch.Parse`, see [Startup, version-check & hot-update](/bootstrap)). In 1.0.364, these switches change what goes on the wire (static-analysis-only):

| Index | Name | Effect when on |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | `DISABLE_NEW_NET_PACKET` | The receive path falls back to the old packet class, without Zstd |
| 5 | `DISABLE_ZSTD` | The client stops sending `isUseLz4` in `Login`, so the server doesn't Zstd-compress |
| 20 | named `ENABLE_CDN_SPEED_TEST` | Sets a `tcpSecurityEnabled` value that the 1.0.364 connection constructor ignores |
| 25 | ShuMei SDK on | When off, `shumeiBoxId` is `""` |
| 26 | `ENABLE_SERVER_WS_CONNECTION` | Connect to `ws_ip` on port 80 with connection type 1 |
| 29 | `ENABLE_CROSS_FORWARD` | Together with the Lua switch `EnableServerRangeRouting`, sets the forward bit and server id on every send |
| 44 | `ENABLE_CONNECT_GAME_WEBSOCKET_FALLBACK` | Every second connect retry uses the WebSocket path |

The forward bit in the 2026-10-04 capture suggests switch 29 is on for the iOS app today; the server still accepts `goclient`'s frames without it. `goclient` doesn't parse `client_config`.

<Check>
**Settled: the shipped client never sends a `Handshake`**

SFS2X's SDK ships a full `Handshake` request (session token negotiation), an AES `CryptoKey` path (`DefaultPacketEncrypter`, keyed over HTTPS from `/BlueBox/CryptoManager`), and a complete MMORoom/AOI (area-of-interest) streaming subsystem. The game uses none of them. The embedded SmartFox2X SDK contains a working `Handshake` (`SendHandshakeRequest`, `SmartFox2X.decompiled.cs:20085-20089`), and the live server answers it when sent (see above), but the game's own transport never calls it. In 1.0.364, `NetConnection` handles only two system actions, `a=1` (`Login`) and `a=29` (ping-pong), and the connect path runs TCP connect, `a=29` probe, then `Login` (static-analysis-only). The 2026-10-04 capture of the real iOS app agrees: no `a=0` on any of the three sockets. A reimplementation should skip it; `goclient` keeps `-handshake` only as an off-by-default experiment. Instead of SFS2X's AOI streaming, the client pulls the world-map viewport and individual points with its own extension requests (see [World map](/world-map)).
</Check>

## Mini-game PvP transport

Two real-time PvP mini-games, BiuBiu (shooting) and GGGo, don't run over the game socket. They use the `Joker.Share` assembly (static-analysis-only):

1. Matchmaking runs over ordinary SFS2X commands (`activity.shoot.pvp.*`). The reply names a separate server: `ip`, `port`, `sessionidgame`, and `sessionidplayer`, a shape that looks like AWS GameLift.
2. The client connects there over TCP, or in "Hybrid" mode over TCP plus UDP.
3. TCP frames are `u32 LE length | i32 opcode | i32 jsonLen | JSON`.
4. UDP datagrams start with `KCPH` and a channel id, and use kcp2k-style Connect, Data, and Disconnect messages, with an MTU of 470.

This is recorded as a transport fact only. Results in these modes are client-computed, and forging them is out of scope (see [Military, hero & battle](/military-battle)).

```

`docs/world-map.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "World map"
description: "The per-server tile grid (1000×1000, or 3000×3000 on season big maps), its linear point-id addressing, the C#-owned viewport block pull, and the other query patterns the client uses instead of SFS2X's unused area-of-interest streaming."
---

A 1000×1000 tile grid per server, addressed by a 1-based linear index; season "nine palaces" maps join nine servers into one 3000×3000 grid. The client streams the visible part of the map itself, through C#-owned block-pull requests, and supplements that with single-point pulls, server-side "find nearest" searches, and bulk per-server datasets. SFS2X's built-in area-of-interest streaming exists in the SDK and is completely unused.

## Tile math

```go
WorldTileCount = 1000   // per-server grid dimension
CityTileCount  = 100    // player-city-interior grid
TileSize       = 2      // Unity world-units per tile

pointId = x + y * tileCount + 1           // 1-based; 0 = "none"
x, y    = (pointId-1) % tileCount, (pointId-1) / tileCount
worldX  = (x + 0.5) * TileSize

// cross-server addressing, 64-bit pack:
worldPos = uint64(serverId) << 32 | uint64(pointId)
```

On a season "nine palaces" map, the 1.0.364 C# sets the world size to **3000** when the palace list holds 9 servers. A tile's server is the grid cell `(x / 1000, y / 1000)`, and its index is `x + y * 3000 + 1`. Battlefield worlds take their size from Lua instead (static-analysis-only).

## Query model

1. **Viewport block pull (C#-owned)**: `world.get.block`, `world.get.new`, and, on the cross-server line, `world.get.cross`. These never appear in the Lua command catalog; C# `WorldPointManager` sends them as the camera moves and handles the replies itself. `world.get.block` asks for up to **160 block indices** per request (static-analysis-only):

   ```text
   world.get.block {bigMap, x, y, serverId, worldId, type, viewLvl (≤ 2), timeStamp,
                    index: IntArray (block ids), blockSize, clearUuidSet (first request only),
                    force, leftBottom, rightTop}
   ```

   `leftBottom` and `rightTop` are tile indices computed on a 3000-wide grid. `world.get.new` is the view-level variant, `{x, y, serverId, type, viewLvl, timeStamp, worldId}`. Replies carry per-server sub-replies (`serverPointArr[]`) or flat `serverId`/`worldId`, with protobuf byte arrays: `points[]` as `WorldPointInfo`, `lands[]` as `LandPointInfo`, `deserts[]` as `DesertInfo`, `alInfos[]`, plus overlays such as `hotSpots`, `triggers`, and `greenPoints`. After the first request with `clearUuidSet=1`, the client drops every previously known point the server didn't return. `push.world.get.block` tells the client to re-request its view.
2. **Single-point pull**: `world.get.detail.new {point, serverId, worldId, previewAssistance, pointType, uid}`. The field is `point`, not `pointId`.
3. **Server-side "find nearest"**: `find.resource`, `find.enemy.point`: the client sends criteria only (level, type), **no coordinates at all**; the server searches from the player's context and returns a single point id. `find.monster` is the same family but (unusually) also sends a `pointId` alongside its criteria.
4. **Bulk per-server/per-alliance push**: `world.get.alliance.city.info`, `lw.req.world.occupy.info`: the entire dataset for a server, no pagination. Pushes are invalidate-then-refetch, not deltas.
5. **Batch pull by uuid list**: radar/detect-event lookups, pipe-delimited uuid lists.

`world.get.march.infos {x, y, needCross}` finds marches passing near a raw tile coordinate. March state then streams as C#-handled pushes: `push.world.march.new` carries a protobuf `WorldMarch` (or a `WorldMarchDeltaMeta` delta), and `push.world.march.del` carries the march `uuid` and `isBattleFail`. In all, 29 world, scene, and season `push.*` messages are handled only in C#.

## Core commands

| cmd | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `world.get.block` / `world.get.new` | Viewport block pull (C#-owned) |
| `world.get.detail.new` | Single-tile dynamic-state pull, keyed by `point` |
| `world.march.formation.new` | Dispatch a march to a target tile (or through a multi-hop `;`-delimited path) |
| `alliance.world.mark.add` | Persistent alliance-shared map marker |
| `world.favo.add` | Personal (non-shared) map bookmark |
| `world.get.alliance.city.info` | Bulk city/stronghold dataset for a server |
